title: Document modeling and BSON types
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB
text: The relational source has customers, orders and order_lines. A literal collection per table is possible, but it does not decide which data should be read/written atomically together. List request predicates, output fields, cardinality, update frequency, consistency requirements and growth before choosing the document boundary.[35] Operation Frequency / invariant Model consequence Render one order Read its lines and historical prices together Embed bounded line items in the order List tenant’s recent orders Tenant equality, descending placement time {tenantId: 1, placedAt: -1} index Update customer’s current contact details Many orders refer to one customer Reference a separate customer document Preserve shipping destination at purchase Historical value must not drift Embed address snapshot on order if needed Reserve stock and create order Both or neither when promised Conditional atomic update plus transaction if spanning documents Customer’s entire order history Potentially unbounded Query orders by customer; never append forever to customer document Keep the administration fixture canonical: order IDs o1001–o1003, tenant t1/t2, customer reference, UTC date, Decimal128 total and a bounded lines array. Additional model examples build on it rather than inventing another database.[35][37] // Read together and modified as one aggregate: { _id: "o1001", tenantId: "t1", customerId: "c1", placedAt: ISODate("2026-09-01T09:00:00Z"), status: "new", total: Decimal128("5.00"), lines: [{sku: "pencil", qty: Int32(2), unitPrice: Decimal128("2.50")}] } The price is an order-time fact, not a pointer to today’s product price. Copying that value is intentional denormalization. Customer current email/name should usually remain on the customer. If historical customer/address facts are legally required, snapshot only the required fields and define retention/deletion obligations.[35] Embed when Reference when Bounded one-to-few relationship Unbounded/high-cardinality relationship Same lifecycle and access pattern Independent updates/lifecycles Atomic update of the aggregate matters Large or shared entities would duplicate heavily Extra copied bytes are acceptable Growth approaches document limits or write contention Arrays must have a growth policy, not merely an initial small size. The fixture validator caps lines at 100 as an application rule. MongoDB’s BSON document limit is 16 MiB; GridFS is an alternative for large binary content, not a reason to put unlimited order history in one customer. Measure BSON size and tail growth, not only averages.[36][37] const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop"); shop.orders.aggregate([ {$project: {_id: 1, bytes: {$bsonSize: "$$ROOT"}, lines: {$size: "$lines"}}}, {$sort: {bytes: -1}}, {$limit: 10} ]).toArray(); Relational meaning BSON/model choice Trap Signed BIGINT identity Long("...") or stable string JavaScript Number cannot exactly represent every 64-bit integer Money DECIMAL Decimal128("5.00") with explicit currency policy Binary floating-point rounding or string sorting UTC instant BSON Date / ISODate(...) Date has no stored timezone; source local timestamp needs a zone decision Date-only business value Validated ISO date string or explicitly modeled parts Midnight UTC silently changes local date semantics Nullable value null when known-empty; missing when absent by design {field: null} also matches missing; choose $exists/type checks deliberately SQL primary key Stable _id plus tenant/business identity policy Do not regenerate IDs on every import/retry ENUM/status String plus validator enum Flexible schema does not enforce the enum by itself Binary/UUID Agreed BSON binary subtype/UUID representation Legacy UUID representations differ across drivers The shell uses BSON constructors; plain JSON cannot express all these types. Use canonical Extended JSON or a driver-aware loader for interchange. Decimal128, Long, BSON Timestamp and BSON Date are different types; oplog timestamps are not ordinary user dates.[74][87] Use the full orders validator to check presence, types, enum and bounded arrays. strict/error rejects invalid writes; it does not retroactively scan/fix existing documents. Before tightening a validator, inspect old shapes, backfill deliberately, test all writers, then enforce. A rollback restores the old validator but does not restore already transformed data.[37][55] MongoDB has no foreign key ensuring customerId exists or matches tenantId. Create/inspect customers in the disposable dataset: const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop"); shop.customers.insertMany([ {_id: "c1", tenantId: "t1", name: "Mira"}, {_id: "c2", tenantId: "t1", name: "Dev"}, {_id: "c3", tenantId: "t2", name: "Asha"} ]); shop.orders.aggregate([ {$lookup: { from: "customers", let: {cid: "$customerId", tenant: "$tenantId"}, pipeline: [{$match: {$expr: {$and: [ {$eq: ["$_id", "$$cid"]}, {$eq: ["$tenantId", "$$tenant"]} ]}}}], as: "customer" }}, {$match: {customer: {$size: 0}}}, {$project: {_id: 1, tenantId: 1, customerId: 1}} ]).toArray(); No results is the expected invariant for this fixture, not measured output. Including the tenant prevents a same-ID/cross-tenant reference from appearing valid. Production referential rules require application/transaction policy plus periodic reconciliation; a nightly orphan report alone does not prevent invalid writes.[35][40] An embedded order update can be atomic without a multi-document transaction. A customer reference plus inventory reservation may require a transaction if the business promises an all-or-nothing change. Keep transactions short, pre-create collections/indexes, and make retries idempotent; see the stock/order transaction.[40] Use indexes for actual predicates, not every optional field. Arrays produce multikey behavior and larger indexes; an index on lines.sku can help product-based searches but increases write cost. Tenant/date and tenant/customer/order indexes serve different patterns. After sharding, query routing and per-shard indexing remain separate: a fast shard index does not prevent scatter-gather.[20][32][36] Schema version fields can support rolling application migrations: deploy readers accepting old/new shapes, backfill bounded batches with checkpointed IDs, deploy new writers, verify no old writers remain, then tighten validation. Do not turn off validation globally merely because one bulk import has old data. Keep business transformations reversible where possible and retain pre-transform data under policy.[35][37] Given source order o1001 for customer c1, and two pencils at exact decimal price 2.50, construct one order document with that line and total 5.00. Copy the source order identity; group child rows by order identity, sort line items deterministically, and preserve quantity/price types. Never compute a migration total with floating-point arithmetic just because the loader is JavaScript.[35][45] An order snapshot and a current customer document answer different questions. Preserve the relational system as authority until bulk load, delta capture and business reconciliation pass. Translate joins/routines/constraints intentionally in the application; SQL query text is not valid MongoDB query language. Continue with migration and cutover.

title: Embed a bounded aggregate; reference independent entities
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB · Document modeling and BSON types
text: // Read together and modified as one aggregate: { _id: "o1001", tenantId: "t1", customerId: "c1", placedAt: ISODate("2026-09-01T09:00:00Z"), status: "new", total: Decimal128("5.00"), lines: [{sku: "pencil", qty: Int32(2), unitPrice: Decimal128("2.50")}] } The price is an order-time fact, not a pointer to today’s product price. Copying that value is intentional denormalization. Customer current email/name should usually remain on the customer. If historical customer/address facts are legally required, snapshot only the required fields and define retention/deletion obligations.[35] Embed when Reference when Bounded one-to-few relationship Unbounded/high-cardinality relationship Same lifecycle and access pattern Independent updates/lifecycles Atomic update of the aggregate matters Large or shared entities would duplicate heavily Extra copied bytes are acceptable Growth approaches document limits or write contention Arrays must have a growth policy, not merely an initial small size. The fixture validator caps lines at 100 as an application rule. MongoDB’s BSON document limit is 16 MiB; GridFS is an alternative for large binary content, not a reason to put unlimited order history in one customer. Measure BSON size and tail growth, not only averages.[36][37] const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop"); shop.orders.aggregate([ {$project: {_id: 1, bytes: {$bsonSize: "$$ROOT"}, lines: {$size: "$lines"}}}, {$sort: {bytes: -1}}, {$limit: 10} ]).toArray();

title: Preserve BSON type meaning
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB · Document modeling and BSON types
text: Relational meaning BSON/model choice Trap Signed BIGINT identity Long("...") or stable string JavaScript Number cannot exactly represent every 64-bit integer Money DECIMAL Decimal128("5.00") with explicit currency policy Binary floating-point rounding or string sorting UTC instant BSON Date / ISODate(...) Date has no stored timezone; source local timestamp needs a zone decision Date-only business value Validated ISO date string or explicitly modeled parts Midnight UTC silently changes local date semantics Nullable value null when known-empty; missing when absent by design {field: null} also matches missing; choose $exists/type checks deliberately SQL primary key Stable _id plus tenant/business identity policy Do not regenerate IDs on every import/retry ENUM/status String plus validator enum Flexible schema does not enforce the enum by itself Binary/UUID Agreed BSON binary subtype/UUID representation Legacy UUID representations differ across drivers The shell uses BSON constructors; plain JSON cannot express all these types. Use canonical Extended JSON or a driver-aware loader for interchange. Decimal128, Long, BSON Timestamp and BSON Date are different types; oplog timestamps are not ordinary user dates.[74][87]

title: Validation and referential integrity
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB · Document modeling and BSON types
text: Use the full orders validator to check presence, types, enum and bounded arrays. strict/error rejects invalid writes; it does not retroactively scan/fix existing documents. Before tightening a validator, inspect old shapes, backfill deliberately, test all writers, then enforce. A rollback restores the old validator but does not restore already transformed data.[37][55] MongoDB has no foreign key ensuring customerId exists or matches tenantId. Create/inspect customers in the disposable dataset: const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop"); shop.customers.insertMany([ {_id: "c1", tenantId: "t1", name: "Mira"}, {_id: "c2", tenantId: "t1", name: "Dev"}, {_id: "c3", tenantId: "t2", name: "Asha"} ]); shop.orders.aggregate([ {$lookup: { from: "customers", let: {cid: "$customerId", tenant: "$tenantId"}, pipeline: [{$match: {$expr: {$and: [ {$eq: ["$_id", "$$cid"]}, {$eq: ["$tenantId", "$$tenant"]} ]}}}], as: "customer" }}, {$match: {customer: {$size: 0}}}, {$project: {_id: 1, tenantId: 1, customerId: 1}} ]).toArray(); No results is the expected invariant for this fixture, not measured output. Including the tenant prevents a same-ID/cross-tenant reference from appearing valid. Production referential rules require application/transaction policy plus periodic reconciliation; a nightly orphan report alone does not prevent invalid writes.[35][40]

title: Index and transaction boundaries
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB · Document modeling and BSON types
text: An embedded order update can be atomic without a multi-document transaction. A customer reference plus inventory reservation may require a transaction if the business promises an all-or-nothing change. Keep transactions short, pre-create collections/indexes, and make retries idempotent; see the stock/order transaction.[40] Use indexes for actual predicates, not every optional field. Arrays produce multikey behavior and larger indexes; an index on lines.sku can help product-based searches but increases write cost. Tenant/date and tenant/customer/order indexes serve different patterns. After sharding, query routing and per-shard indexing remain separate: a fast shard index does not prevent scatter-gather.[20][32][36] Schema version fields can support rolling application migrations: deploy readers accepting old/new shapes, backfill bounded batches with checkpointed IDs, deploy new writers, verify no old writers remain, then tighten validation. Do not turn off validation globally merely because one bulk import has old data. Keep business transformations reversible where possible and retain pre-transform data under policy.[35][37]

title: Worked relational transformation
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB · Document modeling and BSON types
text: Given source order o1001 for customer c1, and two pencils at exact decimal price 2.50, construct one order document with that line and total 5.00. Copy the source order identity; group child rows by order identity, sort line items deterministically, and preserve quantity/price types. Never compute a migration total with floating-point arithmetic just because the loader is JavaScript.[35][45] An order snapshot and a current customer document answer different questions. Preserve the relational system as authority until bulk load, delta capture and business reconciliation pass. Translate joins/routines/constraints intentionally in the application; SQL query text is not valid MongoDB query language. Continue with migration and cutover.

Application access logging plus immutable external log storage can supplement Community, but does not become equivalent by renaming a log.[15][23] Requires enableProfiler/appropriate database administration privilege on shop; reading system.profile also needs access. Connect directly to the intended mongod; profiling is not available on mongos. Scope matters: the profiling level is per database; slow-operation threshold/sample settings affect diagnostic behavior more broadly on that process.[23] const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop"); const before = shop.getProfilingStatus(); printjson(before); // Level 1 + filter, rather than recording every operation: shop.setProfilingLevel(1, {filter: {ns: "shop.orders", millis: {$gte: 50}}}); // Run the authorized representative workload for a short, supervised window. shop.system.profile.find({ns: "shop.orders"}, { ts: 1, millis: 1, planSummary: 1, keysExamined: 1, docsExamined: 1, nreturned: 1 }).sort({$natural: -1}).limit(20); // Restore observed settings, including whether a filter previously existed: shop.setProfilingLevel(before.was, { slowms: before.slowms, sampleRate: before.sampleRate, filter: before.filter || "unset" }); shop.getProfilingStatus(); When a profiler filter is configured it supersedes slowms/sample-rate selection for profiling/slow-log selection as documented. Save the prior state outside the shell before enabling if a disconnect is possible. Level 2 captures all operations and can be expensive; do not leave it on by accident. system.profile is capped and rolls over, so copy required incident evidence promptly under data-access policy. Disabling profiling does not erase already collected sensitive documents.[23][84] Use the three-order fixture. The query is “recent orders for tenant t1,” not a benchmark. executionStats executes the read; it can be expensive on production. No timing or plan result below is claimed to have been measured.[20][24] const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop"); shop.orders.explain("queryPlanner") .find({tenantId: "t1"}).sort({placedAt: -1}).limit(10); shop.orders.explain("executionStats") .find({tenantId: "t1"}).sort({placedAt: -1}).limit(10); // Compare the existing fixture index explicitly, without changing global policy: shop.orders.explain("executionStats") .find({tenantId: "t1"}).sort({placedAt: -1}).hint("tenant_recent").limit(10); Mode/field Read it as queryPlanner Winning/rejected candidate structure without running to completion executionStats Execution statistics for the winning plan; actual work allPlansExecution Additional candidate trial statistics; not full end-to-end runs of every plan nReturned Documents produced; compare with work examined totalKeysExamined Index entries scanned totalDocsExamined Documents fetched/examined; not necessarily unique documents COLLSCAN, IXSCAN, FETCH, SORT Collection/index access, document fetch, explicit sorting; plan layouts vary by execution engine The tiny fixture may make a collection scan reasonable. Check disk and replication lag, schedule builds, and compare sustained workloads before keeping both indexes. An index with tenant equality followed by descending time supports this access pattern; reversing fields can lose that useful prefix.[20] Index feature Use Cost / constraint Compound Match common equality/sort/range patterns Prefix/order matters; one giant index does not serve all queries Multikey Index array values Expansion increases work; a compound multikey index permits at most one indexed array field per document.[79] Unique Enforce business identity Existing duplicates block build; sharded uniqueness must fit shard-key rules Partial Index only documents meeting a filter Queries must imply the filter to use it safely.[76] TTL Expire eligible time-based records Asynchronous deletion; not an exact scheduler or backup retention mechanism.[77] Hidden Exclude an index from planner selection Still maintained and consumes space; unique constraints still enforced Inspect usage/workload, then hide a redundant candidate before deleting it. The experiment below requires a supporting tenant_recent index and explicit approval to alter the second index:[20][36][42] shop.orders.hideIndex("tenant_recent_total"); shop.orders.getIndexes(); // Observe representative application reads and writes. shop.orders.unhideIndex("tenant_recent_total"); Hidden unique indexes still enforce uniqueness and all hidden indexes are maintained on writes.[98] Rollback is unhide, not rebuild. A hidden index cannot be tested by hinting it.[98] Drop only after a complete workload cycle establishes it is unnecessary and the exact name is recorded; dropping it is not rolled back by unhiding. Retain the creation specification if rebuilding is the recovery plan.[42] const s = db.getSiblingDB("admin").serverStatus(); printjson({connections: s.connections, opcounters: s.opcounters, locks: s.locks, wiredTigerCache: s.wiredTiger && s.wiredTiger.cache}); Use a monitoring identity, compare deltas and align timestamps with application latency. Inspect current operations for waits and query shapes. mongostat and mongotop from the separately pinned Database Tools provide repeated samples; run with authentication/TLS like other clients, not an embedded password.[10][104][51] High scan counts: verify predicate types/collation, index prefixes, selectivity and sort coverage before adding RAM. Locks/DDL waits: identify the holder and business operation; cancelling waiters may not remove the cause. Cache eviction + I/O: inspect working-set size, long transactions, index growth and storage latency together. Connection pressure: inspect driver pool counts/limits and application concurrency; raising server limits can amplify overload. Replication lag: correlate disk/write pressure and oplog window; a stale secondary is not a free read-scaling solution. No apparent DB pressure: measure application queuing, network latency, retries and downstream calls before tuning the database. title: Replica sets and high availability
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB
text: rs0 (one dataset) application -> primary db1 -> oplog -> secondary db2 \-> oplog -> secondary db3 election can move primary; driver discovers it Use three data-bearing voting members across independent failure domains. Replica-set copies follow the same MongoDB dataset; they are not SQL logical-replication subscriptions or independent multi-primary writers. A one-member set enables replica-set semantics for a lab but has no redundancy. An arbiter votes but stores no data and cannot supply another durable copy; do not add one to disguise an unavailable data-bearing majority.[30][31] The primary appends replicated changes to the node-local oplog; secondaries copy/apply them asynchronously. Initial sync builds a new member’s data/indexes and catches up from oplog. It requires enough history and resources to complete; a secondary that falls beyond retained history must resync, not skip errors until it looks current.[31][92] New empty hosts, not an in-place production conversion. Provision the pinned packages on db1.example.net, db2.example.net, db3.example.net. These are reserved example DNS names: replace all names consistently in DNS, config, certificate SANs and connection URIs. Each must resolve/reach the others over a private network. Keep inbound firewall rules limited to members and approved clients using the RHEL firewalld matrix. Each data host uses the RPM mongod account, standard data/log paths and enforcing policy; verify those before topology initialization.[13][104] Have a CA-signed node certificate/private key at /etc/mongodb/tls/server.pem and CA bundle at /etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem on each host; each node’s private key/certificate is distinct. Server certificates used for inter-member TLS need appropriate client/server usage. See certificate requirements.[14][58] Generate one shared internal-authentication key and securely distribute it to all members; do not generate a different key on each host. This is an OS-shell provisioning example, never a value to paste into notes:[13] umask 077 openssl rand -base64 756 > rs0.key sudo install -d -o root -g mongod -m 750 /etc/mongodb sudo install -o mongod -g mongod -m 400 rs0.key /etc/mongodb/rs0.key sudo restorecon -Rv /etc/mongodb sudo -u mongod test -r /etc/mongodb/rs0.key sudo ls -lZ /etc/mongodb/rs0.key Remove the staging copy after verified secure distribution/escrow. On each host merge the following with the data/log configuration; substitute that host’s own name in bindIp. Never duplicate YAML net/security keys.[6][13][14] net: port: 27017 bindIp: 127.0.0.1,db1.example.net tls: mode: requireTLS certificateKeyFile: /etc/mongodb/tls/server.pem CAFile: /etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates: true security: authorization: enabled keyFile: /etc/mongodb/rs0.key replication: replSetName: rs0 allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates: true permits SCRAM clients without client certificates; it does not permit plaintext transport or bypass user authorization. Internal keyfile authentication authenticates members; TLS encrypts the connection.[13][14] Start mongod.service on all three hosts only after SELinux, certificate/key access and scoped firewall checks. Check each process is confined (mongod_t) and has no unexplained AVC denials; then verify TLS/member connectivity. Enable boot start only after topology acceptance. On db1, connect through loopback for the localhost exception. Its certificate must include localhost as a SAN for this local TLS bootstrap (in addition to its private DNS name); do not bypass hostname verification:[7][14] mongosh --host localhost --port 27017 --tls --tlsCAFile=/etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem rs.initiate({_id: "rs0", members: [ {_id: 0, host: "db1.example.net:27017"}, {_id: 1, host: "db2.example.net:27017"}, {_id: 2, host: "db3.example.net:27017"} ]}); rs.status(); Initiate once, not on each node. Wait for the elected primary; create useradmin through the localhost exception on that primary, then authenticate and create the operation/application/backup users as in bootstrap. Users replicate with the set. If a different host becomes primary, connect locally there to finish bootstrap.[7][13] mongosh 'mongodb://db1.example.net:27017,db2.example.net:27017,db3.example.net:27017/shop?replicaSet=rs0&authSource=admin' \ --username operator --tls --tlsCAFile=/etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem rs.conf(); rs.status(); db.getSiblingDB("admin").runCommand({hello: 1}); rs.printReplicationInfo(); rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo(); Expected: one writable primary, healthy secondaries, matching set name, intended hostnames, acceptable lag and enough oplog time coverage. Test majority-acknowledged writes and fresh reads with a disposable business record. Never infer health only from three running OS processes.[13][31] Drivers need a seed list and replicaSet=rs0; a fixed primary address or directConnection=true bypasses discovery behavior needed for failover. Direct connections are for controlled member diagnostics/maintenance. Read preference chooses an eligible reader; read/write concern governs visibility/acknowledgement. See consistency controls.[30][44] A member needs majority support to become/remain primary. Loss of the voting majority stops normal writable-primary service; that is protection from competing authoritative histories, not an invitation to force each side writable. Elections interrupt writes and can expose ambiguous outcomes to clients.[30] Event Likely consequence Response Primary unavailable; majority reachable Eligible secondary elected Driver rediscovers; monitor and retry only safe/driver-supported work Minority partition No safe majority on that side Restore connectivity; do not force reconfigure to manufacture quorum Write acknowledged only by old primary May roll back on rejoin Reconcile business state; prefer majority concern for required durability Majority write timeout Outcome uncertain, not automatically absent Check stable request ID; do not duplicate charges/decrements Member returns with divergent history Rollback/recovery may occur Preserve rollback/log evidence; review affected application records A successful majority acknowledgement is tied to the replica-set durability assumptions; it is not a backup against deletion, all-site loss or an administrator forcing unsafe reconfiguration. Avoid mixing priority/votes/delayed members without a reviewed quorum model.[30][31] Use an authorized staging set first; save application error/latency and member-state baselines. Verify another data-bearing member is caught up and eligible. As cluster administrator on the current primary:[30] rs.stepDown(60); Reconnect using the set URI. Confirm a new primary, resumed majority writes, application reconnection and no unexplained duplicate business operations. The old primary should remain/return healthy as a secondary. If stepdown refuses because no eligible secondary is ready, fix lag/health rather than force it. If election fails, inspect majority connectivity, TLS/key agreement and member configuration; restoring the failed node/network is safer than force reconfiguration. A real disaster decision needs a named authority, confirmed surviving data, fencing of obsolete endpoints and an explicit accepted loss window. Do not run rs.initiate() on an existing set to “make a new primary.” Restored replacement sets must remain isolated until the old topology is fenced and clients are cut over exactly once.[22][30] Use the documented member-replacement procedure for the actual failure. A simple secondary replacement preserves the old member’s hostname/port: shut down and fence the old machine, provision a new host with the same identity, keys/TLS and configuration, and an empty dbPath owned by mongod:mongod with the intended persistent SELinux label and mount. Recheck RHEL errata, unit/environment/limits and scoped member firewall rules before starting; let it initial-sync. Never let both old and replacement hosts answer the same member address.[13][92] When host identity must

Never duplicate YAML net/security keys.[6][13][14] net: port: 27017 bindIp: 127.0.0.1,db1.example.net tls: mode: requireTLS certificateKeyFile: /etc/mongodb/tls/server.pem CAFile: /etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates: true security: authorization: enabled keyFile: /etc/mongodb/rs0.key replication: replSetName: rs0 allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates: true permits SCRAM clients without client certificates; it does not permit plaintext transport or bypass user authorization. Internal keyfile authentication authenticates members; TLS encrypts the connection.[13][14] Start mongod.service on all three hosts only after SELinux, certificate/key access and scoped firewall checks. Check each process is confined (mongod_t) and has no unexplained AVC denials; then verify TLS/member connectivity. Enable boot start only after topology acceptance. On db1, connect through loopback for the localhost exception. Its certificate must include localhost as a SAN for this local TLS bootstrap (in addition to its private DNS name); do not bypass hostname verification:[7][14] mongosh --host localhost --port 27017 --tls --tlsCAFile=/etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem rs.initiate({_id: "rs0", members: [ {_id: 0, host: "db1.example.net:27017"}, {_id: 1, host: "db2.example.net:27017"}, {_id: 2, host: "db3.example.net:27017"} ]}); rs.status(); Initiate once, not on each node. Wait for the elected primary; create useradmin through the localhost exception on that primary, then authenticate and create the operation/application/backup users as in bootstrap. Users replicate with the set. If a different host becomes primary, connect locally there to finish bootstrap.[7][13]

title: Connect and verify the set
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Replica sets and high availability
text: mongosh 'mongodb://db1.example.net:27017,db2.example.net:27017,db3.example.net:27017/shop?replicaSet=rs0&authSource=admin' \ --username operator --tls --tlsCAFile=/etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem rs.conf(); rs.status(); db.getSiblingDB("admin").runCommand({hello: 1}); rs.printReplicationInfo(); rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo(); Expected: one writable primary, healthy secondaries, matching set name, intended hostnames, acceptable lag and enough oplog time coverage. Test majority-acknowledged writes and fresh reads with a disposable business record. Never infer health only from three running OS processes.[13][31] Drivers need a seed list and replicaSet=rs0; a fixed primary address or directConnection=true bypasses discovery behavior needed for failover. Direct connections are for controlled member diagnostics/maintenance. Read preference chooses an eligible reader; read/write concern governs visibility/acknowledgement. See consistency controls.[30][44]

title: Elections, majority and rollback
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Replica sets and high availability
text: A member needs majority support to become/remain primary. Loss of the voting majority stops normal writable-primary service; that is protection from competing authoritative histories, not an invitation to force each side writable. Elections interrupt writes and can expose ambiguous outcomes to clients.[30] Event Likely consequence Response Primary unavailable; majority reachable Eligible secondary elected Driver rediscovers; monitor and retry only safe/driver-supported work Minority partition No safe majority on that side Restore connectivity; do not force reconfigure to manufacture quorum Write acknowledged only by old primary May roll back on rejoin Reconcile business state; prefer majority concern for required durability Majority write timeout Outcome uncertain, not automatically absent Check stable request ID; do not duplicate charges/decrements Member returns with divergent history Rollback/recovery may occur Preserve rollback/log evidence; review affected application records A successful majority acknowledgement is tied to the replica-set durability assumptions; it is not a backup against deletion, all-site loss or an administrator forcing unsafe reconfiguration. Avoid mixing priority/votes/delayed members without a reviewed quorum model.[30][31]

title: Planned failover drill
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Replica sets and high availability
text: Use an authorized staging set first; save application error/latency and member-state baselines. Verify another data-bearing member is caught up and eligible. As cluster administrator on the current primary:[30] rs.stepDown(60); Reconnect using the set URI. Confirm a new primary, resumed majority writes, application reconnection and no unexplained duplicate business operations. The old primary should remain/return healthy as a secondary. If stepdown refuses because no eligible secondary is ready, fix lag/health rather than force it. If election fails, inspect majority connectivity, TLS/key agreement and member configuration; restoring the failed node/network is safer than force reconfiguration. A real disaster decision needs a named authority, confirmed surviving data, fencing of obsolete endpoints and an explicit accepted loss window. Do not run rs.initiate() on an existing set to “make a new primary.” Restored replacement sets must remain isolated until the old topology is fenced and clients are cut over exactly once.[22][30]

title: Replace a failed member and watch oplog headroom
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Replica sets and high availability
text: Use the documented member-replacement procedure for the actual failure. A simple secondary replacement preserves the old member’s hostname/port: shut down and fence the old machine, provision a new host with the same identity, keys/TLS and configuration, and an empty dbPath owned by mongod:mongod with the intended persistent SELinux label and mount. Recheck RHEL errata, unit/environment/limits and scoped member firewall rules before starting; let it initial-sync. Never let both old and replacement hosts answer the same member address.[13][92] When host identity must change, as administrator use rs.conf(), locate the exact member by _id, change only its host, then apply rs.reconfig(cfg) through a healthy primary as documented. Retain the old config; wait for health before any next membership change. Do not combine several voting changes or use forced reconfiguration as a routine replacement shortcut.[33] // Inspection before selecting the member/change: const cfg = rs.conf(); printjson(cfg.members); rs.printReplicationInfo(); rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo(); Track lag in time and oplog coverage, not just oplog bytes. Bursts can shrink the history window; long initial sync/maintenance needs capacity for the measured write rate. Oplog resizing/retention settings require a version-specific capacity plan, not manual collection/file deletion. If the old host returns after replacement, keep it fenced and resync it deliberately rather than admitting a stale duplicate identity.[31][33] For horizontal partitioning use sharding, not additional independent primaries holding unsynchronized copies of shop.

title: Hardening, TLS and key rotation
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MongoDB
text: Control Question answered Baseline Network ACL/firewall Which machines can reach the listener? Private interfaces; explicit application/member allowlist TLS identity Is this the expected peer, and is transport encrypted? Trusted CA, matching DNS SAN, requireTLS Authentication Which user/member is connecting? SCRAM-SHA-256 users; keyfile membership in the lab Authorization Which actions on which resources? Explicit least-privilege roles Storage encryption What can a stolen disk/snapshot reveal? Host/volume encryption for Community Backup/secret controls Can recovery work without exposing credentials/data? Encrypted off-host copies, separated keys, restore drills Bind selection is not an access-control list; loopback is a bootstrap boundary, not sufficient isolation against other local users. Keep authorization enabled, patch the OS/server/clients, use a dedicated unprivileged service account, and keep its data/log/key directories unavailable to unrelated users.[6][9][14] Use custom collection roles, not root for an application. User administrators can elevate privileges and need strong custody. Check permissions from fresh allowed and denied sessions; an authenticated ping is not a least-privilege test.[18][85] RHEL 9 uses firewalld zones and separate runtime/permanent configuration. An allow rule is not a deny-all policy: existing broad ports/services, source-based zone selection, trusted/ACCEPT zones, forwarding or upstream ACLs can defeat the intended restriction. Inventory them first and keep an out-of-band administration path; do not move interfaces or remove SSH access blindly.[109][111] sudo firewall-cmd --state sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones sudo firewall-cmd --list-all-zones sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --list-all-zones The worked rule assumes the database interface is already in an approved restrictive public zone and 192.0.2.40/32 is a documentation placeholder for one authorized client. Substitute the actual zone and host source address seen after NAT. Check that no existing rule admits everyone to 27017. Add/test one source-qualified rule at runtime, then persist that exact rule after acceptance; do not save unrelated runtime changes with --runtime-to-permanent.[109] sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public \ --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.0.2.40/32" port port="27017" protocol="tcp" accept' sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public \ --query-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.0.2.40/32" port port="27017" protocol="tcp" accept' # Test a NEW TLS/authenticated connection from the allowed client and # a NEW connection from an unapproved host; the latter must not reach the port. sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public \ --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.0.2.40/32" port port="27017" protocol="tcp" accept' sudo firewall-cmd --check-config sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --list-rich-rules sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-rich-rules Rollback removes that same exact rich rule with --remove-rich-rule in runtime and permanent configuration, followed by readback. A controlled firewall-cmd --reload later proves persistence but replaces runtime-only rules with permanent state; audit those differences before reloading. Test fresh connections after reload/reboot, not an already established session.[109] Destination Approved sources only TCP Standalone/replica member Actual application/backup/monitor hosts; every peer member for a replica set 27017 Router Approved application/admin/backup/monitor hosts 27017 Shard members Peer/internal cluster hosts and authorized maintenance/backup hosts, not general application clients 27018 Config members Peer/internal cluster hosts (including shards/routers) and approved maintenance hosts 27019 Local restore instance None remotely; retain loopback bind, no inbound opening 27018 locally Build the complete private cluster communication matrix: all members need the documented inter-member connections, not just app-to-primary access. Repeat scoped rules for the actual member addresses/ports on each destination. If IPv6 is enabled/bound, implement equivalent family="ipv6" rules with approved /128 or reviewed CIDRs; IPv4 rules do not constrain IPv6. Review egress policy, DNS/CA reachability and upstream firewalls separately. mongod_port_t labels permit daemon use of ports; they do not grant remote hosts access.[103][109] Configuration mutation and restart. Before binding remotely, obtain certificates from the approved CA. Each server PEM contains its own private key, certificate and required intermediate chain. SANs must include the exact DNS names clients/members use; include localhost only where the local TLS bootstrap requires it. Check validity, chain, key match and permitted usage before deployment. For inter-member TLS the node certificate must support its server/client roles.[14][58] Paths used consistently in these notes: /etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem trust bundle, no private key /etc/mongodb/tls/server.pem this host's certificate + private key /etc/mongodb/rs0.key shared membership secret (replica lab) /etc/mongodb/cluster.key shared membership secret (sharding lab) The service must read them, but other users must not read private material. Keep root ownership for policy/config where possible, with controlled group/read access for mongod. Example installation of already approved artifacts on the target host:[13][14] sudo install -d -o root -g mongod -m 750 /etc/mongodb sudo install -d -o root -g mongod -m 750 /etc/mongodb/tls sudo install -o root -g mongod -m 640 approved-ca.pem /etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem sudo install -o mongod -g mongod -m 600 approved-node.pem /etc/mongodb/tls/server.pem sudo restorecon -Rv /etc/mongodb sudo ls -ldZ /etc/mongodb /etc/mongodb/tls sudo ls -lZ /etc/mongodb/tls sudo -u mongod test -r /etc/mongodb/tls/server.pem Use the host policy’s expected /etc/certificate contexts (matchpathcon -V), not home-directory labels carried in by a move. The pinned mongod policy reads generic /etc files and certificate types; DAC still restricts the private key. Do not label secrets as writable database files to force access. test -r checks DAC only: verify actual mongod startup/new TLS connections in mongod_t and review AVCs under enforcing mode.[108][110] Merge into existing /etc/mongod.conf; this example exposes only the chosen private interface plus loopback and allows SCRAM clients without client certificates:[6][14] net: port: 27017 bindIp: 127.0.0.1,db1.example.net tls: mode: requireTLS certificateKeyFile: /etc/mongodb/tls/server.pem CAFile: /etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem allowConnectionsWithoutCertificates: true disabledProtocols: TLS1_0,TLS1_1 security: authorization: enabled Retain any existing keyfile and replica settings; replacing the whole security block and losing keyFile breaks membership authentication. Configure firewall rules before remote start. Restart a standalone in a maintenance window; for existing TLS replica sets use rolling member maintenance and keep quorum. Migrating a live plaintext set requires the documented staged TLS modes and client transition, not switching one member blindly to requireTLS.[14] mongosh --host db1.example.net --port 27017 --username operator \ --authenticationDatabase admin --tls --tlsCAFile=/etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem Acceptance: trusted/hostname-matched connection and protected operation succeed; plaintext, wrong CA, wrong hostname and unauthorized identity fail as expected. Inspect logs without logging secrets. Do not use tlsInsecure, invalid-certificate or invalid-hostname flags to make these negative tests pass. If startup fails, correct certificate permissions/chain/config or restore the last secure known-good config while keeping exposure restricted.[14] SCRAM-SHA-256 authenticates username/password accounts in their authentication database. Use passwordPrompt()/client prompts; never a reusable password literal in a shell command. x.509 client authentication instead maps a certificate subject t

title: SCRAM, x.509 and internal authentication
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MongoDB · Hardening, TLS and key rotation
text: SCRAM-SHA-256 authenticates username/password accounts in their authentication database. Use passwordPrompt()/client prompts; never a reusable password literal in a shell command. x.509 client authentication instead maps a certificate subject to an external user in $external; trust in the CA alone does not grant the client’s database role.[18][58] For an approved client certificate, copy its exact RFC2253 subject from the certificate inspection result—do not guess or normalize its distinguished name. Create the corresponding external user as user administrator:[58] // Replace the marked subject with the EXACT approved certificate subject. const subject = "<EXACT_RFC2253_CLIENT_CERTIFICATE_SUBJECT>"; db.getSiblingDB("$external").createUser({ user: subject, roles: [{role: "read", db: "shop"}] }); mongosh --host db1.example.net --port 27017 --tls \ --tlsCAFile=/etc/mongodb/tls/ca.pem --tlsCertificateKeyFile=/secure/client.pem \ --authenticationMechanism=MONGODB-X509 --authenticationDatabase='$external' Authorize only the intended subject/role; test another valid but unregistered client certificate is denied protected access. Do not reuse cluster-member certificates as client identities.[58] Internal authentication is separate from application authentication. Keyfiles provide shared-secret membership and enable access control; all communicating replica/sharded members need compatible shared keys. File permissions must deny group/world access on Unix. Keyfiles do not encrypt transport; pair them with TLS.[13] For production x.509 membership, use the official member-certificate requirements: trusted chain, required matching organization-related attributes or explicitly configured membership attributes, distinct client-versus-member subjects, and appropriate extended key usage. Configure security.clusterAuthMode: x509 and net.tls.clusterFile/CA options where separate member certificates are used. A conversion from keyfile is a staged rolling procedure (sendKeyFile/sendX509 transitions as documented), not a one-node instant switch. Plan it on a restored staging topology first.[88][91]

title: Rotate without breaking trust
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MongoDB · Hardening, TLS and key rotation
text: TLS rotation and membership-key rotation are different operations. For TLS, retain trusted CA overlap across servers and clients, distribute valid new PEM/CA files at the same paths, preserve ownership/modes and restore/check expected SELinux contexts after replacement, then run on each process with the rotateCertificates privilege:[52] db.getSiblingDB("admin").runCommand({ rotateCertificates: 1, message: "scheduled certificate renewal" }); The command reloads applicable certificate/CA/CRL files. If the private-key file is encrypted, its password must remain the configured password for online rotation; changing that secret requires a different reviewed procedure. Do not infer success for all members from one command. Test new client/member connections after each rotation; existing connections can hide a failed trust change. Keep the old valid files for rollback until acceptance and then remove obsolete trust after every dependent client/member has moved.[52] For shared membership key rotation, use the documented keyfile multi-key rolling process: distribute a file accepting old/new keys to every member, roll while retaining majority, transition the sending/accepted key set, then remove the old key only after all members have converged. Replacing the shared key on one member with a disjoint secret partitions it. Certificate renewal does not rotate this secret. On replica sets the documented sequence is two rolling passes: first every keyfile accepts old and new; then every keyfile contains only the new key, with secondaries first and primary stepdown in each pass.[65][66]

title: At-rest encryption and recovery keys
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MongoDB · Hardening, TLS and key rotation
text: MongoDB Enterprise’s encrypted storage engine and its key-management options are not available as a Community YAML switch. Do not publish security.enableEncryption/KMIP commands as Community instructions. For this baseline, provision OS/volume encryption under the platform’s supported process and verify mount/unlock/reboot/recovery behavior before placing the dbPath there.[11] Boundary Still needs protection Encrypted disk Running privileged processes can read data; logs/temp/swap may live elsewhere TLS Plaintext on client/server endpoints and exported files Backup encryption Keys, metadata, credentials, restore worker and offsite deletion authority Client-side field encryption Driver/library/edition feature compatibility, key vault and application access patterns Do not assume every client-side encryption feature, automatic encryption workflow or Queryable Encryption backup tool is available in every edition. The pinned Tools manuals explicitly exclude mongodump/mongorestore use for Queryable Encryption collections; those require a separately supported backup design.[2][3][11] Escrow recovery keys separately from the only encrypted backup. Record key identifiers and rotation history, not secret bytes in an evidence report. Test restoring an older retained backup after rotation; deleting its last required key makes that backup unrecoverable.

title: Secret, log and incident discipline
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MongoDB · Hardening, TLS and key rotation
text: Use interactive prompts for manual operations. For automated Tools jobs, a protected --config file can carry the documented sensitive fields; use restrictive permissions and a secret manager/rotation policy. Environment variables and command-line URIs can leak through process/environment dumps, shell history, CI logs and copied diagnostics.[2][3] Never store keys/passwords in notes, source control or fixture JSON. Restrict profiler data, shell history/output and diagnostic logs, which can contain query/customer data. FTDC does not sample end-user collection/index data or include query contents; it does include hostnames, OS information and configuration metadata, so inspect its privacy boundary before sharing it.[96] Clear exposed artifacts through an incident process and rotate compromised secrets; simply deleting one history entry does not revoke a leaked credential.[23][43] Lost administrative access is a controlled recovery incident. First use an independently secured administrator or restored access plan. Any exceptional auth-disabled recovery must be isolated at the OS/network level and follow a topology-specific official procedure; this manual intentionally provides no public-listener bypass recipe. Validate allowed/denied operations again after recovery.[7][9]

title: Sharding and resharding
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB
text: application -> mongos router A / router B | reads config metadata from cfgRS +-> shard01 replica set (primary + secondaries) +-> shard02 replica set (primary + secondaries) config servers: cfgRS, three members, cluster metadata A shard owns ranges of collection data. Each shard’s replica set provides redundancy for those ranges. Config servers hold placement/cluster metadata; routers cache that metadata and target requests. Lose a shard’s availability and requests needing its data fail even if other shards are healthy. Lose config-server majority and metadata operations/balancing become unavailable; do not treat router cache as a replacement backup.[34][73] Applications connect to mongos, not directly to shards. Shard-local maintenance access is exceptional, separately authorized, and especially constrained in 8.0. Do not grant directShardOperations to application users or write around the router because a command is rejected.[25][34] For shop.orders, primary accesses are tenant + order ID and tenant + recent date. The worked starting key is {tenantId: 1, _id: 1}. Tenant alone has poor cardinality if there are few tenants, and one very large tenant can become a hotspot. The second field permits subdivisions within a tenant, but sequential IDs can still concentrate new inserts. The fixture is too small to demonstrate real distribution.[32] Candidate Advantage Cost / reject when {tenantId: 1} Tenant routing and zone affinity Few/hot tenants; identical-key range cannot split usefully {placedAt: 1} Time-range locality Monotonically increasing ingest concentrates writes {_id: "hashed"} Distributes many distinct IDs Tenant queries may scatter; hashing does not cure a single repeated hot value {tenantId: 1, _id: 1} Tenant prefix and precise order routing Within-tenant monotonic insert pressure; date scans need their own index {tenantId: 1, customerId: 1, _id: 1} Customer-specific routing/locality Tenant-only reads still span its ranges; changed write predicates required Evaluate cardinality, value frequency, monotonicity, query targeting, write distribution, document growth and zone/residency rules. Use representative production-shaped data and sampled access patterns, not only the three-document exercise. An index can speed work inside a shard without improving router targeting.[20][32] The shard key is not automatically a uniqueness constraint. Unique indexes on sharded collections must satisfy shard-key restrictions; _id may not enforce global uniqueness when it is not the shard key. Generate globally unique business/order IDs and include tenant context in application requests. Do not create an incompatible unique index and discover the conflict only during sharding.[36][39] Use new isolated hosts and the pinned 8.0.29 packages. This procedure uses keyfile membership + TLS for a controlled self-managed lab; MongoDB’s production sharded-deployment guidance recommends x.509 security. Review internal-authentication requirements before promoting the lab to production.[13][34][58] Set/process Hosts Explicit port Role cfgRS cfg1, cfg2, cfg3.example.net 27019 configsvr shard01 s1a, s1b, s1c.example.net 27018 shardsvr shard02 s2a, s2b, s2c.example.net 27018 shardsvr Router router1.example.net 27017 mongos Names are examples, not resolvable infrastructure supplied by these notes. On distinct hosts each mongod may use the package /var/lib/mongo and log path; on shared lab hosts every instance needs a different path/service/socket/port and the custom SELinux integration. title: A sharded cluster contains replica sets
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Sharding and resharding
text: application -> mongos router A / router B | reads config metadata from cfgRS +-> shard01 replica set (primary + secondaries) +-> shard02 replica set (primary + secondaries) config servers: cfgRS, three members, cluster metadata A shard owns ranges of collection data. Each shard’s replica set provides redundancy for those ranges. Config servers hold placement/cluster metadata; routers cache that metadata and target requests. Lose a shard’s availability and requests needing its data fail even if other shards are healthy. Lose config-server majority and metadata operations/balancing become unavailable; do not treat router cache as a replacement backup.[34][73] Applications connect to mongos, not directly to shards. Shard-local maintenance access is exceptional, separately authorized, and especially constrained in 8.0. Do not grant directShardOperations to application users or write around the router because a command is rejected.[25][34]

title: Choose a key from access patterns
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Sharding and resharding
text: For shop.orders, primary accesses are tenant + order ID and tenant + recent date. The worked starting key is {tenantId: 1, _id: 1}. Tenant alone has poor cardinality if there are few tenants, and one very large tenant can become a hotspot. The second field permits subdivisions within a tenant, but sequential IDs can still concentrate new inserts. The fixture is too small to demonstrate real distribution.[32] Candidate Advantage Cost / reject when {tenantId: 1} Tenant routing and zone affinity Few/hot tenants; identical-key range cannot split usefully {placedAt: 1} Time-range locality Monotonically increasing ingest concentrates writes {_id: "hashed"} Distributes many distinct IDs Tenant queries may scatter; hashing does not cure a single repeated hot value {tenantId: 1, _id: 1} Tenant prefix and precise order routing Within-tenant monotonic insert pressure; date scans need their own index {tenantId: 1, customerId: 1, _id: 1} Customer-specific routing/locality Tenant-only reads still span its ranges; changed write predicates required Evaluate cardinality, value frequency, monotonicity, query targeting, write distribution, document growth and zone/residency rules. Use representative production-shaped data and sampled access patterns, not only the three-document exercise. An index can speed work inside a shard without improving router targeting.[20][32] The shard key is not automatically a uniqueness constraint. Unique indexes on sharded collections must satisfy shard-key restrictions; _id may not enforce global uniqueness when it is not the shard key. Generate globally unique business/order IDs and include tenant context in application requests. Do not create an incompatible unique index and discover the conflict only during sharding.[36][39]

title: Shard and inspect the collection
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Sharding and resharding
text: Load the fixture through mongos in the isolated cluster, not directly into a shard. Use the administrator’s cluster-management privileges and approved index/DDL window:[32][34] const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop"); shop.orders.createIndex({tenantId: 1, _id: 1}, {name: "tenant_order_shard"}); sh.shardCollection("shop.orders", {tenantId: 1, _id: 1}); sh.status(); shop.orders.explain("queryPlanner").find({tenantId: "t1", _id: "o1001"}); shop.orders.explain("queryPlanner").find({status: "paid"}); The full-key lookup should be targetable; a status-only query lacks the shard key and may scatter to shards. Inspect the actual router explain output rather than assuming a particular shard count in a tiny dataset. Keep tenant_recent for tenant/date reads: the shard-key index does not replace that sorting access path.[20][24][32] Chunks/ranges describe keyspace ownership, not fixed-size files. Balancing migrates ranges between shards; config metadata records ownership. A migration may create temporary copies/orphan cleanup work, which is why direct shard counts can mislead and backups must coordinate across the topology.[26][38]

title: Balance, zones and maintenance
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Sharding and resharding
text: sh.getBalancerState(); sh.isBalancerRunning(); sh.status(); The enabled setting and a currently active balancing round are different observations. Balancer decisions depend on data distribution/thresholds; adding a shard does not guarantee immediate even document counts. Repeated shard-key values can create unsplittable hot ranges. Investigate data/key design, shard disk, replication lag, migration errors and zone restrictions before manually moving ranges.[32][38] Zones constrain key ranges to selected shards for placement/residency or hardware classes. They do not replace authorization or automatically ensure every copy/backup meets a residency policy. Design zone ranges and matching shard tags together; a missing eligible shard can stop useful balancing.[38] For backup/upgrade windows, record prior state, stop the balancer, wait for active migrations to finish, perform the coordinated work, then restore prior state and validate. Link the same topology inventory to sharded backup and upgrade ordering; a per-shard “done” is not cluster completion.[25][26]

title: Reshard without pretending it is free
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MongoDB · Sharding and resharding
text: 8.0 Community supports resharding. The example changes the key to {tenantId: 1, customerId: 1, _id: 1} only after a measured customer-locality benefit. It is not a fix required by this fixture. Read the 8.0 procedure in full: one collection at a time, majority journaling enabled, no incompatible unique indexes/index builds, sufficient recipient space and CPU/I/O/oplog headroom. The guide’s storage estimate per recipient is 2 × (collection storage + index storage) / shard count; skew and growth require additional margin.[39][64] Rehearse on a representative restored cluster; take a coordinated backup and agree latency/write-block budget. Update application query/identity assumptions for the new key. Save balancer state and stop it. Avoid concurrent DDL/topology changes. Through mongos, run as a role authorized for resharding: db.adminCommand({ reshardCollection: "shop.orders", key: {tenantId: 1, customerId: 1, _id: 1} }); Monitor from another connection with $currentOp on admin, filtering resharding descriptions, and watch per-member disk, lag and errors. The command builds required indexes during its index phase; it is write-intensive and has a write-blocking commit phase. A disconnected client is not proof of cancellation.[39] Before commit, an approved abort can use the command below. Once commit is reached, abort may be rejected; rollback then is another reviewed reshard/migration or restore, not toggling a setting.[63] db.adminCommand({abortReshardCollection: "shop.orders"}); After success, verify key/placement, counts and business totals, uniqueness assumptions and routing of actual queries/writes; restore the prior balancer state. Keep old-key query clients from becoming an unexpected scatter workload. In 8.0 the same-key forceRedistribution option also exists, but it is still a resharding operation with these resource/operational costs, not ordinary balancing.[39][64]

title: WiredTiger, transactions and consistency
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB
text: WiredTiger uses an internal cache plus the OS filesystem cache. On-disk compression and cached document representation differ; database size is not a reliable RAM requirement. The documented default cache is the larger of 50% of (RAM - 1 GB) or 0.256 GB. Multiple instances/container limits require an explicit memory budget, not that default multiplied per process.[10] Mechanism Protects/provides Does not provide Cache Working data, dirty pages, fast access Durable acknowledgement on its own Checkpoint Consistent on-disk recovery point, normally every 60 seconds A separate retained backup Journal Redo of modifications between checkpoints Oplog history or arbitrary PITR Oplog Replication operations in bounded node-local history Indefinite archive or protection from user deletion History store Older versions needed for snapshot visibility User-controlled historical restore points Crash recovery uses a valid checkpoint and journal. Removing journal/history files to free space breaks the storage contract. Find growth in data, indexes, history retention, oplog or logs before acting; retain evidence and restore from a known-good copy if corruption is suspected.[10][31] // Read-only; clusterMonitor const s = db.getSiblingDB("admin").serverStatus(); printjson(s.wiredTiger.cache); printjson(s.connections); printjson(s.locks); Use successive samples: dirty bytes, eviction activity and read I/O rising together are more informative than cache occupancy alone. A full cache is normal; sustained application-thread eviction or disk saturation deserves investigation. Long-running snapshots/transactions retain history and can increase pressure. Do not tune an internal WiredTiger option from an unrelated version’s blog post.[10][40] On the RHEL production host, prefer XFS and verify the actual mounted filesystem, capacity and latency. MongoDB 8.0 has different memory/Transparent Huge Pages guidance from older MongoDB releases: do not inherit a blanket old-version THP-disable script or generic database sysctl profile. Review the 8.0 production notes and coordinate tuning with RHEL tuned, cgroups and the service memory budget; record effective settings after reboot.[62] One document update is atomic, including its embedded fields/arrays. updateMany is not one atomic transaction across all matching documents. WiredTiger provides document-level concurrency with optimistic conflict handling; DDL and metadata operations can still require stronger locks. MVCC snapshots are internal visibility machinery, not a promise that a sequence of unrelated reads shares one snapshot.[10][40][72] For a bounded stock decrement, include the invariant in the filter. This sample expects the shop.inventory document created below and needs readWrite on shop: const shop = db.getSiblingDB("shop"); shop.inventory.insertOne({_id: "pencil", available: Int32(20)}); const r = shop.inventory.updateOne( {_id: "pencil", available: {$gte: 2}}, {$inc: {available: -2}}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority", j: true, wtimeout: 5000}} ); printjson(r); matchedCount: 1 is the expected successful branch, not captured output. Zero means missing item or insufficient stock; it is not permission to retry without the stock condition. An acknowledgement timeout does not prove the write failed: reconcile the business request before issuing a non-idempotent decrement again.[75] Control Example Meaning / trap Read preference primary, secondaryPreferred Where a read may run, not its isolation/durability Read concern local Data visible on that member; can include writes later rolled back Read concern majority Majority-committed data; not necessarily the newest wall-clock write Read concern snapshot Point-in-time view where supported; use for cross-document transaction invariants Write concern {w: 1} Primary acknowledgement, not majority protection Write concern {w: "majority", j: true} Majority acknowledgement plus requested journal durability Write timeout wtimeout: 5000 Bounds waiting for acknowledgement; not server-side undo Causal session causalConsistency: true Orders causally related operations; use majority reads and writes for documented guarantees Do not infer effective defaults from the word “replica set”; topology and cluster default settings matter. Secondary reads can be stale. For read-your-own-writes across eligible nodes, use one causally consistent session and the documented majority concerns; separate sessions do not automatically exchange causal history.[30][44][75] const session = db.getMongo().startSession({causalConsistency: true}); try { const orders = session.getDatabase("shop").orders; orders.updateOne({_id: "o1001"}, {$set: {status: "paid"}}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000}}); printjson(orders.find({_id: "o1001"}).readConcern("majority").toArray()); } finally { session.endSession(); } Use this only after loading the fixture; it mutates order status. Restore the fixture’s business state deliberately, not with an unqualified delete. Multi-document transactions need a replica set or sharded cluster, not a standalone. Create the target collections/indexes before the example: load the three-order fixture and create inventory using the earlier stock example in this same deployment. Confirm pencil has at least two available units and o2001 is absent; do not reset stock on a rerun. Use the replica-set connection, and grant data privileges on both orders and inventory.[40] const session = db.getMongo().startSession(); const shop = session.getDatabase("shop"); try { session.startTransaction({ readConcern: {level: "snapshot"}, writeConcern: {w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000}, readPreference: "primary" }); const stock = shop.inventory.updateOne( {_id: "pencil", available: {$gte: 2}}, {$inc: {available: -2}} ); if (stock.matchedCount !== 1) throw new Error("stock unavailable"); shop.orders.insertOne({ _id: "o2001", tenantId: "t1", customerId: "c1", placedAt: ISODate("2026-09-01T10:00:00Z"), status: "new", total: Decimal128("5.00"), lines: [{sku: "pencil", qty: Int32(2), unitPrice: Decimal128("2.50")}] }); session.commitTransaction(); } catch (e) { try { session.abortTransaction(); } catch (_) { /* may already be ended */ } throw e; } finally { session.endSession(); } This shell walkthrough illustrates boundaries, not a production retry loop. On TransientTransactionError, retry the whole transaction using the driver’s transaction API; on UnknownTransactionCommitResult, resolve/retry the commit as documented rather than resubmitting arbitrary external side effects. A duplicate o2001 on rerun should abort; do not erase it to make the example appear successful. Keep payment/email calls outside retryable transaction callbacks.[78] After an unambiguous commit, inspect order and stock in a fresh majority read. After an unambiguous abort, neither mutation should persist. If commit outcome is uncertain, look up the stable order/business request ID before retrying. Transactions add cost and do not make an unbounded document model sensible; prefer one atomic aggregate where the access pattern permits it.[35][40]

title: Read preference, read concern, write concern
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB · WiredTiger, transactions and consistency
text: Control Example Meaning / trap Read preference primary, secondaryPreferred Where a read may run, not its isolation/durability Read concern local Data visible on that member; can include writes later rolled back Read concern majority Majority-committed data; not necessarily the newest wall-clock write Read concern snapshot Point-in-time view where supported; use for cross-document transaction invariants Write concern {w: 1} Primary acknowledgement, not majority protection Write concern {w: "majority", j: true} Majority acknowledgement plus requested journal durability Write timeout wtimeout: 5000 Bounds waiting for acknowledgement; not server-side undo Causal session causalConsistency: true Orders causally related operations; use majority reads and writes for documented guarantees Do not infer effective defaults from the word “replica set”; topology and cluster default settings matter. Secondary reads can be stale. For read-your-own-writes across eligible nodes, use one causally consistent session and the documented majority concerns; separate sessions do not automatically exchange causal history.[30][44][75] const session = db.getMongo().startSession({causalConsistency: true}); try { const orders = session.getDatabase("shop").orders; orders.updateOne({_id: "o1001"}, {$set: {status: "paid"}}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000}}); printjson(orders.find({_id: "o1001"}).readConcern("majority").toArray()); } finally { session.endSession(); } Use this only after loading the fixture; it mutates order status. Restore the fixture’s business state deliberately, not with an unqualified delete.

title: A two-collection transaction
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MongoDB · WiredTiger, transactions and consistency
text: Multi-document transactions need a replica set or sharded cluster, not a standalone. Create the target collections/indexes before the example: load the three-order fixture and create inventory using the earlier stock example in this same deployment. Confirm pencil has at least two available units and o2001 is absent; do not reset stock on a rerun. Use the replica-set connection, and grant data privileges on both orders and inventory.[40] const session = db.getMongo().startSession(); const shop = session.getDatabase("shop"); try { session.startTransaction({ readConcern: {level: "snapshot"}, writeConcern: {w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000}, readPreference: "primary" }); const stock = shop.inventory.updateOne( {_id: "pencil", available: {$gte: 2}}, {$inc: {available: -2}} ); if (stock.matchedCount !== 1) throw new Error("stock unavailable"); shop.orders.insertOne({ _id: "o2001", tenantId: "t1", customerId: "c1", placedAt: ISODate("2026-09-01T10:00:00Z"), status: "new", total: Decimal128("5.00"), lines: [{sku: "pencil", qty: Int32(2), unitPrice: Decimal128("2.50")}] }); session.commitTransaction(); } catch (e) { try { session.abortTransaction(); } catch (_) { /* may already be ended */ } throw e; } finally { session.endSession(); } This shell walkthrough illustrates boundaries, not a production retry loop. On TransientTransactionError, retry the whole transaction using the driver’s transaction API; on UnknownTransactionCommitResult, resolve/retry the commit as documented rather than resubmitting arbitrary external side effects. A duplicate o2001 on rerun should abort; do not erase it to make the example appear successful. Keep payment/email calls outside retryable transaction callbacks.[78] After an unambiguous commit, inspect order and stock in a fresh majority read. After an unambiguous abort, neither mutation should persist. If commit outcome is uncertain, look up the stable order/business request ID before retrying. Transactions add cost and do not make an unbounded document model sensible; prefer one atomic aggregate where the access pattern permits it.[35][40]

title: Upgrades and feature compatibility
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MongoDB
text: The selected target is the vendor RHEL 9 x86_64 RPM 8.0.29-1.el9. A patch update within 8.0 is not a 7.0 → 8.0 major upgrade. featureCompatibilityVersion (FCV) gates persistent feature compatibility; changing it does not install a binary. Running 8.0 binaries at FCV 7.0 after a major upgrade is a deliberate burn-in phase, not evidence of an unfinished package install.[4][27][28] Starting point Route Supported earlier 8.0 patch Review intervening patch notes/advisories; rolling binary replacement in a healthy replica set; retain FCV 7.0 series, all members FCV 7.0 Rehearse documented 7.0 → 8.0 procedure; secondaries first; FCV last 6.0 or older Sequential major upgrades to 7.0 first; review each intermediate version’s own procedure Standalone Backup, write outage, clean shutdown, replace/start/validate; no rolling HA Sharded cluster Config servers, shard replica sets, then routers; coordinated FCV through mongos Do not skip majors by pointing a new executable at an old dbPath. Do not interpret “FCV still 7.0” as permission for arbitrary binary downgrade: MongoDB’s 8.0 documentation states binary downgrade needs support assistance; Community binary downgrades are not supported. The independent recovery plan is a rehearsed pre-upgrade backup restore or compatible logical/application migration, with an explicit post-upgrade-write loss/reconciliation decision.[25][27][56] Use the administrative identity and connect to each member directly for node-local inspection, preserving TLS/auth. Record effective config, exact packages, drivers, operating system, FCV, replica configuration and backup recovery credentials.[27][29] const admin = db.getSiblingDB("admin"); admin.runCommand({buildInfo: 1}); admin.runCommand({getParameter: 1, featureCompatibilityVersion: 1}); admin.runCommand({replSetGetStatus: 1}); Before a 7.0 → 8.0 upgrade: Bring all members to the required 7.0-series baseline and FCV 7.0; verify none are in ROLLBACK/RECOVERING or doing initial sync. Restore a recent backup into staging, exercise the exact upgrade and application workload, and measure startup/recovery/index behavior. Review driver compatibility, removed options/commands, query changes and feature compatibility. 8.0 deprecates server-side JavaScript features; do not conceal warnings by dropping code paths untested. Inspect invalid non-time-series system.buckets collections as the official guide requires. Preserve data before any rename/drop; do not paste a wildcard removal command. Confirm majority remains while each member is unavailable, disk/cache/connection headroom, an oplog window longer than maintenance, and working backups. Retain old artifacts/config for forensic/recovery use, but do not promise they can simply reopen upgraded files.[27][29][31] On RHEL record rpm -q for server/router/shell/Tools, the installed SELinux policy revision and local fcontext/port mappings, systemctl cat/show including drop-ins and /etc/sysconfig/mongod, filesystem mounts and both firewalld configurations. Rehearse any OS-major migration separately; swapping an el8 RPM onto an el9 machine is not an OS migration procedure. Recheck current RHEL kernel/glibc errata and MongoDB advisories.[100][101][104] Application acceptance should include authentication, representative queries/plans, transactions/retries, change stream consumers where used, backup tooling and operational monitoring. “Server started” is insufficient. Service disruption; potential election. Three healthy data-bearing members are assumed. Use exact approved packages, not an unattended broad dnf upgrade. For a 7.0 → 8.0 migration, configure the 8.0 repository as in installation; leave shell/Tools versions separately controlled.[27][104] Pick a secondary; verify its role immediately before stopping. Stop only its mongod service. Delete only the server component’s version lock, install the exact target NEVRA, verify/relock it, then restart. Do not clear the whole lock list. A router package is upgraded on router hosts, not used as evidence that a data member changed. Wait until it is healthy SECONDARY, caught up and error-free; check the actual server version. Abort the rollout if it cannot rejoin. Repeat for the next secondary, never taking down a voting majority together. On the current primary, step down without forcing. Wait until another upgraded member is PRIMARY; only then stop/upgrade/restart the old primary.[27] # On the chosen stopped member only; package versions must already be available. sudo systemctl stop mongod sudo dnf versionlock delete mongodb-org-server sudo dnf install mongodb-org-server-8.0.29-1.el9.x86_64 rpm -q mongodb-org-server sudo dnf versionlock add mongodb-org-server sudo dnf versionlock list sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo restorecon -v /usr/bin/mongod /usr/lib/systemd/system/mongod.service /etc/mongod.conf sudo systemctl start mongod sudo journalctl -u mongod -n 100 --no-pager // Primary maintenance action, cluster administration privilege rs.stepDown(60); // Reconnect through the set URI, then inspect: rs.status(); If package installation fails, do not continue the sequence or relock an assumed version: inspect rpm -q/DNF transaction state and keep the node stopped until resolved. Retain /etc/mongod.conf and review any .rpmnew/.rpmsave, unit and environment changes rather than overwriting security settings. Recheck mongod_t, labels, effective service limits and AVCs after the upgrade; rpm -V differences on an intentionally changed config require review, not blind reset.[100][101][110] Connection interruption can be expected during stepdown. No eligible caught-up secondary or failure to elect is a stop condition, not a reason to add force: true. Repair health while preserving majority; application drivers must tolerate the election and resolve uncertain write outcomes.[27][30] For an 8.0 patch update, follow the same healthy-member discipline but do not change FCV merely because the patch number changed. Observe release-specific instructions/advisories before treating that as universally sufficient.[4][28] Inventory every config-server member, every shard member and every mongos. Confirm the whole cluster is at 7.0/FCV 7.0 before a major upgrade, and have a coordinated backup including config metadata. Direct shard checks require authorized shard-local maintenance identities; cluster users on mongos are not automatically shard-local users.[25] On mongos, save balancer state, call sh.stopBalancer(), and verify it stopped with no migration still running. Upgrade the config-server replica set secondary-by-secondary, then step down/upgrade its primary; wait for complete health. Upgrade each shard replica set, secondaries then stepped-down primary. Verify health before moving on. Upgrade/restart mongos routers individually, maintaining available client entry points. On each stopped router use the same DNF lock/delete/install/relock discipline for mongodb-org-mongos-8.0.29-1.el9.x86_64 and verify mongos --version.
