title: Storage engines, transactions and InnoDB
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MySQL
text: Engine Use and limits NDB / NDBCLUSTER Distributed, highly available storage engine in the separate MySQL NDB Cluster product; not InnoDB Group Replication. MEMORY RAM-resident table data; definitions persist but rows do not survive a server restart. Not all optimizer temporary tables use this engine. CSV Stores table rows in CSV files; no indexes, with CSV-specific constraints. Useful for bounded interchange, not a transactional replacement. BLACKHOLE Discards written data; specialized replication/logging experiments need binlog-format analysis. ARCHIVE Compressed archival storage with restricted operations/index support; not a backup format. MyISAM Nontransactional engine with table-level locking. Some workloads may favor it; “smaller and faster” is not a general rule. Prefer InnoDB when transactions, foreign keys and crash recovery are required. [16] ACID property InnoDB MyISAM Atomicity Transaction rollback uses undo; application must handle statement errors, deadlocks and rollback scope. DDL commonly causes implicit commits. No transactional rollback. Consistency Enforces supported constraints including foreign keys; application/business invariants remain the application’s responsibility. Supports some constraints such as unique indexes, but not InnoDB-style foreign keys. Isolation MVCC plus record/gap locks and selectable isolation levels. Table-level locking coordinates statements but does not provide multi-statement transactional isolation. Durability Redo, recovery, doublewrite and correctly configured flushing/storage. Not independent of settings or hardware. No transactional crash recovery; table repair is not committed-transaction recovery. InnoDB is the default engine in 8.4 (historically the default since 5.5). Official architecture diagram is linked rather than republished. [11][13][14][16] The buffer pool, log buffer and internal structures use RAM; some cached structures have durable on-disk backing.MySQL 8.4 · memory / persistencePages and logs do different jobsRedo recordsLog buffer · RAMRecords changes; it is not a list of dirty pages.→ write / flushRedo log · storageSupports crash recovery. Write-ahead logging makes the required redo durable before the corresponding data-page write.Data & index pagesBuffer pool · RAMHolds clean and dirty pages. Reads can fetch pages into the pool; updates dirty cached pages.→ page flushingDoublewrite → tablespacesWith normal doublewrite protection, page images go through doublewrite files before their final locations. This protects against torn page writes.Undo has another role. Undo records support rollback and older visible versions for consistent reads. Persistent undo tablespaces are separate from redo; long snapshots can delay purge.The binary log is separate. It belongs to the MySQL server, not the InnoDB buffer pool. It supports replication and point-in-time recovery; redo is not a substitute.This is not a commit timeline. Commit durability and page flushing are different events; committing does not require every changed page to be written to its final location. Redo/binlog flush settings and storage that must honor flush requests matter. Group commit and background work are not shown.The existing LRU drawing below explains the old/new page policy. Flushing is not eviction. Optional change buffering and the adaptive hash index are omitted here; both are disabled by default in 8.4.Teaching simplification: two persistence paths and their purposes, not an exact engine schematic or a promise of fixed I/O ordering across all transactions. This is InnoDB, not a shared PostgreSQL/MongoDB storage model.Read the sources Buffer pool [7] · Redo [10] · Doublewrite [11] · Versions and undo [13] · Undo tablespaces [131] · Durability settings [21] · 8.4 defaults [90]External reference, not republished: Official InnoDB architecture image Buffer pool Caches clean and dirty table/index pages. Default configuration starts small (128 MiB); size to the measured working set and total memory budget, including connections, other engines and the OS. “80% of RAM” is not universal, especially on shared or container-limited hosts. The LRU diagram below shows the usual old/new midpoint policy. The old portion defaults to 3/8; flushing dirty pages and evicting pages are different operations. [7][21][129] +-----------------------------+ | InnoDB LRU List | +-----------------------------+ | | | Young (New) Sublist (5/8) | | +---------------------+ | | | Head |<--+-- Most recently accessed page | | Most accessed pages | | | | ... | | | | Tail | | | +---------------------+ | | | | Old Sublist (3/8) | | +---------------------+ | | | Head |<--+-- Newly loaded page | | Less accessed pages | | | | ... | | | | Tail |<--+-- Candidate for eviction; dirty pages must be flushed safely | +---------------------+ | +-----------------------------+ [7] Change buffer Buffers eligible changes to secondary-index pages absent from the buffer pool, then merges them when needed or in the background. It has in-memory and persistent parts. In 8.4 innodb_change_buffering=none by default. When enabled, innodb_change_buffer_max_size defaults to 25% of the pool, with maximum 50%; this is a limit, not a permanent reservation. Adaptive hash index Built by InnoDB from hot B-tree search patterns when enabled. It points to buffered index pages and can speed suitable lookups, but can also add contention. Disabled by default in 8.4. Benchmark before enabling; it is not a user-created secondary index or optimizer hint. Log buffer Holds redo records describing changes, not a catalog of dirty pages. Writes/flushes are affected by commits, capacity and periodic flushing. innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 and sync_binlog=1 are the usual strongest server settings for durable InnoDB/binlog commits; storage must honor flushes. [8][9][10][21][129][90] Redo Logs Write-ahead logging Persistent log of changes, before applied to on-disk pages Changes can be reapplied to data pages if system crashes before/during writing Durability depends on redo/binlog flush settings and storage guarantees; committed data can be lost with relaxed settings or faulty storage. [10][21] Temporary redo logs (#ib_redoXXX_tmp) - internal, pre-created spare files to handle log resizing and rotation Tablespaces System tablespace (ibdata1): stores the change buffer and may hold table/index data when not using file-per-table or general tablespaces. The 8.4 dictionary lives in mysql.ibd; default undo and doublewrite storage are separate. Old diagrams putting all of them in ibdata1 describe historical layouts. General tablespace (.ibd): shared InnoDB container for multiple tables. Moving/dropping tables does not automatically shrink the file. File-per-table (.ibd): one table’s data/index storage (or separate files for partitions). Availability of transportable tablespaces depends on table features and import restrictions. Session temporary tablespaces (#innodb_temp/*.ibt): a pool starts with ten files. A session can receive two: one for user temporary tables and one for internal on-disk temporary tables. They are truncated/reused on release. Inspect INNODB_SESSION_TEMP_TABLESPACES; not all internal temp work reaches disk. Global temporary tablespace (ibtmp1): remains supported in 8.4, not deprecated simply because session files exist. Stores rollback segments for user-created temporary tables. Default is auto-extending, initially slightly over 12 MiB. innodb_temp_data_file_path, for example ibtmp1:12M:autoextend:max:1G, bounds growth but can cause statements to fail at the limit. It is recreated on restart. Never delete it while the server is running; a normal controlled restart reclaims it without a manual deletion recipe. Undo tablespaces: hold undo records for transaction rollback and consistent reads. They are not a network-delivery rollback mechanism. Long-running snapshots can delay purge and grow undo storage. Doublewrite files: protect against torn page writes; normally separate .dblwr f

title: Glossary
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MySQL · Storage engines, transactions and InnoDB
text: InnoDB data changes run in transactions. With the usual autocommit=1, each statement forms its own transaction unless an explicit transaction is active. Use START TRANSACTION for a deliberate multi-statement unit; many DDL statements implicitly commit. [140] The default isolation level is REPEATABLE READ. A normal consistent read establishes a read view at the first consistent read in a transaction (or use WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT where applicable). Later consistent reads reuse it. READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot for each consistent read. The read view tracks transaction visibility boundaries and active transaction IDs. Later transactions do not become visible merely because they commit. A row’s transaction ID and undo chain allow reconstruction of an older visible version; a transaction sees its own changes. Locking reads (FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE) and DML do not simply reuse the nonlocking snapshot. Their locks and record-selection behavior depend on statement and isolation level. Mixing locking and consistent reads can expose different states. Undo supports both rollback and MVCC; purge removes versions no active read view needs. Term Meaning Page Basic InnoDB storage/buffer unit, 16 KiB by default; configurable at instance initialization. Not the smallest OS write or individual SQL change. Clustered key Explicit primary key; otherwise the first suitable UNIQUE NOT NULL index; otherwise an internal generated row ID. Clustered index One per InnoDB table; leaf records contain the row data ordered by clustered key. Secondary key Indexed columns used for alternate access paths, including columns that may overlap the primary key. Example: searching WHERE name='A'. Secondary index Leaf records contain secondary-key columns plus the clustered key to locate the row. A covering query can avoid the extra clustered lookup. Additional indexes cost storage and write work. [13][14][15]

title: Installing MySQL on Linux
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL
text: These package/service notes target RHEL 9, x86-64, Oracle MySQL Community 8.4 LTS RPMs. They are not Ubuntu/Debian or Windows commands. Enterprise packages require the corresponding entitlement/download source. Before installing, inventory existing MySQL/MariaDB packages, data and services; replacing an existing server is an upgrade/migration, not a fresh install. Obtain the current EL9 repository-configuration RPM from the official MySQL Yum download page linked by the installation manual. Its filename/build and signing key change; do not copy the old EL8 release-RPM URL or import every historical key. Verify the package signature and the signing-key fingerprint through the official download/signature instructions. Keep gpgcheck=1; a missing/expired key is not a reason to disable verification. rpm -K downloaded-package.rpm checks a downloaded RPM against trusted keys; a key imported from an unverified source does not prove authenticity. Install that verified repository package using dnf. Inspect /etc/yum.repos.d/mysql-community.repo and enable the 8.4 LTS server channel, with other server-series channels disabled. Verify the repository’s actual IDs; current guidance names mysql-8.4-lts-community. Inspect the transaction before accepting installation of mysql-community-server. DNF resolves dependencies. EL8’s module-disable step is specific to EL8 and must not be copied unconditionally to EL9. Read-only inventory examples and the install command after those prerequisites: dnf repolist enabled rpm -qa 'mysql*' 'mariadb*' sudo dnf install mysql-community-server Do not add -y until the selected repository, architecture and package transaction have been reviewed. The RPM unit initializes an empty data directory on first start; confirm this is a deliberately new instance and that required storage is mounted. Start/manage it with the vendor systemd unit, then use the initial-password mechanism documented for that package and secure the root account. Do not copy initial passwords into scripts or notes. Download matching 8.4 builds for EL9 from official distribution/archives, verify signatures, and use DNF on the complete selected local package set. Do not force RPM dependencies or mix EL8/EL9, Community/Enterprise or server-series packages. mysql-community-server client and common runtime requirements mysql-community-client mysql-community-libs mysql-community-client-plugins mysql-community-common This is a functional dependency sketch, not a fixed resolver graph: use package metadata for the exact selected build. Optional package/data class Purpose and qualification ICU data Unicode support where the selected package split requires it. Test Test programs/data; not required to run production workloads. Debuginfo Symbols and source locations for diagnosis; normally separated to reduce installed size, not to secure secret internals. Devel Headers/libraries for building against client APIs. Libs-compat Older client ABI compatibility, only where offered and required; not a reason to mix arbitrary packages. A generic tarball contains a prebuilt server/client layout, libraries, documentation and support files, not every host dependency or a guaranteed systemd unit. Match architecture/glibc and required libraries to the selected build. Verify the download, create a dedicated OS account, choose a new empty datadir, initialize with the selected server binary as documented, and secure the generated administrative account. Preserve package-managed installations separately. Supplied SysV examples are not modern systemd integration. Use the configuration chapter for paths and a service decision checklist. Do not place downloaded configuration files directly over /etc/my.cnf. The production baseline is RHEL 9 x86_64 with Oracle MySQL Community 8.4 LTS RPMs from Oracle’s MySQL Yum repository. Use a maintained RHEL 9 minor release and an approved current 8.4 maintenance build. Oracle’s platform matrix includes this OS/architecture. This is not a claim that a RHEL subscription supports Oracle’s independently supplied database RPMs; confirm the required vendor support entitlement separately. RHEL also supplies MySQL through AppStream, with its own packaging and lifecycle: Red Hat documents 8.0 as the initial RHEL 9 stream and 8.4 from RHEL 9.6. Its mysql-server / dnf module install mysql:8.4/server route is an alternative, not a prerequisite to the selected mysql-community-server route. Both use a mysqld service name, which does not make their helper scripts, multiple-instance support or upgrade procedures interchangeable. Do not mix Red Hat and Oracle server packages or run AppStream module switching against this Oracle-RPM installation. Red Hat documents containers for its multiple-instance route; the named vendor template in these notes is the Oracle-RPM route. Before approving a host, record /etc/redhat-release, uname -m, the enabled repository IDs, full installed package versions/vendor, and the installed unit/config file list. Resolve existing MariaDB/MySQL packages or enabled competing streams as a migration decision; do not force replacement or erase their data. Download the EL9 repository RPM and corresponding current public signing key through Oracle’s official HTTPS download/signature pages. title: Choose one installation method
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Installing MySQL on Linux
text: These package/service notes target RHEL 9, x86-64, Oracle MySQL Community 8.4 LTS RPMs. They are not Ubuntu/Debian or Windows commands. Enterprise packages require the corresponding entitlement/download source. Before installing, inventory existing MySQL/MariaDB packages, data and services; replacing an existing server is an upgrade/migration, not a fresh install.

title: Repository installation and GPG trust
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Installing MySQL on Linux
text: Obtain the current EL9 repository-configuration RPM from the official MySQL Yum download page linked by the installation manual. Its filename/build and signing key change; do not copy the old EL8 release-RPM URL or import every historical key. Verify the package signature and the signing-key fingerprint through the official download/signature instructions. Keep gpgcheck=1; a missing/expired key is not a reason to disable verification. rpm -K downloaded-package.rpm checks a downloaded RPM against trusted keys; a key imported from an unverified source does not prove authenticity. Install that verified repository package using dnf. Inspect /etc/yum.repos.d/mysql-community.repo and enable the 8.4 LTS server channel, with other server-series channels disabled. Verify the repository’s actual IDs; current guidance names mysql-8.4-lts-community. Inspect the transaction before accepting installation of mysql-community-server. DNF resolves dependencies. EL8’s module-disable step is specific to EL8 and must not be copied unconditionally to EL9. Read-only inventory examples and the install command after those prerequisites: dnf repolist enabled rpm -qa 'mysql*' 'mariadb*' sudo dnf install mysql-community-server Do not add -y until the selected repository, architecture and package transaction have been reviewed. The RPM unit initializes an empty data directory on first start; confirm this is a deliberately new instance and that required storage is mounted. Start/manage it with the vendor systemd unit, then use the initial-password mechanism documented for that package and secure the root account. Do not copy initial passwords into scripts or notes.

title: Local RPM packages
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Installing MySQL on Linux
text: Download matching 8.4 builds for EL9 from official distribution/archives, verify signatures, and use DNF on the complete selected local package set. title: Generic Linux archive
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Installing MySQL on Linux
text: A generic tarball contains a prebuilt server/client layout, libraries, documentation and support files, not every host dependency or a guaranteed systemd unit. Match architecture/glibc and required libraries to the selected build. Verify the download, create a dedicated OS account, choose a new empty datadir, initialize with the selected server binary as documented, and secure the generated administrative account. Preserve package-managed installations separately. Supplied SysV examples are not modern systemd integration. Use the configuration chapter for paths and a service decision checklist. Do not place downloaded configuration files directly over /etc/my.cnf.

title: RHEL package origin and support contract
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Installing MySQL on Linux
text: The production baseline is RHEL 9 x86_64 with Oracle MySQL Community 8.4 LTS RPMs from Oracle’s MySQL Yum repository. Use a maintained RHEL 9 minor release and an approved current 8.4 maintenance build. Oracle’s platform matrix includes this OS/architecture. This is not a claim that a RHEL subscription supports Oracle’s independently supplied database RPMs; confirm the required vendor support entitlement separately. RHEL also supplies MySQL through AppStream, with its own packaging and lifecycle: Red Hat documents 8.0 as the initial RHEL 9 stream and 8.4 from RHEL 9.6. Its mysql-server / dnf module install mysql:8.4/server route is an alternative, not a prerequisite to the selected mysql-community-server route. Both use a mysqld service name, which does not make their helper scripts, multiple-instance support or upgrade procedures interchangeable. Do not mix Red Hat and Oracle server packages or run AppStream module switching against this Oracle-RPM installation. Red Hat documents containers for its multiple-instance route; the named vendor template in these notes is the Oracle-RPM route. Before approving a host, record /etc/redhat-release, uname -m, the enabled repository IDs, full installed package versions/vendor, and the installed unit/config file list. title: Migrating MySQL to Oracle
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MySQL
text: Source target: MySQL 8.4 LTS. Migration-workflow reference: Oracle SQL Developer 24.3, targeting an independently patched/supported Oracle Database 19c installation with the chosen PDB/service, character set and licensing approved by its DBA. This is a migration to Oracle, not PostgreSQL or MongoDB. The 24.3 migration guide still names old Connector/J releases in its MySQL preparation section. That is not evidence that those drivers support MySQL 8.4 authentication/TLS, nor proof of a certified end-to-end 8.4 migration path. Before using the wizard, validate the exact SQL Developer/JDK/Connector-J/server tuple against vendor compatibility guidance and a representative disposable rehearsal. If that tuple is not supported/working, choose a supported export/transform/load path with equivalent validation; do not downgrade authentication or install an obsolete driver just to match an old screenshot. Back up both systems and rehearse recovery. Inventory schemas, row counts, keys, types/collations, routines/triggers/events, views, definers, privileges, dependencies and application SQL. Establish outage/CDC requirements and an agreed reconciliation plan. Obtain a Connector/J release compatible with the actual MySQL 8.4/JDK/security requirements from Oracle’s official Connector/J distribution. Check its license and support terms. In SQL Developer, add its JAR through Tools → Preferences → Database → Third Party JDBC Drivers and restart if required. Do not mix unrelated drivers in the same classpath. Create/test the MySQL source connection with metadata/data access needed for capture, not a root account. Verify TLS identity and character/timezone handling. An account that cannot see routine definitions cannot migrate them merely because it can execute the routine. Create/test the Oracle connection to the intended PDB/service, not accidentally the root container or SYSTEM schema. Keep repository, deployment operator and application-owner responsibilities separate. The repository is an Oracle schema storing captured and converted models. The wizard repository connection must be Oracle, not the MySQL source. SQL Developer manages repository association; if no repository exists, create/provision and associate one before the wizard. Right-click the Oracle repository connection → Migration Repository → Associate Migration Repository. Do not reuse the old GRANT ... IDENTIFIED BY account-creation syntax or grant unlimited quota on SYSTEM. Oracle 19c creates an account with CREATE USER, then grants authorized privileges separately. Use a dedicated approved non-SYSTEM permanent tablespace, appropriate temporary tablespace and bounded quota sized for the captured metadata/data needs. A DBA supplies the credential securely; no literal password is included here. Identity Minimum-scope decision MySQL capture account Read only the chosen schemas/metadata, including routine/view definitions as needed; no blanket replication/admin privileges merely for capture. Oracle repository owner The SQL Developer guide specifies RESOURCE plus CREATE SESSION, CREATE VIEW and CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW for its repository, with extra admin privileges for multischema workflows. Review what RESOURCE grants on the actual 19c installation; do not infer a universally minimal custom grant list from its name. Grant only the documented features used, with bounded tablespace quota. Oracle DDL deployment operator Generated cross-schema DDL can require powerful ANY/admin privileges listed by SQL Developer. Do not grant this entire set to the persistent repository/application account by default. Have a DBA review/split the generated script and deploy under controlled temporary authority or schema-owner sessions where possible; audit and revoke temporary grants afterward. Oracle application owner/runtime Own only intended target objects; runtime account receives only needed object privileges, not RESOURCE/DBA or ANY privileges as a shortcut. The official migration guide’s broad deployment privilege list is a tooling requirement for certain automated cross-schema operations, not a least-privilege production role. If unattended wizard deployment cannot fit the site’s authorization model, export the generated DDL and use the reviewed deployment path instead. Never migrate as SYS. Keep the repository after cutover only as long as needed and protect it as sensitive metadata. Open Tools → Migration → Migrate after compatibility and accounts are validated. Wizard stage What to supply/check Repository The Oracle repository connection. Do not select MySQL here; review any truncate/clear-existing-project choice because it deletes repository history. Project Explicit project name/output directory; protect generated scripts and avoid overwriting another migration. Source database Online MySQL connection, or a supported offline capture path. Capture privileges determine what is visible. Capture Select the exact databases/objects; compare captured inventory to the source. Missing definitions are not successful exclusions. Convert Review every mapping and conversion warning. Do not accept defaults without evaluating semantics. Target database Intended Oracle PDB/service/schema and reviewed DDL deployment identity. Inspect generated CREATE/ALTER/DROP statements before execution. Move data Choose online transfer for an appropriate bounded workload or supported offline unload/load. Ensure source consistency and define the cutover/delta boundary. Summary Review logs, rejected records, object failures and incomplete conversions; “Finish” is not acceptance. MySQL feature/data Oracle review TINYINT, INT, unsigned ranges Often map to NUMBER with chosen precision/scale; preserve full signed/unsigned range and application boolean conventions, not just the type name. AUTO_INCREMENT Review identity/sequence generation and next-value synchronization, including explicit existing IDs and concurrent writers. Character data/collation Character sets, case/accent comparison, length semantics and index limits can change query/uniqueness behavior. Empty strings and NULL Oracle character semantics differ; test sentinel values and constraints explicitly. Dates/timestamps Check zero/invalid dates, range, fractional seconds, timezone conversion and defaults. JSON, ENUM/SET, binary/LOBs Choose a supported 19c representation and transformations; do not assume a textual CAST preserves semantics or indexes. Routines, triggers, events MySQL procedural SQL is not PL/SQL; manually review transactional behavior, exceptions, delimiters, definers and scheduling equivalents. Indexes/defaults/constraints Names and syntax can change; preserve meaning and dependencies. Test foreign keys, unique constraints and generated/default expressions. title: Scope and compatibility gate
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MySQL · Migrating MySQL to Oracle
text: Source target: MySQL 8.4 LTS. Migration-workflow reference: Oracle SQL Developer 24.3, targeting an independently patched/supported Oracle Database 19c installation with the chosen PDB/service, character set and licensing approved by its DBA. This is a migration to Oracle, not PostgreSQL or MongoDB. The 24.3 migration guide still names old Connector/J releases in its MySQL preparation section. That is not evidence that those drivers support MySQL 8.4 authentication/TLS, nor proof of a certified end-to-end 8.4 migration path. Before using the wizard, validate the exact SQL Developer/JDK/Connector-J/server tuple against vendor compatibility guidance and a representative disposable rehearsal. If that tuple is not supported/working, choose a supported export/transform/load path with equivalent validation; do not downgrade authentication or install an obsolete driver just to match an old screenshot.

title: Prepare and connect
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MySQL · Migrating MySQL to Oracle
text: Back up both systems and rehearse recovery. Inventory schemas, row counts, keys, types/collations, routines/triggers/events, views, definers, privileges, dependencies and application SQL. Establish outage/CDC requirements and an agreed reconciliation plan. Obtain a Connector/J release compatible with the actual MySQL 8.4/JDK/security requirements from Oracle’s official Connector/J distribution. Check its license and support terms. In SQL Developer, add its JAR through Tools → Preferences → Database → Third Party JDBC Drivers and restart if required. Do not mix unrelated drivers in the same classpath. Create/test the MySQL source connection with metadata/data access needed for capture, not a root account. Verify TLS identity and character/timezone handling. An account that cannot see routine definitions cannot migrate them merely because it can execute the routine. Create/test the Oracle connection to the intended PDB/service, not accidentally the root container or SYSTEM schema. Keep repository, deployment operator and application-owner responsibilities separate.

title: Migration repository and least privilege
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MySQL · Migrating MySQL to Oracle
text: The repository is an Oracle schema storing captured and converted models. The wizard repository connection must be Oracle, not the MySQL source. SQL Developer manages repository association; if no repository exists, create/provision and associate one before the wizard. Right-click the Oracle repository connection → Migration Repository → Associate Migration Repository. Do not reuse the old GRANT ... IDENTIFIED BY account-creation syntax or grant unlimited quota on SYSTEM. Oracle 19c creates an account with CREATE USER, then grants authorized privileges separately. Use a dedicated approved non-SYSTEM permanent tablespace, appropriate temporary tablespace and bounded quota sized for the captured metadata/data needs. A DBA supplies the credential securely; no literal password is included here. Identity Minimum-scope decision MySQL capture account Read only the chosen schemas/metadata, including routine/view definitions as needed; no blanket replication/admin privileges merely for capture. Oracle repository owner The SQL Developer guide specifies RESOURCE plus CREATE SESSION, CREATE VIEW and CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW for its repository, with extra admin privileges for multischema workflows. Review what RESOURCE grants on the actual 19c installation; do not infer a universally minimal custom grant list from its name. Grant only the documented features used, with bounded tablespace quota. Oracle DDL deployment operator Generated cross-schema DDL can require powerful ANY/admin privileges listed by SQL Developer. Do not grant this entire set to the persistent repository/application account by default. Have a DBA review/split the generated script and deploy under controlled temporary authority or schema-owner sessions where possible; audit and revoke temporary grants afterward. Oracle application owner/runtime Own only intended target objects; runtime account receives only needed object privileges, not RESOURCE/DBA or ANY privileges as a shortcut. The official migration guide’s broad deployment privilege list is a tooling requirement for certain automated cross-schema operations, not a least-privilege production role. If unattended wizard deployment cannot fit the site’s authorization model, export the generated DDL and use the reviewed deployment path instead. Never migrate as SYS. Keep the repository after cutover only as long as needed and protect it as sensitive metadata.

context: Databases · Store data and handle change · MySQL
text: Use a database name you are authorized to inspect. Definition visibility depends on privileges; SHOW output can expose definer accounts and routine source. Object List objects Show definition Procedure SHOW PROCEDURE STATUS WHERE Db='app'; SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE app.procedure_name\G Function SHOW FUNCTION STATUS WHERE Db='app'; SHOW CREATE FUNCTION app.function_name\G View SHOW FULL TABLES IN app WHERE Table_type='VIEW'; SHOW CREATE VIEW app.view_name\G Trigger SHOW TRIGGERS FROM app; SHOW CREATE TRIGGER app.trigger_name\G; Information Schema exposes ACTION_STATEMENT too. Event SHOW EVENTS FROM app; SHOW CREATE EVENT app.event_name\G Names ending _name above are identifiers to substitute, not objects this chapter creates. In the interactive mysql client, status or \s reports connection details and selected server status such as uptime, threads, open tables, slow queries and average query rate. It is a client command, not SQL usable through every connector. mysqladmin --user=operator --password status provides related server counters; processlist --sleep=2 polls sessions rather than status counters. SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST; SELECT * FROM sys.processlist; These show connection IDs, account/host/database, command, elapsed state time and current state/query. Visibility into other users’ sessions requires additional privilege. The INFORMATION_SCHEMA.PROCESSLIST implementation is deprecated in 8.4; prefer the Performance Schema-based interfaces. KILL QUERY connection_id cancels a statement; KILL CONNECTION connection_id terminates the connection. connection_id is a MySQL connection/thread identifier, not an OS PID. Confirm the current owner/query before acting because IDs can be reused. Cancellation can trigger expensive rollback; do not repeatedly kill a recovering operation. Account privileges govern which sessions you may kill. [23][24][35][36][42][89][136]  Source setting/operation Correct 8.4 interpretation innodb_data_file_path=ibdata1:10M:autoextend:max:512M Startup system-tablespace layout example, not a live resize or shrink command. Do not apply a different initial size over an existing file. A small maximum can stop writes. Plan initialization/growth against actual files and backup/restore requirements. innodb_autoextend_increment=64 Growth increment in MiB for the auto-extending system tablespace; not a universal size for every .ibd. CREATE TABLESPACE ... INITIAL_SIZE=100M INITIAL_SIZE belongs to NDB syntax, not an InnoDB initial-allocation option. For InnoDB general tablespaces, AUTOEXTEND_SIZE controls extension increments (multiple of 4 MiB), not an arbitrary initial file size. ALTER TABLE table_name AUTO_INCREMENT=value is a schematic DDL operation: choose a permitted value above existing generated values. It does not renumber old rows or safely recycle identifiers. Concurrent inserts and engine rules affect the next value. The examples in this section are independent of the later data generator. First select a deliberately created empty scratch schema with USE your_scratch_schema; (replace that identifier); app elsewhere means an existing application schema, not this fixture. A complete temporary-table example: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE customers ( customer_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL ) ENGINE=InnoDB; The table is session-local and disappears when that session ends. A same-named permanent table can be hidden in that session; explicitly identify scratch objects and do not assume temporary-table DDL follows ordinary rollback semantics. The following creates new objects and requires a scratch schema, suitable privileges, an unused datafile name and disk space: CREATE TABLESPACE ts ADD DATAFILE 'ts.ibd' ENGINE=InnoDB; CREATE TABLE t1 ( id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50) ) TABLESPACE ts ENGINE=InnoDB; A relative datafile location is resolved under the applicable datadir rules. Do not copy/move the file manually while the server owns it. Dropping a table does not return a general tablespace’s allocated file size to the OS. [21][25][26][129] Back up and rehearse before conversion. ALTER TABLE table_name ENGINE=InnoDB; can rebuild the table, change locking/storage behavior and consume substantial extra space. Check unsupported engine-specific features and dependent code; verify row counts, constraints and application behavior before accepting the conversion. Reverting the engine is not a substitute for a tested backup. The original procedure created successively numbered tables and generated one million SHA-256 values through a recursive CTE. Keep this as a load-generation task, not a production tuning command. A million-row run needs a deliberate resource budget; start with at most 1,000 rows in a disposable schema, never a shared schema named test whose ownership is unknown. The procedure below preserves dynamic table creation, numeric suffix discovery, prepared statements, recursive CTE generation and hash values, but takes a bounded row count. It must run in the interactive mysql client (DELIMITER is not server SQL). The following CREATE DATABASE must succeed for a new scratch_mysql schema (stop if it already exists); do not reuse another exercise’s schema. Use that new empty schema and use a single session; concurrent calls can choose the same table number. The procedure deliberately leaves its created table for inspection. DDL is not rolled back if later insertion fails. CREATE DATABASE scratch_mysql; DELIMITER $$ CREATE PROCEDURE scratch_mysql.create_dummy_data(IN row_limit INT) BEGIN DECLARE n INT; IF row_limit IS NULL OR row_limit < 1 OR row_limit > 1000 THEN SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT='row_limit must be 1..1000'; END IF; IF @@session.cte_max_recursion_depth < row_limit THEN SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT='session recursion limit is too small'; END IF; SELECT COALESCE(MAX(CAST(SUBSTRING(table_name,2) AS UNSIGNED)),0)+1 INTO n FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='scratch_mysql' AND table_name REGEXP '^t[0-9]+$'; SET @dummy_table=CONCAT('scratch_mysql.t',n); SET @dummy_sql=CONCAT('CREATE TABLE ',@dummy_table, ' (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, hash CHAR(64)) ENGINE=InnoDB'); PREPARE dummy_stmt FROM @dummy_sql; EXECUTE dummy_stmt; DEALLOCATE PREPARE dummy_stmt; SET @dummy_sql=CONCAT('INSERT INTO ',@dummy_table,' (hash) ', 'WITH RECURSIVE cte(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM cte WHERE n<', row_limit,') SELECT SHA2(n,256) FROM cte'); PREPARE dummy_stmt FROM @dummy_sql; EXECUTE dummy_stmt; DEALLOCATE PREPARE dummy_stmt; END$$ DELIMITER ; CALL scratch_mysql.create_dummy_data(100); Inspect the created table’s count and hashes and the actual resource use; no expected output is fabricated here. For a larger load, deliberately revise/test a generator in a disposable instance, choose batches or an appropriate nonrecursive data-generation method, and budget redo/binlog/disk/replication load. Do not just set cte_max_recursion_depth=1000000 in an unrelated session. Remove only the confirmed disposable objects when finished. [26][27]

title: Database vocabulary, editions and tools
context: Databases · Understand the moving parts · MySQL
text: MySQL is an RDBMS. In MySQL, database and schema are synonyms for a namespace of tables and other objects. A table definition describes columns, types, indexes and constraints; a schema can also contain views, routines, triggers and events. Foreign keys express relationships where the storage engine supports them. Community and Enterprise are distributions/licensing offerings, not simply the same server with a fixed extra-utility list. Check the purchased edition and component package before planning a feature. Original category Availability and purpose in the 8.4 family mysqlbackup MySQL Enterprise Backup, separately versioned commercial physical-backup product. mysqlmonitoragent, Enterprise Monitor Commercial monitoring product/agent, not a core mysqld executable; deployment and lifecycle are separate. MySQL Router Available with Community as well as commercial offerings; routes client connections and is not an Enterprise-only backup tool. Audit, Firewall, Thread Pool Enterprise features; they are not automatically installed or enabled merely because the server starts. PAM and LDAP authentication Enterprise authentication integrations; depend on platform, plugin and identity-service configuration. Keyring A framework with different implementations: component_keyring_file is available in Community; encrypted-file and external key-management choices have edition-specific availability. Loading a keyring does not encrypt tables. Connectors Separately versioned drivers with their own compatibility/support and licensing terms; “Advanced Connectors” is not a universal server feature switch. Choose a supported 8.4 LTS maintenance release rather than assuming the first 8.4.0 build is the deployment target. The official release policy gives LTS a stable feature set and five years of Premier plus three years of Extended Support; entitlement terms and platform support still apply. [1][72][84][93][155]

title: Execution plans, indexes and diagnostics
context: Databases · See what the server is doing · MySQL
text: Substitute an existing table/condition/index in the schematic statements below. On production, ANALYZE TABLE can affect plans and acquire locks; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and can be expensive. Rehearse with a bounded SELECT on representative test data before applying changes. ANALYZE TABLE your_table; EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON SELECT * FROM your_table WHERE your_condition; EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM your_table WHERE your_condition; Estimated costs/rows are not elapsed runtime. EXPLAIN ANALYZE provides actual timings/rows/loops in TREE format in this target, not an assurance that every supported EXPLAIN form can be executed safely. For a single-session optimizer trace, save the prior settings and read the trace immediately after the statement: SET @old_trace = @@session.optimizer_trace; SET SESSION optimizer_trace='enabled=on'; SELECT * FROM your_table WHERE your_condition; SELECT TRACE FROM information_schema.OPTIMIZER_TRACE\G SET SESSION optimizer_trace=@old_trace; Trace output can contain sensitive SQL. Statement execution and trace collection add work. Operation Schematic SQL and interpretation Suggest eligible indexes SELECT * FROM your_table USE INDEX (idx_name) WHERE your_condition; restricts considered named indexes but does not force their use; a table scan remains possible. Stronger index hint FORCE INDEX (idx_name) changes scan cost treatment; measure rather than assume it improves the query. Index hints can become stale as data changes. Disable index merge in this session Save @@session.optimizer_switch, then SET SESSION optimizer_switch='index_merge=off';. Restore the saved string after the comparison. Reset defaults SET SESSION optimizer_switch='default'; resets defaults, not necessarily the session’s original custom settings. Inspect switches SHOW SESSION VARIABLES LIKE 'optimizer_switch'; List indexes SHOW INDEX FROM your_table; Add candidate covering index CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON your_table(col1, col2, col3); only covers queries whose needed columns fit; column order matters for predicates/order/grouping. Remove an index DROP INDEX idx_name ON your_table; only after checking constraints and workload dependence; plan DDL resource/lock costs and a recreation path. Compare plans, latency distribution, rows examined, write overhead and storage before/after. A full scan is not automatically a missing-index defect; it can be cheapest for small tables or broad predicates. [32][34][94] These are diagnostic views, not independent copies of application data. Their results depend on enabled instrumentation and collection/reset history. View Meaning and caution sys.user_summary User-level statement, I/O and connection aggregates. sys.user_summary_by_file_io File I/O operations and latency by user. sys.innodb_buffer_stats_by_table Buffer-page information grouped by schema/table. Querying this view can itself harm production performance; reproduce on a test instance unless its cost has been explicitly accepted. sys.schema_tables_with_full_table_scans Reports table-access statistics with full scans; a scan is not automatically an indexing defect. sys.processlist Detailed current session/process information, based on Performance Schema. [132][133][134][135][136] Table Description | information_schema.tables | Table/database/engine metadata. InnoDB TABLE_ROWS is an estimate; counts, timestamps and sizes have engine-specific meaning. | | information_schema.table_privileges | Table-level privileges visible to the current account; does not alone enumerate global/schema/role-derived effective access. Combine with SHOW GRANTS and role review. | [36][39][40]

For a single-session optimizer trace, save the prior settings and read the trace immediately after the statement: SET @old_trace = @@session.optimizer_trace; SET SESSION optimizer_trace='enabled=on'; SELECT * FROM your_table WHERE your_condition; SELECT TRACE FROM information_schema.OPTIMIZER_TRACE\G SET SESSION optimizer_trace=@old_trace; Trace output can contain sensitive SQL. Statement execution and trace collection add work. Operation Schematic SQL and interpretation Suggest eligible indexes SELECT * FROM your_table USE INDEX (idx_name) WHERE your_condition; restricts considered named indexes but does not force their use; a table scan remains possible. Stronger index hint FORCE INDEX (idx_name) changes scan cost treatment; measure rather than assume it improves the query. Index hints can become stale as data changes. Disable index merge in this session Save @@session.optimizer_switch, then SET SESSION optimizer_switch='index_merge=off';. Restore the saved string after the comparison. Reset defaults SET SESSION optimizer_switch='default'; resets defaults, not necessarily the session’s original custom settings. Inspect switches SHOW SESSION VARIABLES LIKE 'optimizer_switch'; List indexes SHOW INDEX FROM your_table; Add candidate covering index CREATE INDEX idx_covering ON your_table(col1, col2, col3); only covers queries whose needed columns fit; column order matters for predicates/order/grouping. Remove an index DROP INDEX idx_name ON your_table; only after checking constraints and workload dependence; plan DDL resource/lock costs and a recreation path. Compare plans, latency distribution, rows examined, write overhead and storage before/after. A full scan is not automatically a missing-index defect; it can be cheapest for small tables or broad predicates. [32][34][94]

title: Source-replica replication and recovery
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MySQL
text: MySQL asynchronous replication transfers binlog events from a source to one or more replicas. Circular/two-source (A↔B) and chained/ring (A→B→C→A) layouts are possible but not automatic conflict resolution or HA. Prefer a single-writer design unless conflict handling, failover/fencing and recovery have been explicitly engineered. Auto-increment offsets only reduce one class of generated-key collision; they do not resolve conflicting updates, deletes or explicit keys.MySQL 8.4 · source / replicaReceived is not the same as appliedSource · intended application writerTransactions & binary logThe source records binlog events for replication. Its local commit durability still depends on configuration and storage.Send binlog eventsA replication connection streams the requested history over the network. The replica needs a matching seed and available source history.Asynchronous: source commits do not wait for a replica to receive or apply the changes.Replica · independently progressingReceiverReceives the source’s binlog events and writes them to the relay log.Relay logQueues received events locally. Received history can be ahead of applied history.Applier → replica dataThe applier reads relay-log events and applies transactions. Parallel workers may be involved; lag and errors must be checked.Semisync acknowledgment goes back from receipt, not from applied data. It reports that the configured number of replicas have received and flushed events to relay log, not that their appliers have committed them. The wait point is configurable; a timeout can fall back to asynchronous operation.GTIDs identify transaction history; they do not compare row contents. Promotion still needs data checks, routing and old-writer fencing. This diagram does not describe Group Replication, PostgreSQL streaming replication or MongoDB replica-set elections.Teaching simplification of one MySQL source and one replica channel, not an exact thread schematic. Network delivery, durable receipt and application are distinct milestones; this topology alone is not automatic failover or zero-data-loss HA.Read the sources Channel configuration [52] · GTID setup [53] · Replica options [56] · Semisync acknowledgment [57] · Failover boundaries [152]External reference, not republished: Earlier replication image Original replication diagram — external reference. Linked only; rights to republish are unverified. Inventory all members and choose unique nonzero server_id values and unique server UUIDs. Binary logging must be enabled; retain enough history to seed and catch up replicas. For 8.4 GTID replication, all participating servers must be in an appropriate compatible GTID state. For a new topology, configure gtid_mode=ON and enforce_gtid_consistency=ON before workload starts. For an existing OFF topology use the coordinated online-transition procedure, not a direct jump or reset. Provision a dedicated source account restricted to the actual replica host(s), with REPLICATION SLAVE and TLS requirements. Use a securely generated/provisioned credential; the source example’s literal secret is not retained as a usable password. Take a consistent seed backup and record its matching GTID set or binlog file/position using the selected backup tool’s documented procedure. Securely transfer/restore it to an isolated replica; preserve data and correct replication metadata. Example account creation, replacing the documentation address with the approved replica host; capture the generated secret securely without session transcript logging: CREATE USER 'replica'@'192.0.2.20' IDENTIFIED BY RANDOM PASSWORD REQUIRE SSL; GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'replica'@'192.0.2.20'; SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS; SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS is the 8.4 statement; older notes use SHOW MASTER STATUS. Neither requires a reset beforehand. Historical RESET MASTER and 8.4 RESET BINARY LOGS AND GTIDS erase history and are not provisioning prerequisites. For intentionally coordinated circular writers, the old auto_increment_increment=2 / offsets 1 and 2 illustrate distinct sequences. Choose values for the actual number of writers, test application assumptions and still implement conflict prevention. Do not enable circular writes merely by uncommenting these settings. [46][52][53][91][152][156] Use unique server_id, a stable relay-log basename and independent datadir/socket paths. For example, relay_log=/var/lib/mysql/relaylog belongs to that instance, not a shared directory. Set read_only=ON and normally super_read_only=ON to deter local writes; the replication applier can still apply events. Privileged operators can alter these settings, so they are not a security boundary by themselves. Use named channels for multi-source designs. Current MySQL stores replication metadata in tables; old master_info_repository/relay_log_info_repository variables are not an 8.4 setup recipe. Do not import MariaDB metadata names into MySQL procedures. After verifying the seed, stop the relevant channel and choose one positioning method: GTID: SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1 requests the transactions missing from the replica’s recorded GTID state. The seed’s data and GTID history must match; never clear history to hide errant transactions. File/position: set SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=0, the backup’s exact SOURCE_LOG_FILE and SOURCE_LOG_POS. Do not invent coordinates or combine them with auto-position. Account for purged logs before starting. The following is a complete statement template for a GTID channel. Replace every site input, including the conspicuous secret placeholder, through your secure provisioning workflow; it is not a runnable universal recipe. Disable client history/transcripts around secrets. Paths are on the replica server, not the machine running the client. STOP REPLICA FOR CHANNEL 'app'; CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_HOST='source.example.com', SOURCE_PORT=3306, SOURCE_USER='replica', SOURCE_PASSWORD='<SUPPLY_SECURELY_AT_DEPLOYMENT>', SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1, SOURCE_SSL=1, SOURCE_SSL_CA='/var/lib/mysql/tls/ca.pem', SOURCE_SSL_VERIFY_SERVER_CERT=1 FOR CHANNEL 'app'; START REPLICA FOR CHANNEL 'app'; SHOW REPLICA STATUS FOR CHANNEL 'app'\G For a new channel, the initial STOP can be omitted if no channel exists; do not suppress an unexpected error without checking identity/state. If the source account requires client certificates, add SOURCE_SSL_CERT and SOURCE_SSL_KEY to that same statement before FOR CHANNEL, with the private key readable only by the required service identity. There is no semicolon between its option lines and no trailing comma before FOR CHANNEL. With verified TLS, GET_SOURCE_PUBLIC_KEY=1 is unnecessary. RSA password-exchange public keys are not TLS certificates or SSH keys. Do not weaken transport verification to cure an authentication error. CHANGE REPLICATION FILTER and option-file filters must be designed for the channel/binlog format and tested with cross-schema/routine behavior. Filtering can create intentional partial replicas that are unsuitable as full failover targets. SOURCE_CONNECTION_AUTO_FAILOVER=1 requires GTID auto-positioning (SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1) and is optional after populating and validating alternative sources with the failover functions. For example, asynchronous_connection_failover_add_source('app','source2.example.com',3306,'',100) adds a source with a priority weight; use the documented delete function to remove stale entries. Inspect performance_schema.replication_asynchronous_connection_failover. Every listed source must serve the same intended history, support the account/TLS policy and retain needed GTIDs. Review SOURCE_RETRY_COUNT and SOURCE_CONNECT_RETRY: their default retry window can delay switching substantially. This changes connection source selection, not application-writer election/fencing. Verify receiver/applier state, error fields and worker status as well as lag, GTID convergence and actual data. Seconds_Behind_Source=0 alone is not proof of consistency. context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MySQL · Source-replica replication and recovery
text: CHANGE REPLICATION FILTER and option-file filters must be designed for the channel/binlog format and tested with cross-schema/routine behavior. Filtering can create intentional partial replicas that are unsuitable as full failover targets. SOURCE_CONNECTION_AUTO_FAILOVER=1 requires GTID auto-positioning (SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1) and is optional after populating and validating alternative sources with the failover functions. RESET REPLICA discards connection/relay state according to its options; ALL also affects stored connection information. Neither is a routine “start clean” step, and neither substitutes for reseeding mismatched data.

title: Planned single-writer switchover acceptance
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MySQL · Source-replica replication and recovery
text: A channel’s source-connection failover does not promote an application writer. For an approved planned GTID switchover between equivalent unfiltered instances, rehearse this sequence with compatible versions, routing and rollback ownership: Fence application writes and scheduled jobs on the old source; set/verify its read-only protections, drain active write transactions, and retain an administrative session. Infrastructure fencing must prevent the old writer returning unexpectedly; SQL read-only flags alone do not supply that guarantee. Record the old source’s final @@GLOBAL.gtid_executed. On the intended candidate, check receiver/applier errors and wait for that exact set with WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET(captured_gtid_set, approved_timeout_seconds). These are explicit SQL inputs supplied from the captured evidence. 0 means the wait succeeded; 1 is timeout; an error is failure. Stop on any failure, errant history or unresolved data discrepancy. A successful GTID wait alone does not compare rows or prove that a prior skipped transaction had its effects applied. After data/application checks and positive old-writer fencing, stop only the candidate’s intended channel, preserve its metadata, deliberately remove candidate read-only restrictions and redirect the approved writer endpoint. Verify one writable primary, new client TLS identity, writes/reads and replica progress. Do not reset binlogs/GTIDs as part of promotion. Repoint/reseed remaining replicas from the new authority only with compatible history and retained logs. Keep the old source fenced until it is reconciled and reintroduced safely. Once the new writer accepts changes, reverting a router entry is not rollback: catch up/reconcile the old instance or use the rehearsed restore path. For unplanned loss, that final old-source boundary may be unavailable. Establish the most complete trusted survivor, quantify any loss against RPO, fence the failed writer and follow the incident runbook; never label a zero-lag counter as proof of zero data loss. Group Replication has separate quorum/outage-recovery rules and must not use this asynchronous promotion sequence blindly. [52][53][56][70][149][152][164][165]

title: Recover from an applier error without hiding divergence
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MySQL · Source-replica replication and recovery
text: Stop the affected channel, record full error/worker status, failing transaction identity and source/replica data. Preserve backup/logs before changing anything. Diagnose the cause: schema mismatch, duplicate/missing row, unauthorized local write, missing source logs, privilege error or storage failure. Correct configuration/permissions only if doing so does not alter transaction meaning. Prefer restoring/reseeding a replica from a consistent source when history or data cannot be proved equivalent. Do not reset GTIDs to make the error disappear. Only after explicit reconciliation and approval consider skipping a transaction. With GTIDs enabled, the documented method identifies and marks the exact GTID using the prescribed empty-transaction process; this permanently records it as executed without its original effects. It can propagate if logged. Audit and validate all affected rows and downstream replicas first. sql_replica_skip_counter is for the documented non-GTID mode cases, not a generic GTID cure. It counts events/event groups rather than intuitively “N bad SQL statements”; transaction boundaries matter. No blind SET ...=N recovery recipe is recommended here. Restart the intended channel only after resolving the cause; verify both applier/receiver and independent data reconciliation. Document any intentionally skipped history.

title: Crash recovery
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MySQL · Source-replica replication and recovery
text: MySQL 8.4 uses transactional replication metadata (including mysql.slave_relay_log_info and mysql.slave_worker_info) and GTID execution state where enabled. The source’s mysql.gtid_replica_pos is not the MySQL 8.4 metadata model. relay_log_recovery=ON is a startup, not dynamic, setting. It reconstructs receiver progress from applier/transaction state and may fetch events again from the source; the source must retain required binlogs. Configure the documented durable relay/applier settings before failure, retain purging behavior compatible with recovery, and rehearse crash recovery. Do not try SET GLOBAL relay_log_recovery=ON after a crash or manually erase relay files as a universal repair.

title: Semisynchronous replication
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · MySQL · Source-replica replication and recovery
text: Semisync waits for acknowledgments that the configured number of replicas have received and flushed the events to relay log; it does not mean their SQL appliers have committed those changes. rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point determines the wait point, and timeout can fall back to asynchronous operation. Monitor whether semisync is actually active and acknowledge the durability/failover implications of each wait point. For compatible 8.4 builds, choose source/replica plugins deliberately: Side Installation/loading and enabling Source Runtime INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source SONAME 'semisync_source.so';, then enable rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled; or the corresponding plugin_load_add startup configuration. Replica Runtime INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_replica SONAME 'semisync_replica.so';, then enable rpl_semi_sync_replica_enabled; or equivalent startup settings. Check for an already installed plugin before issuing INSTALL. Runtime enablement alone is not restart persistence. A replica receiver thread that was already running needs the documented stop/start of its IO_THREAD (and intended channel) to advertise semisync capability. Test source status, acknowledgments, timeout/fallback, lag and failover before relying on the setup; installing the library is not verification. [55][56][57][109]

title: Startup, OS security and multiple instances
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL
text: For the selected EL9 RPM service: systemctl status mysqld.service journalctl -u mysqld.service -b mysqld --verbose --help Read the configured MySQL error log as well. Verify configuration syntax, port/socket conflicts, free space, mounted data/key directories, OS ownership and SELinux denials. sudo systemctl reset-failed mysqld.service clears the start-limit state after fixing the cause; it does not repair MySQL. Do not reinitialize a nonempty datadir to cure startup errors.  Firewalld zones/rich rules can constrain traffic by source address, service, port and protocol. Inspect the active interface’s zone first; the default zone may not be the one serving MySQL. firewall-cmd --get-active-zones firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all Choose the actual zone and approved application/replica source CIDRs. Prefer a source-restricted rich rule to opening mysql to an entire untrusted zone. --add-service=mysql refers to the service definition’s ports; a custom port uses --add-port=3307/tcp. These are alternatives, not requirements to expose both ports. Test a runtime rule, preserve console access and existing SSH rules, then persist only the approved rule. --reload applies permanent configuration and can discard temporary rules; review before doing so. Do not expose X Protocol or replication-internal ports merely because a classic-protocol client needs 3306. Keep enforcement enabled. Inspect the installed policy and AVC denials; label the intended path/port, not every similarly named directory. semanage port -l | grep mysqld semanage fcontext -l | grep mysqld For a deliberately selected new port 3307 that is not already assigned to another type, the policy operation is semanage port -a -t mysqld_port_t -p tcp 3307; an existing entry may need -m after inspection. Use -d only to remove a rule you intentionally own. For a moved standard datadir, follow the configuration chapter’s equivalence mapping and restorecon procedure; it preserves differentiated data/socket rules instead of labeling every object as database data. If an entry already exists, review/modification is required instead of repeating -a. Match log/socket/key paths to their appropriate policy types, and restore the previous mapping if rolling back. OS permissions and SELinux policy must both permit access. Mechanism What it actually does processname & Runs asynchronously in the shell’s job context; TTY/session/hangup behavior depends on shell and process. The TTY is not the parent process. nohup processname & Ignores SIGHUP and conditionally redirects terminal streams; does not create a complete supervised service. setsid processname Starts a new session when possible; does not automatically close inherited descriptors, drop privileges, restart on failure or guarantee reparenting to PID 1. systemd unit Supervises a service with explicit identity, environment, lifecycle and resource controls. Use this for the RPM MySQL instance. Historical nohup mysqld --defaults-group-suffix=1 & / setsid mysqld ... examples demonstrated shell detachment, not a recommended way to bypass the installed unit. Starting a second server against the same datadir is unsafe. Use named units and unique datadirs/ports/sockets instead. Use this only after authorizing the interface, zone, source network and listener. Here public and 192.0.2.0/24 are documentation inputs to replace, not a production recommendation. Inspect both runtime and permanent zone settings first: a broader existing mysql service/port/rich rule or trusted source can already admit traffic, and adding a narrow allow rule does not revoke that access. sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --list-all sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.0.2.0/24" port port="3306" protocol="tcp" accept' --timeout=300 Test a new identity-verified TLS connection from an allowed host, rejection from a disallowed host, and a new SSH management connection before the temporary rule expires. IPv6 needs its own deliberately restricted policy; an IPv4 allow test does not validate IPv6. Preserve console access. If accepted, add the same exact rule with --permanent (without --timeout) and as a non-timed runtime rule after removing the timed copy if still present. Query both copies with --query-rich-rule and test again. Avoid --runtime-to-permanent when unrelated transient rules are present. A later planned reload/reboot must retain only the approved access. Rollback removes only this exact rule from runtime and permanent configuration with --remove-rich-rule; do not flush the zone or stop firewalld. A firewall opening cannot make an unbound or SELinux-denied listener work. For SELinux tooling on RHEL 9 install policycoreutils-python-utils through the approved Red Hat repositories if absent. Inspect getenforce, ls -lZ, matchpathcon, ps -eZ and sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC -ts recent to distinguish DAC/path labeling, port labeling and genuine policy needs. Repair the specific cause; do not use setenforce 0, disable SELinux, or blindly generate audit2allow policy as the operating solution. [19][22][106][107][117][154][157][162] Dimension Separate instances Multiple databases in one instance Data integrity Separate dictionaries/storage; no cross-instance foreign-key enforcement. Never share one datadir between processes. Cross-schema relations can be supported within one server/engine. Availability Independent restart boundaries, but same-host instances share host/storage failure. HA requires a designed topology and failure domains. A server outage affects all schemas. Security Separate accounts/configs can reduce blast radius; same OS account/root access can defeat isolation. No automatic regulatory compliance guarantee. Grants/roles can restrict schemas, but share privileged administration and server resources. Backup/maintenance/recovery Each instance needs its own jobs, monitoring and restore plan; selective maintenance can spare others. Fewer server jobs, but consistency and restore scope need attention. Cost More operational/resource overhead; dedicated tenant instances may be justified. Simpler consolidation for workloads that can safely share limits. Performance Separate buffer pools and processes, not reserved CPU/RAM/I/O unless OS/cgroup/storage controls allocate them. Sum all budgets. Workloads contend within the same server; schema separation is not a resource governor. Scalability An instance can be moved/scaled independently after dependency review. Adding schemas is simple but does not remove instance limits. For RPM templates use [mysqld@replica01] with the matching mysqld@replica01.service. Give each instance a unique datadir, socket, classic/X ports where enabled, PID/error/relay/binlog paths and replication identity. The instance appendix preserves and corrects the template. Never clone a datadir as a generic way to create independent server UUIDs. [19][53]  Historical source example for reading, not a tested procedure or executable download. Applies to MySQL Server 8.4 LTS; the production baseline is RHEL 9 x86_64 with Oracle MySQL Community RPMs from the MySQL Yum repository. Separately licensed products and other platforms are identified explicitly.[1][72] Target: RHEL 9 x86-64 Oracle MySQL 8.4 RPMs. Use the package-provided mysqld@.service; the original template below is historical, not a portable service download. See the single-instance appendix for the common directive-by-directive review, including the incorrect EnvironmentFile assignment, notify/forking mismatch and deprecated identity control. title: Diagnose startup in order
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Startup, OS security and multiple instances
text: For the selected EL9 RPM service: systemctl status mysqld.service journalctl -u mysqld.service -b mysqld --verbose --help Read the configured MySQL error log as well. Verify configuration syntax, port/socket conflicts, free space, mounted data/key directories, OS ownership and SELinux denials. sudo systemctl reset-failed mysqld.service clears the start-limit state after fixing the cause; it does not repair MySQL. Do not reinitialize a nonempty datadir to cure startup errors.

title: firewalld
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Startup, OS security and multiple instances
text: Firewalld zones/rich rules can constrain traffic by source address, service, port and protocol. Inspect the active interface’s zone first; the default zone may not be the one serving MySQL. firewall-cmd --get-active-zones firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all Choose the actual zone and approved application/replica source CIDRs. Prefer a source-restricted rich rule to opening mysql to an entire untrusted zone. --add-service=mysql refers to the service definition’s ports; a custom port uses --add-port=3307/tcp. These are alternatives, not requirements to expose both ports. Test a runtime rule, preserve console access and existing SSH rules, then persist only the approved rule. --reload applies permanent configuration and can discard temporary rules; review before doing so. Do not expose X Protocol or replication-internal ports merely because a classic-protocol client needs 3306.

title: SELinux
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Startup, OS security and multiple instances
text: Keep enforcement enabled. Inspect the installed policy and AVC denials; label the intended path/port, not every similarly named directory. semanage port -l | grep mysqld semanage fcontext -l | grep mysqld For a deliberately selected new port 3307 that is not already assigned to another type, the policy operation is semanage port -a -t mysqld_port_t -p tcp 3307; an existing entry may need -m after inspection. Use -d only to remove a rule you intentionally own. For a moved standard datadir, follow the configuration chapter’s equivalence mapping and restorecon procedure; it preserves differentiated data/socket rules instead of labeling every object as database data. If an entry already exists, review/modification is required instead of repeating -a. Match log/socket/key paths to their appropriate policy types, and restore the previous mapping if rolling back. OS permissions and SELinux policy must both permit access.

title: Background processes are not service management
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Startup, OS security and multiple instances
text: Mechanism What it actually does processname & Runs asynchronously in the shell’s job context; TTY/session/hangup behavior depends on shell and process. The TTY is not the parent process. nohup processname & Ignores SIGHUP and conditionally redirects terminal streams; does not create a complete supervised service. setsid processname Starts a new session when possible; does not automatically close inherited descriptors, drop privileges, restart on failure or guarantee reparenting to PID 1. systemd unit Supervises a service with explicit identity, environment, lifecycle and resource controls. Use this for the RPM MySQL instance. Historical nohup mysqld --defaults-group-suffix=1 & / setsid mysqld ... examples demonstrated shell detachment, not a recommended way to bypass the installed unit. Starting a second server against the same datadir is unsafe. Use named units and unique datadirs/ports/sockets instead.

title: A source-restricted runtime rule with explicit acceptance
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Startup, OS security and multiple instances
text: Use this only after authorizing the interface, zone, source network and listener. Here public and 192.0.2.0/24 are documentation inputs to replace, not a production recommendation. Inspect both runtime and permanent zone settings first: a broader existing mysql service/port/rich rule or trusted source can already admit traffic, and adding a narrow allow rule does not revoke that access. sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --list-all sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.0.2.0/24" port port="3306" protocol="tcp" accept' --timeout=300 Test a new identity-verified TLS connection from an allowed host, rejection from a disallowed host, and a new SSH management connection before the temporary rule expires. IPv6 needs its own deliberately restricted policy; an IPv4 allow test does not validate IPv6. Preserve console access. If accepted, add the same exact rule with --permanent (without --timeout) and as a non-timed runtime rule after removing the timed copy if still present. Query both copies with --query-rich-rule and test again. Avoid --runtime-to-permanent when unrelated transient rules are present. A later planned reload/reboot must retain only the approved access. Rollback removes only this exact rule from runtime and permanent configuration with --remove-rich-rule; do not flush the zone or stop firewalld. A firewall opening cannot make an unbound or SELinux-denied listener work. For SELinux tooling on RHEL 9 install policycoreutils-python-utils through the approved Red Hat repositories if absent. Inspect getenforce, ls -lZ, matchpathcon, ps -eZ and sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC -ts recent to distinguish DAC/path labeling, port labeling and genuine policy needs. Repair the specific cause; do not use setenforce 0, disable SELinux, or blindly generate audit2allow policy as the operating solution. [19][22][106][107][117][154][157][162]

title: Multiple instances versus multiple databases
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Startup, OS security and multiple instances
text: Dimension Separate instances Multiple databases in one instance Data integrity Separate dictionaries/storage; no cross-instance foreign-key enforcement. Never share one datadir between processes. Cross-schema relations can be supported within one server/engine. Availability Independent restart boundaries, but same-host instances share host/storage failure. HA requires a designed topology and failure domains. A server outage affects all schemas. Security Separate accounts/configs can reduce blast radius; same OS account/root access can defeat isolation. No automatic regulatory compliance guarantee. Grants/roles can restrict schemas, but share privileged administration and server resources. Backup/maintenance/recovery Each instance needs its own jobs, monitoring and restore plan; selective maintenance can spare others. Fewer server jobs, but consistency and restore scope need attention. Cost More operational/resource overhead; dedicated tenant instances may be justified. Simpler consolidation for workloads that can safely share limits. Performance Separate buffer pools and processes, not reserved CPU/RAM/I/O unless OS/cgroup/storage controls allocate them. Sum all budgets. Workloads contend within the same server; schema separation is not a resource governor. Scalability An instance can be moved/scaled independently after dependency review. Adding schemas is simple but does not remove instance limits. For RPM templates use [mysqld@replica01] with the matching mysqld@replica01.service. Give each instance a unique datadir, socket, classic/X ports where enabled, PID/error/relay/binlog paths and replication identity. The instance appendix preserves and corrects the template. Never clone a datadir as a generic way to create independent server UUIDs. [19][53]
