title: Instance expansion and path isolation
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Startup, OS security and multiple instances
text: The source’s ExecStartPre=... %I passes the unescaped instance name to the RPM helper. --defaults-group-suffix=@%I makes instance replica01 read [mysqld@replica01] in addition to common groups. It does not read [mysqld1]. Verify the installed unit’s exact command rather than copying an ordering of --defaults-file and suffix options that the server will reject. A per-instance option-file illustration, after its distinct directory/ownership/mount/SELinux plan is prepared: [mysqld@replica01] datadir=/var/lib/mysql-replica01 socket=/var/lib/mysql-replica01/mysql.sock port=3307 log-error=/var/log/mysqld-replica01.log This is not a complete replication configuration. Decide unique server IDs/UUIDs, binlog/relay-log locations, PID files and X Protocol listener/socket if enabled. A common inherited pid-file, mysqlx_port or log path can still collide even with separate classic ports. Sum memory budgets and use OS resource controls if resource isolation is required; shared-host instances do not provide host-failure HA. Inventory vendor/common settings and existing instances; ensure new paths are empty intentionally, not unmounted production data. Configure each unique suffix group, owned paths and security policy, then validate the selected configuration. Start the specific instance with systemctl start mysqld@replica01.service. Inspect that exact unit’s journal and error log; connect using its socket/port and verify @@datadir, @@port, server identity and intended objects. Only after verification, decide whether systemctl enable mysqld@replica01.service should make it start at boot. Test mount/order dependencies. On failure stop/repair only the intended instance. Keep prior config/data for rollback and do not run both units over the same datadir. All original template fields are retained in the historical text. Their common meanings are unchanged from the single-instance review except for %I, @%I and the need to avoid shared runtime/storage resources.

title: Provision the named instance’s RHEL paths
context: Databases · Get a server running · MySQL · Startup, OS security and multiple instances
text: Keep this second instance local initially: add bind_address=127.0.0.1, mysqlx=OFF (unless separately provisioned), pid-file=/run/mysqld/replica01.pid and a chosen unique nonzero server_id to [mysqld@replica01]. Retain the standard package-managed /run/mysqld runtime directory and verify the installed unit/tmpfiles setup recreates it at boot. Do not inherit the default instance’s PID/socket/log paths. The datadir below must be a deliberately new empty directory; creating it on top of missing storage is not acceptable. After reviewing existing SELinux local rules and approving this path: sudo install -d -o mysql -g mysql -m 0750 /var/lib/mysql-replica01 sudo semanage fcontext -a -e /var/lib/mysql /var/lib/mysql-replica01 sudo restorecon -Rv /var/lib/mysql-replica01 matchpathcon /var/lib/mysql-replica01/mysql.sock matchpathcon /var/log/mysqld-replica01.log semanage port -l | grep mysqld Confirm the socket’s expected type is mysqld_var_run_t; verify/restore the named error log’s mysqld_log_t after creation and inspect the PID label. The Oracle RPM helper only assists automatic error-log creation for its documented /var/log/mysql*.log pattern; an arbitrary new log directory is your provisioning responsibility. Register port 3307 as mysqld_port_t only if needed after inspecting the actual policy; do not reassign a port owned by another service. No firewall opening is needed for this loopback-only initial instance. Check all inherited groups and run /usr/sbin/mysqld --defaults-group-suffix=@replica01 --validate-config with appropriate config-read authority. If NO_INIT=true is already set for existing production units, do not turn it off globally just to create this one instance. After verifying the new empty paths/options, explicitly initialize only this instance using sudo /usr/sbin/mysqld --defaults-group-suffix=@replica01 --initialize --user=mysql; inspect its own protected error log for the temporary password. Otherwise the reviewed vendor helper may perform first initialization. These are alternative paths: never initialize twice or use --initialize-insecure to avoid credential handling. Start mysqld@replica01.service, complete its interactive account hardening against its explicit socket, and verify it with mysql --protocol=SOCKET --socket=/var/lib/mysql-replica01/mysql.sock --user=root --password. Compare both instances’ datadir, server UUID, ports, PID and logs; verify stopping the new unit leaves the original instance healthy. Add per-instance mount dependencies where needed and test restart before boot enablement. Remote exposure then follows the TLS/SELinux/firewall procedure for 3307, not a copied 3306 service rule. All instances share one installed server binary/package update: separate units do not provide independent MySQL versions or rolling binary upgrades on one host. [19][20][53][105][106][107][157][163][18][58]

title: Upgrades and rollback planning
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · MySQL
text: Target: MySQL Server 8.4 LTS. Record the full source patch, distribution, architecture, OS, plugins, client drivers, replication topology and desired 8.4 target patch. A table that says 8.0.x → 8.4 or 8.4 → 9.x is not a support matrix. Use the official upgrade-path table and the selected release notes/prerequisites before choosing packages. Source-era path from the old notes Correct disposition Older than 5.7 → 5.7 Historical intermediate migration, not an 8.4 direct in-place path. Plan supported intermediate steps or reviewed logical transformation for the actual source. 5.7 → 8.0.15 Historical pre-auto-upgrade behavior used mysql_upgrade; it is not a recommendation to deploy that old patch now. 5.7 → 8.0.16+ 8.0.16 introduced server-performed upgrade tasks. Reach a source version eligible for the next hop; do not jump 5.7 directly to 8.4. 8.0 → 8.4 LTS Supported adjacent-series class (the manual gives 8.0.37 → 8.4.x as an example), subject to exact versions, removed features, readiness checks and release notes. Update to an eligible maintained source patch first where required. 8.4 → a later Innovation/LTS Outside this deployment target. Only follow a specifically documented supported path; “all 9.x” is false. A required LTS cannot be skipped. Within 8.4 LTS maintenance update; still review release notes, plugin/tool compatibility and rollback support for the exact pair. Back up all data, binlogs, key material, effective configuration, grants/routines and package inventory. Rehearse restoring them to an isolated old-version instance; merely saving old packages does not undo a dictionary upgrade. Use a MySQL Shell build whose checker understands the chosen target, and supply the exact targetVersion. The 8.4 API supports this option; omitting it checks against the Shell release, which may not be the intended target. configPath can include checks of a local copy of the source option file. The checker’s documented account needs RELOAD, PROCESS and SELECT; use temporary controlled access, not a permanently privileged application account. Connect without an embedded password and call util.checkForServerUpgrade(connectionData, {targetVersion: approvedTargetVersion, configPath: sourceConfigPath}) in Shell JavaScript. Those names represent explicitly supplied values. Save the report; resolve errors and understand warnings. Passing the checker is necessary evidence, not an application/replication/backup test. Rehearse the exact package/binary upgrade and restart on the restored copy. Check changed authentication defaults, removed variables/plugins, charset/collation, SQL behavior, optimizer changes and app drivers. Rehearse topology sequencing, including replicas and Router where used. During the approved production window, stop writes as required, take the final consistent backup/boundary, apply only the reviewed packages from the intended 8.4 channel, and start with monitored logs. Do not use a blanket yum localupdate over an arbitrary directory. Validate server version, tables/routines/accounts, application results, performance, backups and all replicas before cutover is accepted. mysqld --upgrade= Meaning AUTO Default: performs dictionary/server upgrade steps as needed. MINIMAL Limits upgrade to required dictionary, Performance Schema and INFORMATION_SCHEMA work; skips other server-upgrade work. Not proof that user/system objects have passed all checks. FORCE Forces server-upgrade checks/work even when normally considered current; not a magic repair for arbitrary corruption. NONE Suppresses upgrade work; startup fails if a required dictionary upgrade is needed. Not a way to run new binaries against an incompatible old dictionary. Do not start old binaries on a newly upgraded datadir unless the exact downgrade is expressly supported. The 8.4 LTS policy permits some within-series in-place downgrades; cross-series and feature-specific restrictions are separate. Safest rehearsed fallback is the untouched old instance/backup plus a plan for writes accepted after cutover. A logical export may require unsupported-feature/type/SQL transformations and is not universally loadable into an older version. Test rollback and its data-loss window before upgrading. Use the same Oracle repository origin, selected 8.4 channel and approved package transaction; inventory server, client, Shell, Router, backup tool, plugins and SELinux policy compatibility. A Red Hat AppStream module-switch command is not this upgrade method. Review every active mysqld@... unit as well as mysqld.service: package replacement changes their shared binaries, so plan all affected instances even when they have separate datadirs. Back up drop-ins, /etc/my.cnf includes and /etc/sysconfig/mysql; compare RPM configuration artifacts rather than overwriting working local settings. For a supported asynchronous rolling upgrade, upgrade/test replicas before the writer where the exact-version replication matrix allows old-source to new-replica traffic. Stop if any required channel, plugin or client version is unsupported; new-source to old-replica traffic must not be assumed. For Group Replication, use its exact mixed-version/primary restrictions and preserve quorum while upgrading one member at a time. Do not bootstrap during an ordinary rolling update. Keep a separately restored old-version fallback, and record the point after which new writes make it stale. These are topology acceptance gates, not a universal execution sequence for unspecified source/target versions. [1][49][50][51][86][90][97][158][19][165][166]

title: Access control, passwords and recovery
context: Operating systems
text: Filesystems organize names and metadata in directories and allocate storage for file data. Ownership, permissions, labels and mount options affect access; they do not replace backups.[23] At-rest encryption protects stored data under a defined key-management model; in-transit encryption, such as SSH or TLS, protects communications. One does not automatically provide the other. An unlocked encrypted filesystem remains accessible to authorized processes; protect encryption keys and recovery material separately.[83][30]  Traditional Unix DAC uses ownership plus owner/group/other mode bits (rwx). Access Control Lists can express additional per-user/per-group permissions; the basic mode bits are not themselves an arbitrary ACL. Directory write/search permissions govern directory-entry creation and removal; file write permission governs modifying file content.[19][88] See permissions and umask.  Authentication verifies an asserted identity. Passwords, biometrics and SSH public-key authentication are different mechanisms. PAM-aware services can delegate relevant checks to configured PAM stacks; SSH keys also require correct server policy and account authorization.[7][30]  SELinux implements mandatory access control using labels and policy enforced in the kernel. In normal access checks, passing DAC is not enough: SELinux can still deny access. SELinux does not simply override ownership permissions to grant access. Policy can restrict a process’s access to files, network ports and other resources; roles and domains are policy concepts, not synonyms for Unix groups.[143] RHEL 9 commonly uses firewalld with zones, services, ports and optional rich rules to control traffic. A rule can combine a source address with a service or port restriction. Packet filtering, SELinux application permissions and service authentication are separate controls. Before changing firewall rules remotely, retain console access and verify both the intended application path and the management path; a rule that drops SSH can end the maintenance session.[57] On RHEL 9, semanage is provided by policycoreutils-python-utils; install it through the approved Red Hat repositories if missing. Keep enforcement enabled. Inspect the service’s actual OS permissions, process context and file labels before assuming a database authentication or firewall problem:[143] getenforce ps -eZ sudo semanage fcontext -l -C sudo semanage port -l sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC,SELINUX_ERR,USER_SELINUX_ERR -ts recent Record the actual denied process, operation and target. For a custom service path, compare ls -lZ with matchpathcon /actual/path; check parent-directory search access and ACLs as well as file modes. semanage fcontext changes persistent path mappings; restorecon applies those mappings to existing objects. A one-off chcon is not a durable replacement. When moving a whole standard directory tree, a reviewed semanage fcontext -a -e OLD_ROOT NEW_ROOT equivalence mapping can preserve distinct labels for data, sockets and other children. These uppercase arguments are placeholders for verified paths, not literal directory names. Inspect existing local rules before adding/modifying/removing one.[143] Ports have policy types too: inspect the current assignment before adding a nondefault service port, and never reassign a port owned by another service merely to silence a denial. Labels must match the actual daemon’s documented policy, not a type copied from another database. Re-test the denied operation, persistent label restoration and the next controlled service restart. Stop if the policy need is unexplained; do not leave SELinux permissive/disabled or blindly install audit2allow output. Preserve the original local mapping for targeted rollback.[143] Inspect firewall-cmd --get-active-zones, the actual zone’s runtime --list-all, and its --permanent --list-all before editing. The default zone is not necessarily the interface’s zone. A service definition admits its listed ports; a database’s nondefault port is not automatically covered. An additional narrow allow rule does not remove existing broader access.[57][142] For a separately authorized IPv4 example, replace public, 192.0.2.0/24 and 3306 with the actual zone, approved source network and listener port. Test temporarily before persistence: sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.0.2.0/24" port port="3306" protocol="tcp" accept' --timeout=300 The timeout is runtime-only and cannot be combined with --permanent. Verify a fresh application connection from an allowed host, denial from an unapproved host, and a new management session before expiry. Check IPv6 separately when present. An open socket alone does not establish reachability or authenticated TLS.[142] If accepted, remove the timed copy if still active, add the identical non-timed runtime rule and add that exact rule with --permanent. Use --query-rich-rule for both stores and test again. Avoid --runtime-to-permanent unless every other transient runtime change is intended to persist. A reload replaces runtime policy with permanent policy; schedule/test it rather than casually discarding unrelated runtime rules. Rollback uses --remove-rich-rule for only the introduced rule in both stores, preserving SSH and other existing rules. Confirm intended access survives the next controlled reload/reboot; never stop the firewall as the fix.[142][57] These examples target RHEL 9 local accounts. Directory-backed identities may have policy elsewhere. Account changes require delegated administrative authority. title: File system management
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: Filesystems organize names and metadata in directories and allocate storage for file data. Ownership, permissions, labels and mount options affect access; they do not replace backups.[23]

title: Encryption
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: At-rest encryption protects stored data under a defined key-management model; in-transit encryption, such as SSH or TLS, protects communications. One does not automatically provide the other. An unlocked encrypted filesystem remains accessible to authorized processes; protect encryption keys and recovery material separately.[83][30]

title: Authorization
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery

title: Discretionary access control (DAC)
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: Traditional Unix DAC uses ownership plus owner/group/other mode bits (rwx). Access Control Lists can express additional per-user/per-group permissions; the basic mode bits are not themselves an arbitrary ACL. Directory write/search permissions govern directory-entry creation and removal; file write permission governs modifying file content.[19][88] See permissions and umask.

title: Security
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery

title: Authentication
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: Authentication verifies an asserted identity. Passwords, biometrics and SSH public-key authentication are different mechanisms. PAM-aware services can delegate relevant checks to configured PAM stacks; SSH keys also require correct server policy and account authorization.[7][30]

title: Authorization
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery

title: SELinux
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: SELinux implements mandatory access control using labels and policy enforced in the kernel. In normal access checks, passing DAC is not enough: SELinux can still deny access. SELinux does not simply override ownership permissions to grant access. Policy can restrict a process’s access to files, network ports and other resources; roles and domains are policy concepts, not synonyms for Unix groups.[143]

title: Firewall
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: RHEL 9 commonly uses firewalld with zones, services, ports and optional rich rules to control traffic. A rule can combine a source address with a service or port restriction. Packet filtering, SELinux application permissions and service authentication are separate controls. Before changing firewall rules remotely, retain console access and verify both the intended application path and the management path; a rule that drops SSH can end the maintenance session.[57]

title: Enforcing SELinux: diagnose before changing policy
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: On RHEL 9, semanage is provided by policycoreutils-python-utils; install it through the approved Red Hat repositories if missing. Keep enforcement enabled. Inspect the service’s actual OS permissions, process context and file labels before assuming a database authentication or firewall problem:[143] getenforce ps -eZ sudo semanage fcontext -l -C sudo semanage port -l sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC,SELINUX_ERR,USER_SELINUX_ERR -ts recent Record the actual denied process, operation and target. For a custom service path, compare ls -lZ with matchpathcon /actual/path; check parent-directory search access and ACLs as well as file modes. semanage fcontext changes persistent path mappings; restorecon applies those mappings to existing objects. A one-off chcon is not a durable replacement. When moving a whole standard directory tree, a reviewed semanage fcontext -a -e OLD_ROOT NEW_ROOT equivalence mapping can preserve distinct labels for data, sockets and other children. These uppercase arguments are placeholders for verified paths, not literal directory names. Inspect existing local rules before adding/modifying/removing one.[143] Ports have policy types too: inspect the current assignment before adding a nondefault service port, and never reassign a port owned by another service merely to silence a denial. Labels must match the actual daemon’s documented policy, not a type copied from another database. Re-test the denied operation, persistent label restoration and the next controlled service restart. Stop if the policy need is unexplained; do not leave SELinux permissive/disabled or blindly install audit2allow output. Preserve the original local mapping for targeted rollback.[143]

title: Firewall changes: narrow rule, live test, then persistence
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: Inspect firewall-cmd --get-active-zones, the actual zone’s runtime --list-all, and its --permanent --list-all before editing. The default zone is not necessarily the interface’s zone. A service definition admits its listed ports; a database’s nondefault port is not automatically covered. An additional narrow allow rule does not remove existing broader access.[57][142] For a separately authorized IPv4 example, replace public, 192.0.2.0/24 and 3306 with the actual zone, approved source network and listener port. Test temporarily before persistence: sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.0.2.0/24" port port="3306" protocol="tcp" accept' --timeout=300 The timeout is runtime-only and cannot be combined with --permanent. Verify a fresh application connection from an allowed host, denial from an unapproved host, and a new management session before expiry. Check IPv6 separately when present. An open socket alone does not establish reachability or authenticated TLS.[142] If accepted, remove the timed copy if still active, add the identical non-timed runtime rule and add that exact rule with --permanent. Use --query-rich-rule for both stores and test again. Avoid --runtime-to-permanent unless every other transient runtime change is intended to persist. A reload replaces runtime policy with permanent policy; schedule/test it rather than casually discarding unrelated runtime rules. Rollback uses --remove-rich-rule for only the introduced rule in both stores, preserving SSH and other existing rules. Confirm intended access survives the next controlled reload/reboot; never stop the firewall as the fix.[142][57]

title: Reset root password via GRUB
context: Operating systems · Access control, passwords and recovery
text: Authorized recovery only, on a RHEL 9 system you administer. This interrupts the machine and bypasses the normal login path. Obtain maintenance approval, a verified recovery backup and physical or trusted out-of-band console access. Confirm any bootloader credential and encrypted-volume unlock material are available. If boot policy prevents editing, use the organization’s approved rescue process rather than disabling security controls. Reboot into the GRUB menu, select the intended RHEL entry and press e. Append rd.break to the line beginning with linux. This is a temporary edit for this boot; do not save it as a permanent kernel argument. Press Ctrl+x. At the switch_root prompt, remount the installed root and enter it: mount -o remount,rw /sysroot chroot /sysroot passwd root touch /.autorelabel exit exit Enter the replacement password only at passwd’s prompts. touch /.autorelabel is run inside the chroot, so it marks the installed root for SELinux relabelling. The first exit leaves the chroot; the second leaves the early-boot shell and resumes boot. Relabelling may take time and cause a further reboot; do not interrupt it.[8] After normal boot, verify an authorized login, whoami, expected SELinux mode with getenforce, and required services.[143] Confirm the temporary rd.break argument is absent on the next normal boot. If recovery fails, return to the approved console/rescue process; do not leave an early-boot shell or permissive security configuration as the operating state. See boot stages.

title: Inspect or change the target
context: Operating systems · From power-on to login
text: Task Command List loaded active targets systemctl list-units --type=target Show boot default systemctl get-default Legacy compatibility view runlevel (where installed); does not enumerate all active targets Switch this boot to text multi-user mode sudo systemctl isolate multi-user.target Set text multi-user mode for future boots sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target Changing targets is authorized maintenance: isolate can stop services and terminate the current desktop/session. Save work, verify what depends on the current target, record the prior default, and retain console access. set-default changes future boot selection, not the current running target. Verify active units/default afterward; restore the recorded target/default if required. Do not substitute poweroff.target or reboot.target as a harmless exercise.[48] Legacy init N compatibility requests a numbered runlevel; prefer the explicit systemd operation above on RHEL 9 rather than treating init # as literal syntax.

title: 6. Login and session management

text: A getty/login path or a display manager handles user login. A successful login creates the user’s session. A GUI is not simply a login shell.[128][17] See shell startup files and systemd service types.

title: Devices, kernel services and isolation
context: Operating systems
text: Kernel functionality may be built into the kernel or supplied by loadable modules. A driver is not necessarily a loadable module.[94] Hardware can signal an interrupt request (IRQ). Drivers register handlers with the kernel interrupt subsystem. A hard-interrupt handler should do bounded, non-sleeping work; defer longer work to an appropriate threaded handler or other deferred-work mechanism.[132] Interrupt controllers route and prioritize interrupts. On x86, APICs are part of this machinery. MSI/MSI-X are message-signalled interrupt mechanisms, not a generic component called an “MSI controller.”[93] Device drivers handle hardware such as network adapters and storage controllers; CPU/platform support also lives in the kernel. Filesystem implementations (for example ext4 or NTFS implementations) manage on-disk structures and filesystem operations through the kernel’s filesystem/I/O layers. Buffering and caching involve shared kernel facilities, not only the device driver.[3][43] Linux-PAM is a userspace framework, not a Linux kernel module subsystem. PAM-aware applications use libraries and configured module stacks for authentication, account checks, password changes and session setup. A shared-library PAM module is different from a loadable kernel module.[7] See password policy. The kernel implements networking protocols, including IP and the TCP and UDP transports. Depending on the build, networking features can be built in or modular. TCP and UDP both operate over IP; “TCP/IP” is not a peer of UDP in a clean protocol-layer taxonomy.[90] LSM provides hooks for security decisions involving files, networking, process operations and other kernel objects. SELinux is one implementation that applies its security policy through these hooks. It is distinct from PAM’s userspace login/session decisions.[4][82] Exceptions, hardware interrupts, and system calls are different entry paths into privileged kernel handling. Linux “softirqs” are a specific deferred-processing mechanism; the term is not a synonym for every system call or exception.[132][85] Applications request kernel services through interfaces such as read(), write(), getpid(), pipe(), socket() and execve(). The exec*() family includes library wrappers; exec() is not one universal Linux syscall name. time() is a familiar time interface, but a library/vDSO implementation need not trap into the kernel on every call.[92][91] A syscall enters kernel mode, validates the request and permissions, performs the operation where permitted, and returns a result or error; it does not grant the caller unrestricted privilege.[61] Namespaces give groups of processes distinct views of resources such as process IDs, network stacks, mount points and user IDs. They are building blocks for containers and sandboxes, not by themselves a complete security boundary.[5] Cgroups organize processes for resource accounting and control: CPU, memory and I/O are important examples. Namespaces answer “which resources are visible?”; cgroups answer “how are resources accounted for and constrained?” Available controllers and delegation rules depend on the kernel and configuration.[6] For service-level limits, see resource controls.

context: Operating systems · Devices, kernel services and isolation
text: Hardware can signal an interrupt request (IRQ). Drivers register handlers with the kernel interrupt subsystem. A hard-interrupt handler should do bounded, non-sleeping work; defer longer work to an appropriate threaded handler or other deferred-work mechanism.[132] Interrupt controllers route and prioritize interrupts. On x86, APICs are part of this machinery. MSI/MSI-X are message-signalled interrupt mechanisms, not a generic component called an “MSI controller.”[93] Device drivers handle hardware such as network adapters and storage controllers; CPU/platform support also lives in the kernel. Filesystem implementations (for example ext4 or NTFS implementations) manage on-disk structures and filesystem operations through the kernel’s filesystem/I/O layers. Buffering and caching involve shared kernel facilities, not only the device driver.[3][43]

title: Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)
context: Operating systems · Devices, kernel services and isolation
text: Linux-PAM is a userspace framework, not a Linux kernel module subsystem. PAM-aware applications use libraries and configured module stacks for authentication, account checks, password changes and session setup. A shared-library PAM module is different from a loadable kernel module.[7] See password policy.

title: Network protocol support
context: Operating systems · Devices, kernel services and isolation
text: The kernel implements networking protocols, including IP and the TCP and UDP transports. Depending on the build, networking features can be built in or modular. TCP and UDP both operate over IP; “TCP/IP” is not a peer of UDP in a clean protocol-layer taxonomy.[90]

title: Linux Security Modules (LSM)
context: Operating systems · Devices, kernel services and isolation
text: LSM provides hooks for security decisions involving files, networking, process operations and other kernel objects. SELinux is one implementation that applies its security policy through these hooks. It is distinct from PAM’s userspace login/session decisions.[4][82]

title: Kernel services
context: Operating systems · Devices, kernel services and isolation
text: Exceptions, hardware interrupts, and system calls are different entry paths into privileged kernel handling. Linux “softirqs” are a specific deferred-processing mechanism; the term is not a synonym for every system call or exception.[132][85] Applications request kernel services through interfaces such as read(), write(), getpid(), pipe(), socket() and execve(). The exec*() family includes library wrappers; exec() is not one universal Linux syscall name. time() is a familiar time interface, but a library/vDSO implementation need not trap into the kernel on every call.[92][91] A syscall enters kernel mode, validates the request and permissions, performs the operation where permitted, and returns a result or error; it does not grant the caller unrestricted privilege.[61]

title: Namespaces
context: Operating systems · Devices, kernel services and isolation
text: Namespaces give groups of processes distinct views of resources such as process IDs, network stacks, mount points and user IDs. They are building blocks for containers and sandboxes, not by themselves a complete security boundary.[5]

title: Control groups (cgroups)
context: Operating systems · Devices, kernel services and isolation
text: Cgroups organize processes for resource accounting and control: CPU, memory and I/O are important examples. Namespaces answer “which resources are visible?”; cgroups answer “how are resources accounted for and constrained?” Available controllers and delegation rules depend on the kernel and configuration.[6] For service-level limits, see resource controls.

title: Memory and virtual memory
context: Operating systems
text: Pages divide virtual memory into fixed-size units; physical page frames provide RAM backing. Page size is architecture-dependent, and larger page sizes may also be supported. Page tables describe mappings and access attributes.[1] Segments are variable-size logical regions in the classic segmentation model, such as code, data and stack. Do not confuse a program’s logical regions with the fixed-size pages backing them; modern Linux virtual memory is primarily described through mappings and pages.[86][1] Virtual memory gives programs virtual addresses that the CPU and kernel map to physical memory or other backing. It supports separate address spaces, controlled sharing, protection, demand allocation and file mappings. It works even when no swap is configured.[1] A page fault can demand allocation or loading of a valid page; an invalid access can instead fault the process. File-backed pages may be read from a file; clean cached pages can be discarded and read again. Eligible anonymous pages may be written to swap and brought back later. Swap is backing storage, not extra RAM with RAM’s latency. Reclaim and compaction respond to memory pressure. If memory cannot be made available, an allocation may fail or the out-of-memory mechanism may select a task to kill.[1] Use memory and I/O statistics to investigate pressure; do not infer a memory leak merely from low “free” RAM, because caches also consume RAM.

title: Networking, SSH and file transfer
context: Operating systems
text: Examples use RHEL 9 with NetworkManager. Interface names such as enp1s0 are examples; discover the actual interface and active connection profile before changes. Read-only inspection: nmcli device status nmcli connection show --active ip address show ss -tuln Connection changes can disconnect you. For authorized maintenance, retain out-of-band console access, record the active profile/address/routes/DNS, back up relevant profile configuration, and prepare a tested rollback before changing a remote interface. Do not release/flush the interface carrying your only administrative session. Command Meaning nmcli NetworkManager command-line client, not a “BSD-style” networking subsystem nmcli device Show device status (d is an accepted abbreviation) nmcli device show IFACE Show interface properties nmcli device connect IFACE Ask NetworkManager to connect the device; may activate a matching profile or create a suitable one nmcli device disconnect IFACE Disconnect the device; can terminate remote sessions nmcli --ask device wifi connect 'SSID' Connect to Wi-Fi, prompting for the secret when required instead of putting it in shell history or the process argument list ss -tu TCP/UDP sockets, with selection depending on other flags ss -tuln Listening TCP/UDP sockets, numeric addresses/ports.[89] netstat -tuln Legacy net-tools equivalent where installed; prefer ss for routine inspection.[126] Socket listeners are not proof of firewall reachability. Verify the intended connection from an authorized client after a change; keep the prior working profile until the new path is verified.[28][33] Syntax is rsync [OPTIONS] SOURCE DEST; one endpoint may be remote, for example user@host:/path/. Ordinary rsync does not accept two remote endpoints in one transfer. The examples below use SSH transport.[29] Option Meaning -a Archive mode (-rlptgoD): recursive, links, permissions, times, group, owner, devices/special files as privileges allow; not hard links, ACLs or extended attributes -r Recurse without implying archive metadata preservation -v Verbose -z Compress transfer data; benefit depends on content and link -P --partial --progress: keep partial files and report progress; lowercase -p instead means permissions --delete Delete extraneous destination entries within the synchronized scope; excluded/protected entries and delete timing/options matter --exclude=PATTERN Exclude matching paths according to rsync’s filter rules -n / --dry-run Preview without writing the transfer A trailing slash matters: source/ copies its contents, while source includes that directory level. A partial file is not an integrity-verified backup, and -P is not a promise to resume every file from exactly the last byte. Add -H, -A, or -X only when hard links, ACLs or xattrs are required and both ends support them.[29] Example preview for an approved test destination, with deletion deliberately absent: rsync -anvi -e ssh -- /srv/example-source/ user@host.example:/srv/example-copy/ Before enabling a mirror’s --delete, obtain authorization for the destination, confirm both roots/trailing slashes, maintain a separate recoverable backup or protected snapshot, and inspect the itemized dry run with the exact intended filters. Do not mirror into a live database directory. Stop if the source is unexpectedly empty or unavailable. After an approved transfer, verify expected files and application-consistent recovery separately; a zero exit status alone is not a restore test.[29] Protocol/tool Default port SSH, SFTP, SCP over SSH TCP 22, unless server/client configuration selects another port.[124] SFTP is a file-transfer protocol over SSH, not FTP with TLS. Upstream OpenSSH scp uses SFTP by default from 9.0; distribution packages can backport this change, so do not infer protocol behavior from the command name alone.[32] Command Meaning ssh user@host.example Open an authenticated remote session scp FILE user@host.example:/approved/path/ Copy local to remote; quote paths as required scp -r DIR user@host.example:/approved/path/ Recursive directory copy; validate destination and symlink behavior scp user@host1.example:/path/FILE user@host2.example:/path/ Remote-to-remote copy; data routing/authentication behavior depends on scp options/version ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C 'admin@example.invalid' Create an RSA keypair if allowed by organizational policy; use an interactive passphrase and a new filename rather than overwriting an existing key ssh-copy-id user@host.example Install an appropriate public key after authenticating the server and account; review key selection and server policy.[109] ssh-keygen -l -f KEYFILE.pub Display a public-key fingerprint ssh-keygen -R host.example Remove that host’s stored known-hosts trust entry; use only after the identity checks below Keep the private key private; a passphrase protects it at rest and an agent can assist use. “Key login” is not synonymous with “no authentication.” RSA key type does not require enabling obsolete SHA-1 ssh-rsa signatures.[30][31] Do not fix a warning by immediately deleting known_hosts or disabling StrictHostKeyChecking. Confirm the expected host and new fingerprint through a trusted independent channel (for example the console or an authenticated administrator/asset record). A fresh network scan alone does not establish identity.[30] Only after confirming an authorized key rotation/rebuild: preserve the old trust record, remove the precise stale entry with ssh-keygen -R, reconnect, and compare the displayed fingerprint to the verified value before accepting. Non-default ports use the known-hosts form [host.example]:PORT; check aliases and IP entries individually. Stop and investigate if verification fails.[31] Prefer NetworkManager connection profiles for persistent RHEL 9 configuration. Direct ip address changes are runtime changes and may be overwritten by the manager.[28][33] Operation Command/reference Inspect interface addresses ip address show dev enp1s0 Add a runtime IPv4 address ip address add 192.0.2.10/24 dev enp1s0 Remove that specific runtime address ip address del 192.0.2.10/24 dev enp1s0 Reapply supported changes to an active device nmcli device reapply enp1s0 Flush matching addresses ip address flush dev enp1s0 — disruptive; can remove both IPv4 and IPv6 selections, not a normal repair step 192.0.2.10/24 is a documentation address, not a value to assign to a production network. Do not execute add/delete/flush until the maintenance prerequisites above are met, the interface and address plan are verified, and an explicit inverse change or prior profile can be restored from the console. reapply applies only changes NetworkManager can update without full reconnection; it is not a guarantee against interruption.[28] The older pattern dhclient -r && dhclient IFACE releases leases too broadly and can conflict with NetworkManager. On RHEL 9, do not start an independent DHCP client on a NetworkManager-managed device. Refresh/reconnect the intended profile through NetworkManager during approved maintenance instead; a profile down/up still interrupts traffic. For a genuinely unmanaged interface, use the distribution’s documented DHCP client procedure rather than this generic release-all chain. After any approved change, inspect addresses, routes and DNS, test the gateway and intended service from the correct network, and verify a new management connection before closing the console. If it fails, restore the recorded profile/addresses from that console—not by stacking further speculative changes.

title: Processes and scheduling
context: Operating systems
text: Non-preemptive scheduling lets a running task keep the CPU until it exits, blocks or voluntarily yields. Preemptive scheduling can take the CPU away without that cooperation—for example when a higher-priority task becomes runnable. A fixed time slice is one policy, not the definition of preemption: Linux SCHED_FIFO has no time slice, whereas SCHED_RR does.[2][84] A process control block (PCB) is the textbook record of process state. Linux represents execution contexts with kernel task structures rather than a single portable PCB layout. The fields below describe the conceptual model, not a binary layout to inspect or edit.[117][122] Field What it records PID Process/task identity State Running, runnable, sleeping, stopped, and other lifecycle states Pointers Links to queues and related kernel objects Priority Scheduling policy and priority information Program counter Instruction location needed to resume execution CPU registers Saved execution context I/O information Open resources and pending/waiting operations Accounting information CPU time and other usage statistics The conceptual job queue is the collection of submitted jobs/processes awaiting or under system management; the ready queue contains tasks eligible to run; a device/wait queue contains tasks waiting for an event such as I/O completion. Linux has multiple scheduling and wait structures, not one universal queue of each kind. ps is a snapshot of process state, not a dump of all scheduler queues.[38][117] Long-term/admission scheduling: decides which jobs enter a workload; a textbook role, not a separate required Linux scheduler daemon. Short-term/CPU scheduling: selects a runnable task for a CPU. Dispatch changes its role from ready to running. Medium-term scheduling: the textbook suspension/resumption role, sometimes associated with swapping.[117] A task blocked on I/O need not be swapped out. Linux normally reclaims memory at page granularity: discard reconstructible clean file-backed pages, write dirty file-backed pages to their backing file, or move eligible anonymous pages to swap. Swapping an entire process is a useful historical model, not a description of every Linux scheduling decision.[1] The kernel saves the outgoing task’s CPU execution state and restores the incoming task’s state. Switching address spaces may also change memory mappings and translation context; it does not copy all process memory into a PCB. Threads in the same process share an address space.[85][123] The selection rules below are textbook models; SJN is also commonly called shortest job first (SJF).[84] Model Selection rule First come, first served (FCFS) Arrival order; typically non-preemptive Shortest job next (SJN) Smallest estimated CPU burst; non-preemptive Priority Highest eligible priority; can be preemptive or non-preemptive Shortest remaining time (SRT) Preemptive counterpart of shortest-job scheduling Round robin Rotate eligible tasks after a time quantum Multilevel queue Separate workload queues, with a policy between and within queues; unlike multilevel feedback, this label alone does not imply moving tasks between queues.[136] These are conceptual models, not interchangeable Linux command-line settings. Linux exposes policies such as SCHED_OTHER, SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR and SCHED_DEADLINE; normal scheduling internals depend on the kernel version. Real-time priorities can starve ordinary work and require a deliberate capacity and privilege policy.[2] For observation and safe signalling, see process tools.

Linux exposes policies such as SCHED_OTHER, SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR and SCHED_DEADLINE; normal scheduling internals depend on the kernel version. Real-time priorities can starve ordinary work and require a deliberate capacity and privilege policy.[2] For observation and safe signalling, see process tools.

title: Systemd service types
context: Operating systems
text: Type= describes the startup protocol, not a guarantee that an application is healthy. These five types are relevant to RHEL 9; the upstream systemd 252 manual provides the reference semantics. Consult the installed man systemd.service for the exact packaged version and backports.[12] Type When startup is considered complete Main point simple After systemd forks the service process, before successful executable invocation is confirmed Run the main service in the foreground; follow-up jobs can begin before the executable is ready exec After successful execution of the service binary (execve) Detects invocation failures such as a missing executable; it does not wait for application readiness notify After a valid READY=1 notification The program must implement the notification protocol; setting this type alone cannot add readiness support forking After the original process exits as part of daemonization Intended for traditional forking daemons. Use a reliable PIDFile= where appropriate; identifying the main process by guessing can be unreliable oneshot After the start command(s) finish successfully Suitable for finite setup work. With RemainAfterExit=yes, systemd can regard the unit as active after the commands exit; otherwise it normally becomes inactive Service processes are tracked as a group; do not reduce systemd tracking to “the orphan happened to be adopted by PID 1.” Choose the type matching the program’s actual behavior. After= expresses ordering, while requirement dependencies such as Requires= have different semantics.[99] An exec service that has started can still fail during its own initialization.[12] For boot targets, see init system; for resource policy, see limits and cgroups. RHEL’s packaged unit and its vendor-defined OS identity are the starting point. A familiar unit name does not establish package origin or prove that another distributor’s helper script exists. Use read-only inspection on the actual host; sshd.service below is an inspection example, not an instruction to restart remote access: systemctl cat sshd.service systemctl show sshd.service -p FragmentPath -p DropInPaths -p User -p Group systemctl status sshd.service journalctl -u sshd.service -b systemctl cat shows the unit and drop-ins; show exposes manager properties, while the journal records startup/runtime messages. An empty User= for a system service does not mean no OS identity: the service may begin with the manager’s default root identity and drop privileges internally.[48][55] For a separately approved service change, preserve the installed configuration and existing drop-ins, then use systemctl edit UNIT (replace UNIT) for a narrow override in /etc/systemd/system/. Do not overwrite /usr/lib/systemd/system/ or shadow the complete vendor unit merely to change one limit. Use the installed systemd-analyze verify on the actual unit path; after editing, systemctl daemon-reload reloads unit definitions, not the application’s own configuration. Plan a service reload/restart only when that service supports the required operation and its maintenance/recovery conditions are met.[48][99] For a service depending on a custom data mount, a [Unit] drop-in can use RequiresMountsFor=/srv/service-data for the approved actual path. This adds mount requirements/ordering, not a test that the correct volume, files or encryption keys are present. Check mount identity and service data before start. After=network-online.target is also not a guarantee that a remote database or DNS endpoint is healthy.[99] After the planned change, verify the intended unit, effective properties, application readiness, logs, listeners and a fresh client connection; distinguish enabled (boot policy) from active (current state). Test persistence/restart during the maintenance window. If it fails, restore only the changed drop-in/application settings, reload the manager and recover the intended service; do not remove unrelated overrides or repeatedly reset a failed unit without resolving its cause.[48]

title: Finding, editing and protecting files
context: Operating systems
text: Examples use Bash and GNU/Linux tools on RHEL 9. Command names, options and most file names are case-sensitive. In synopsis notation, brackets mean optional arguments, not literal characters to type; replace names such as DIR, FILE, DEVICE and USER with the verified target.[18][19] command [-f] [--flag] arguments Inspect with unprivileged commands first. Administrative commands below require the appropriate authorization; do not add sudo to a command merely to hide a permission error. The command table distinguishes discovery from actions that change mounts, databases, host identity or time.[20][19][54] Command Meaning command -v CMD Bash-aware command lookup; may report a builtin, function, alias or path which CMD External PATH lookup where installed; does not reliably describe every shell construct.[125] find DIR -name '*.conf' Search below DIR by basename; quote patterns so the shell does not expand them first find DIR -wholename '*/config/*' GNU find full-path match; -path is the more portable spelling locate PATTERN Search a prebuilt filename database if a locate implementation is installed; results may be stale or exclude paths.[131] updatedb Rebuild that locate database with the implementation’s configuration, often /etc/updatedb.conf; an authorized maintenance action that can traverse many files whatis CMD Short manual-page description from the manual index.[127] man CMD Manual page; specify a section such as man 5 passwd when needed.[112] CMD --help Built-in help for commands supporting this convention df -h FILE Filesystem space usage for the filesystem containing FILE; omit FILE to list filesystems du -h -d 1 DIR Storage usage for DIR and one level of subdirectories; allocated blocks need not equal apparent file size lsblk / lsblk -f Block-device topology / filesystem information.[100] findmnt Current mount information.[101] mount DEVICE MOUNTPOINT Mount a verified filesystem; requires appropriate privileges/policy umount MOUNTPOINT Unmount; it may fail while files or working directories are in use Ctrl+r / history Search / list Bash command history; never place passwords in commands to begin with w Logged-in sessions and activity, including TTY, login/idle and CPU information.[110] who Logged-in sessions and terminals last Login history where records exist; not proof that every access path was audited.[111] whoami Effective user name; not necessarily the original login identity who am i Login record for the current terminal, if one exists users Names associated with current login records finger Optional user-information utility; frequently absent or restricted; not required for administration stat FILE Metadata including access, modification and status-change times. ctime is not creation time date Print date/time. Setting time is a separate privileged action and can disrupt logs/authentication hostnamectl status Systemd host/OS/kernel information; /etc/os-release describes the OS hostnamectl set-hostname NAME Set hostname when authorized; coordinate DNS, monitoring and application identities first uname -a Kernel/system information; not the full distribution/package inventory Before mounting, verify the source device and destination with lsblk -f and findmnt; mounting over a nonempty directory hides its existing contents until unmount.[102] Do not unmount a filesystem with active database/application work or force-detach it as a routine fix.[103] For new filesystems and destructive operations, use the partition procedure. Use these operations inside a known working directory. cp, mv, redirection and archive extraction can overwrite existing data. rm has no general undo: inspect expanded names and protect backups before removal. Do not experiment on system, database or shared directories.[19][21] Command Meaning cd PATH / cd - Change directory / return to the previous directory ls List directory entries ls -l Long format. ll works only if your environment defines that alias/function ls -a Include dot entries and hidden names ls -lh Human-readable sizes with long format ls -lu Display access time instead of modification time in long format; -u also interacts with sorting lsof List open files; visibility depends on privileges and process namespace.[113] cp SOURCE DEST Copy; existing destination data can be overwritten cp -r DIR DEST Recursive copy; choose -a when the intended semantics are metadata-preserving archive copy mv SOURCE DEST Move/rename; can replace a destination mkdir DIR / mkdir -p parent/child Create a directory / create required parents rm FILE Remove a file name; irreversible without another copy rm -r DIR Recursively remove a directory tree; verify every selected path first rm -f FILE Suppress prompts and ignore nonexistent operands; does not make removal safer rmdir DIR Remove an empty directory touch FILE Update timestamps; create an empty file if it does not exist echo 'text' Write text to standard output; use printf when portable escape/option behavior matters cat FILE1 FILE2 Concatenate content to standard output CMD > FILE / CMD 1> FILE Redirect stdout, truncating FILE CMD 2> FILE Redirect stderr, truncating FILE CMD &> FILE Bash: redirect stdout and stderr to one file CMD >> FILE Append stdout; use 2>> for stderr or Bash &>> for both grep -v 'word' FILE Exclude lines matching the expression grep -w 'word' FILE Match the expression as a whole word awk '{print $1, $2}' FILE Print the first two whitespace-separated fields cut -c1 FILE Select the first character position of each line sed -n '5p' FILE Print only line 5 CMD | less Page through command stdout; there is no stout command head FILE / tail FILE Show the beginning/end of a file tar -cvf archive.tar FILES Create an uncompressed tar archive tar -Avf a1.tar a2.tar Concatenate the members of uncompressed a2.tar onto a1.tar; does not merge compressed archives tar -rvf a1.tar FILES Append files to an uncompressed archive tar -czvf archive.tar.gz DIR Create a gzip-compressed tar archive tar -tf archive.tar.gz List archive members; GNU tar recognizes compression when reading a file tar -xvf archive.tar.gz Extract into the current directory; use only after listing and selecting a safe destination gzip FILE Compress, normally replacing the input with FILE.gz; gzip -k FILE retains it For the filter examples, grep matches text, sed selects a line here, and Awk selects fields; these are distinct languages with their own quoting rules.[73][74][75] gzip normally replaces its input; use its keep option when retaining the original is required.[76] Expansion happens before the command runs. The source-style expression file00{4,5,6} expands to three names; f3* can match many more than intended. Inspect instead of deleting while learning: printf '%s\n' file1 file2 f3* file00{4,5,6} For an archive, first list its contents, then extract as an unprivileged user into a new, empty, dedicated directory, not over a live tree. Treat untrusted archives as untrusted files even when tar rejects common traversal paths. Appending to a tar file or creating an archive with an existing output name changes that file; preserve the prior archive if it is a backup.[21][18] The split orientation names refer to the separating boundary: horizontal splits are stacked, vertical splits are side by side.[22] The editing and formatting commands below follow Vim’s editing and option manuals.[77][78] Command Meaning vim -o file1 file2 Open stacked horizontal splits vim -O file1 file2 Open side-by-side vertical splits :r FILE Insert a file’s content below the current line :set textwidth=80 Set an automatic formatting width; behavior depends on formatting options and insertion/reformatting, not display-only wrapping of all existing lines :split FILE / :vsplit FILE Horizontal / vertical split :qa Quit all windows; refuses when unsaved changes require attention :only Close other windows, subject to modified-buffer checks :wq / ZZ Write and quit; ZZ writes only if the buffer changed Ctrl+w then an arrow Move to th

title: Ownership, permissions and attributes
context: Operating systems · Finding, editing and protecting files
text: Change permissions only on files you are authorized to administer. Broad recursive ownership/permission changes can expose secrets or break services; inspect the exact path and current settings first.[19] Command or notation Meaning chown USER:GROUP PATH Change owner and group (requires suitable privilege); chown USER PATH changes the owner chgrp GROUP PATH Change group ownership subject to permissions chmod u=rw,g=r,o= FILE Explicit symbolic mode example; u, g, o mean owner, group and other; +, -, = add/remove/set selected bits chmod 640 FILE Numeric mode: read = 4, write = 2, execute/search = 1 for each owner/group/other digit chmod +t DIR / chmod -t DIR Set/remove sticky bit. In a writable directory it restricts removal/rename to authorized owners or privileged processes; it does not prevent modification of writable file contents t versus T in ls -l Sticky bit with / without the other-execute bit chattr +a FILE Append-only attribute on supporting filesystems; writes must append. Setting/clearing protected attributes requires appropriate privilege chattr +i FILE Immutable attribute on supporting filesystems; a suitably privileged administrator can clear it, so it is not protection from all root actions lsattr FILE Inspect supported file attributes umask Display the current creation mask umask 022 Mask group/other write on future creations in this shell and descendants, subject to the requested mode and default ACLs Without a default ACL, creation permissions are requested mode AND the complement of umask. For the usual requested modes, mask 022 gives files 0644 from 0666 and directories 0755 from 0777; mask 002 gives files 0664. This is bit clearing, not a universally valid subtraction formula, and does not alter existing files. Default ACL inheritance can change the calculation.[88][19] Append-only and immutable attributes are filesystem-specific controls, separate from mode bits.[53]

title: Filesystems, RAID, directories and partitions
context: Operating systems
text: RHEL 9’s usual local choices are XFS and ext4. Btrfs and OpenZFS below are cross-platform comparisons, not instructions to deploy unsupported RHEL filesystem packages. Features depend on format options, software version and storage layout.[23] Filesystem Crash consistency Integrity checks Native snapshots Integrated multi-device/RAID Typical fit ext4 Journaling, with mode-dependent data handling Metadata checksums when enabled; no general file-data checksum No; lower layers such as LVM can snapshot No; use a separate storage layer General-purpose Linux filesystems Btrfs Copy-on-write Data and metadata checksums, with exceptions for configured modes such as NODATASUM Yes Yes; profiles have distinct limits and failure behavior Linux deployments needing subvolumes/snapshots and validated Btrfs support XFS Metadata journaling Metadata checksums on modern formats; not general file-data checksums No native volume snapshots; reflink file clones are different No; use a separate storage layer Scalable general/server storage; RHEL 9 default.[133][140] OpenZFS Copy-on-write transactional storage Data and metadata checksums; some data checksum properties are configurable Yes Yes, through pool/vdev layouts including mirrors and RAIDZ Storage deployments that support and deliberately operate OpenZFS Btrfs checksum exceptions and OpenZFS pool/checksum properties must be read with their selected layout and property settings.[70][68][69] A checksum detects corruption; repair also needs a sound redundant copy. Neither journaling nor copy-on-write guarantees that every unflushed application write survives a power loss. Choose by supported workload and recovery requirements, not “small files versus big files” alone.[59][24][44] A directory maps names to inode numbers. An inode describes a file’s metadata and data layout; regular-file data blocks hold its content. This is more precise than saying that every directory simply “points to data.” ext4 uses metadata checksums for supported structures; it does not generally checksum file contents.[59][67] Redundant Array of Independent Disks describes families of layouts with different capacity, performance and failure tradeoffs. Hardware controllers, Linux software RAID and LVM RAID implement different management layers. RAID 0 stripes data without redundancy; other levels tolerate only specified failure patterns.[83][141] RAID is not a backup. It does not independently protect against deletion, malicious changes, application corruption or loss of the whole host. A local snapshot is also not an independent backup. Keep restorable copies in a separate failure domain and verify recovery; after a disk failure, a rebuild is a period of additional risk, not proof the data is safe.[23][44] The following is a systemd/Linux layout reference. RHEL 9 uses a merged /usr layout, so several traditional root directories are compatibility symlinks.[14] Path Purpose / Root of the filesystem namespace /boot Kernel/initramfs and boot-related files; the ESP may be mounted at /boot/efi /dev Device nodes and related interfaces /bin Traditional essential command path; commonly a symlink to /usr/bin /sbin Traditional system-administration commands; commonly a symlink to /usr/sbin /usr Installed userspace binaries, libraries and shareable data; not users’ home directories. Can be read-only in an appropriate deployment /opt Optional/add-on application trees /lib, /lib64 Traditional library paths, commonly linked into /usr; kernel modules conventionally under /lib/modules /home Ordinary users’ home directories /root Root user’s home /etc Host-specific configuration /var Variable persistent data such as logs, spool and application state; individual subpaths may have different retention /tmp Temporary files; may be cleared on boot or by age-based cleanup. Not guaranteed to last a session or survive reboot /var/tmp Temporary files normally retained across boots, but still subject to cleanup policy /mnt Conventional temporary mount location /proc Virtual process/kernel interface, including per-PID directories /sys Virtual interface to devices and other kernel objects Inspection and creation are different operations. These examples target the RHEL 9 util-linux/e2fsprogs/GNU Parted tools; the first commands only inspect.[100][101][26] lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS,MODEL,SERIAL findmnt sudo fdisk -l sudo parted --list Tool Role parted Inspect/edit GPT or MBR partition tables; print is inspection, creating/deleting partitions writes metadata fdisk Interactive partition-table editor supporting GPT and MBR, not only legacy MBR; -l lists tables partprobe Requests that the kernel update its view of partition-table changes; busy devices can prevent a safe reread.[137] mkfs.ext4 DEVICE or mke2fs -t ext4 DEVICE Create an ext4 filesystem, overwriting filesystem metadata on the selected device Formatting destroys the selected filesystem. Use only an explicitly approved, expendable test partition or approved maintenance target with a verified backup. Identify it by capacity, serial/WWN and storage ownership—not by assuming /dev/sda1 is spare. Confirm it is neither mounted nor swap and is not a live RAID/LVM member; stop dependent workloads and obtain console access before changing a boot/storage device.[26][27][52] Schematic alternatives—not a paste-ready device selection: mkfs.ext4 /dev/disk/by-id/VERIFIED-TEST-PARTITION # Equivalent filesystem choice, not a second required step: mke2fs -t ext4 /dev/disk/by-id/VERIFIED-TEST-PARTITION After an authorized change, inspect lsblk -f and the partition layout, mount only at an approved empty test mount point, and verify access/ownership before allowing workloads onto it. Do not force a partition reread on a busy production disk. Formatting has no general “undo”; restore from backup if the wrong data was destroyed. For basic mounting, see file commands.

text: Redundant Array of Independent Disks describes families of layouts with different capacity, performance and failure tradeoffs. Hardware controllers, Linux software RAID and LVM RAID implement different management layers. RAID 0 stripes data without redundancy; other levels tolerate only specified failure patterns.[83][141] RAID is not a backup. It does not independently protect against deletion, malicious changes, application corruption or loss of the whole host. A local snapshot is also not an independent backup. Keep restorable copies in a separate failure domain and verify recovery; after a disk failure, a rebuild is a period of additional risk, not proof the data is safe.[23][44]

title: Directory structure
context: Operating systems · Filesystems, RAID, directories and partitions
text: The following is a systemd/Linux layout reference. RHEL 9 uses a merged /usr layout, so several traditional root directories are compatibility symlinks.[14] Path Purpose / Root of the filesystem namespace /boot Kernel/initramfs and boot-related files; the ESP may be mounted at /boot/efi /dev Device nodes and related interfaces /bin Traditional essential command path; commonly a symlink to /usr/bin /sbin Traditional system-administration commands; commonly a symlink to /usr/sbin /usr Installed userspace binaries, libraries and shareable data; not users’ home directories. Can be read-only in an appropriate deployment /opt Optional/add-on application trees /lib, /lib64 Traditional library paths, commonly linked into /usr; kernel modules conventionally under /lib/modules /home Ordinary users’ home directories /root Root user’s home /etc Host-specific configuration /var Variable persistent data such as logs, spool and application state; individual subpaths may have different retention /tmp Temporary files; may be cleared on boot or by age-based cleanup. Not guaranteed to last a session or survive reboot /var/tmp Temporary files normally retained across boots, but still subject to cleanup policy /mnt Conventional temporary mount location /proc Virtual process/kernel interface, including per-PID directories /sys Virtual interface to devices and other kernel objects

title: Inspect and manage partitions
context: Operating systems · Filesystems, RAID, directories and partitions
text: Inspection and creation are different operations. These examples target the RHEL 9 util-linux/e2fsprogs/GNU Parted tools; the first commands only inspect.[100][101][26] lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS,MODEL,SERIAL findmnt sudo fdisk -l sudo parted --list Tool Role parted Inspect/edit GPT or MBR partition tables; print is inspection, creating/deleting partitions writes metadata fdisk Interactive partition-table editor supporting GPT and MBR, not only legacy MBR; -l lists tables partprobe Requests that the kernel update its view of partition-table changes; busy devices can prevent a safe reread.[137] mkfs.ext4 DEVICE or mke2fs -t ext4 DEVICE Create an ext4 filesystem, overwriting filesystem metadata on the selected device Formatting destroys the selected filesystem. Use only an explicitly approved, expendable test partition or approved maintenance target with a verified backup. Identify it by capacity, serial/WWN and storage ownership—not by assuming /dev/sda1 is spare. Confirm it is neither mounted nor swap and is not a live RAID/LVM member; stop dependent workloads and obtain console access before changing a boot/storage device.[26][27][52] Schematic alternatives—not a paste-ready device selection: mkfs.ext4 /dev/disk/by-id/VERIFIED-TEST-PARTITION # Equivalent filesystem choice, not a second required step: mke2fs -t ext4 /dev/disk/by-id/VERIFIED-TEST-PARTITION After an authorized change, inspect lsblk -f and the partition layout, mount only at an approved empty test mount point, and verify access/ownership before allowing workloads onto it. Do not force a partition reread on a busy production disk. Formatting has no general “undo”; restore from backup if the wrong data was destroyed. For basic mounting, see file commands.

title: Package cleanup and RPM database recovery
context: Operating systems · Users, processes and resource monitoring
text: On RHEL 9, yum is a compatibility interface to DNF. dnf autoremove selects packages marked as dependencies that are no longer required according to package-manager state; that does not prove the application owner no longer needs them.[50] Preview before any approved cleanup: sudo dnf --assumeno autoremove Review every proposed removal and dependency, protect explicitly required packages, and have a tested recovery path before applying a removal transaction. Verify applications afterward. rpm --rebuilddb / rpmdb --rebuilddb rebuilds the installed-package database; it does not reinstall files or repair arbitrary filesystem damage. Use only for a diagnosed database problem under the distribution’s recovery procedure: prevent concurrent package transactions, take a recoverable backup of the actual configured database, preserve logs and investigate storage errors first. rpmdb --verifydb verifies database integrity; it is not package-file verification. Recheck database queries and application/package health after recovery. Do not delete database files as a speculative “fix.”[49]

title: Windows tools and licensing
context: Operating systems
text: Windows Terminal hosts command-line applications, including Command Prompt, PowerShell and WSL shells. It supplies tabs, panes and rendering; it is not itself the command language.[40] PowerShell is a shell and automation language built around commands and objects. PowerShell 7.x is cross-platform; it is distinct from the Windows PowerShell 5.1 component. Bash commands elsewhere in these notes are Linux examples, not PowerShell syntax.[41][139] Use the product edition, acquisition channel and governing agreement to determine licensing rights. Installation or activation alone is not an inventory of an organization’s entitlements. Keep license records and route compliance questions, reports or vendor audit requests through the organization’s licensing/legal team.[42] Reporting channels, third-party auditors and enforcement practices vary by vendor, agreement and jurisdiction; no particular auditor or reporting organization is universally involved. This is an administration reminder, not legal advice or a statement about any employer’s compliance.
