title: Objects, roles and administration
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL
text: A role may own objects, receive privileges, belong to other roles and optionally log in. Do not make the application the database owner or a superuser simply to avoid grant errors. Ownership includes powers that ordinary grants cannot remove; a no-login owner plus narrow runtime roles gives a clearer boundary.[18][19][59] Role in this example Login Allowed work postgres Local OS peer administration Bootstrap, maintenance requiring superuser; never the application identity. notes_owner No Own database/schema/objects; assumed only by authorized migrations. notes_read No Read objects explicitly granted in notes. notes_write No Read and modify rows plus use identity sequences; no schema creation. notes_app Yes Inherits notes_write; cannot become the object owner. Run the following once in a fresh cluster as postgres. Stop on errors/name collisions; do not repurpose existing roles without reviewing their memberships. \set ON_ERROR_STOP on CREATE ROLE notes_owner NOLOGIN; CREATE ROLE notes_read NOLOGIN; CREATE ROLE notes_write NOLOGIN; CREATE ROLE notes_app LOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOREPLICATION; GRANT notes_write TO notes_app WITH INHERIT TRUE, SET FALSE; CREATE DATABASE adminlab OWNER notes_owner; REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE adminlab FROM PUBLIC; GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE adminlab TO notes_read, notes_write; CREATE DATABASE cannot run inside a transaction block. Set a password interactively with psql \password notes_app after confirming SHOW password_encryption is scram-sha-256; never put a password in command history or these notes. The initial local peer policy requires the matching OS identity, so an app without that OS account connects by loopback TCP/SCRAM; remote access additionally requires TLS.[13][15] \connect adminlab REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC; SET ROLE notes_owner; CREATE SCHEMA notes AUTHORIZATION notes_owner; GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA notes TO notes_read, notes_write; ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE notes_owner IN SCHEMA notes GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO notes_read; ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE notes_owner IN SCHEMA notes GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO notes_write; ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE notes_owner IN SCHEMA notes GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON SEQUENCES TO notes_write; ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE notes_owner REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC; RESET ROLE; Default privileges apply to future objects created by the specified role, not all future objects in a database and not existing objects. Migrations must SET ROLE notes_owner before creating tables; inherited membership alone does not make that role the creator. A schema-level default grant is additive to global defaults, which is why the function EXECUTE revocation above has no IN SCHEMA clause.[20] Use only the new adminlab database. This fixture supports later plan, permission, backup and replication examples; it is not production schema advice. The deterministic generator inserts 2,000 rows. Existing joins teaching remains in the canonical joins lesson, not duplicated here. \set ON_ERROR_STOP on BEGIN; SET LOCAL ROLE notes_owner; CREATE TABLE notes.orders ( order_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, customer_id integer NOT NULL CHECK (customer_id > 0), amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount >= 0), status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('new','paid','cancelled')), created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ); INSERT INTO notes.orders (customer_id, amount, status, created_at) SELECT (g % 100) + 1, (g % 500)::numeric / 10, CASE WHEN g % 3 = 0 THEN 'paid' ELSE 'new' END, timestamptz '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' + g * interval '1 minute' FROM generate_series(1,2000) AS g; CREATE VIEW notes.paid_orders AS SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE status = 'paid'; CREATE FUNCTION notes.touch_order() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY INVOKER SET search_path = pg_catalog AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at := CURRENT_TIMESTAMP; RETURN NEW; END; $$; CREATE TRIGGER orders_touch BEFORE UPDATE ON notes.orders FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION notes.touch_order(); COMMIT; ANALYZE notes.orders; SELECT count(*), min(order_id), max(order_id), sum(amount) FROM notes.orders; A trigger function returns the row to store; SECURITY INVOKER uses the caller’s privileges instead of elevating to the owner. This timestamp trigger is not an audit trail: it records neither old values nor authenticated actor. A normal view is stored query text, not a physical copy; its owner’s access can matter, so review view security before using one to expose restricted data.[50][77] Identity generates values through an implicit sequence; the primary key separately enforces uniqueness. Allocations can have gaps. A manual import of explicit IDs must resynchronize the sequence before writers resume; see migration.[48][60] For existing objects that predate the defaults, apply grants explicitly as owner: SET ROLE notes_owner; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA notes TO notes_read; GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA notes TO notes_write; GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA notes TO notes_write; RESET ROLE; Do not grant TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, ownership or CREATE just to support ordinary inserts. Extension installation is separate: first install its reviewed package for major 18, inspect pg_available_extensions, then CREATE EXTENSION in the intended database using required privileges. Some modules additionally require preloading and a restart.[19][54] \du+ \dn+ \dp notes.* \ddp SELECT has_database_privilege('notes_app','adminlab','CONNECT'), has_schema_privilege('notes_app','notes','USAGE'), has_table_privilege('notes_app','notes.orders','INSERT'), has_schema_privilege('notes_app','notes','CREATE'); Connect in a new session as notes_app using the approved endpoint. Do not trust only an inspection query executed as superuser. Use the bootstrap loopback SCRAM endpoint before hardening, or the verified TLS endpoint afterward.[14][18][19] SELECT current_user, current_database(); SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders ORDER BY order_id LIMIT 3; BEGIN; INSERT INTO notes.orders(customer_id, amount, status) VALUES (42, 1.25, 'new') RETURNING order_id; ROLLBACK; The row insert must succeed and leave no row after rollback; its consumed identity value is not reclaimed.[60] Separately, in interactive psql (not in the setup script), run CREATE TABLE notes.denied_test(id integer); and SET ROLE notes_owner;. Both must fail with a permission error. If either succeeds, stop: review unexpected memberships/ownership before any application use. Do not silently drop an unexpectedly created object as though the test passed. Test readers separately because another inherited group can restore a revoked permission. Change Command Limit Block new logins ALTER ROLE notes_app NOLOGIN; Existing sessions remain; separately review termination. Remove a membership REVOKE notes_write FROM notes_app; Direct/other inherited grants may still allow access. Restore login ALTER ROLE notes_app LOGIN; HBA/password/database grants must also permit it. Change password \password notes_app Rotation does not disconnect old sessions. Remove a role DROP ROLE role_name First resolve ownership and dependencies in every database. For decommissioning, inventory owned/shared objects, reassign ownership to the approved successor, and revoke remaining privileges in each database before dropping the role. DROP OWNED can delete objects; it is not a harmless grant cleanup when the role still owns data. Keep a dependency report and backup. HBA is a connection filter, not an alternative to object grants.[14][19] Command/option Purpose Scope/caution \conninfo, \l+, \dn+ Connection, databases, schemas Check port/database before mutation. \dt notes.*, \d+ notes.orders, \di notes.* Tables, table detail, indexes Pattern and search path affect what is shown. \df+ notes.*, \dv notes.*, \dx Functions

Migrations must SET ROLE notes_owner before creating tables; inherited membership alone does not make that role the creator. A schema-level default grant is additive to global defaults, which is why the function EXECUTE revocation above has no IN SCHEMA clause.[20]

title: Build one small administration fixture
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL · Objects, roles and administration
text: Use only the new adminlab database. This fixture supports later plan, permission, backup and replication examples; it is not production schema advice. The deterministic generator inserts 2,000 rows. Existing joins teaching remains in the canonical joins lesson, not duplicated here. \set ON_ERROR_STOP on BEGIN; SET LOCAL ROLE notes_owner; CREATE TABLE notes.orders ( order_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, customer_id integer NOT NULL CHECK (customer_id > 0), amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount >= 0), status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('new','paid','cancelled')), created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ); INSERT INTO notes.orders (customer_id, amount, status, created_at) SELECT (g % 100) + 1, (g % 500)::numeric / 10, CASE WHEN g % 3 = 0 THEN 'paid' ELSE 'new' END, timestamptz '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' + g * interval '1 minute' FROM generate_series(1,2000) AS g; CREATE VIEW notes.paid_orders AS SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE status = 'paid'; CREATE FUNCTION notes.touch_order() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY INVOKER SET search_path = pg_catalog AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at := CURRENT_TIMESTAMP; RETURN NEW; END; $$; CREATE TRIGGER orders_touch BEFORE UPDATE ON notes.orders FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION notes.touch_order(); COMMIT; ANALYZE notes.orders; SELECT count(*), min(order_id), max(order_id), sum(amount) FROM notes.orders; A trigger function returns the row to store; SECURITY INVOKER uses the caller’s privileges instead of elevating to the owner. This timestamp trigger is not an audit trail: it records neither old values nor authenticated actor. A normal view is stored query text, not a physical copy; its owner’s access can matter, so review view security before using one to expose restricted data.[50][77] Identity generates values through an implicit sequence; the primary key separately enforces uniqueness. Allocations can have gaps. A manual import of explicit IDs must resynchronize the sequence before writers resume; see migration.[48][60] For existing objects that predate the defaults, apply grants explicitly as owner: SET ROLE notes_owner; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA notes TO notes_read; GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA notes TO notes_write; GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA notes TO notes_write; RESET ROLE; Do not grant TRUNCATE, TRIGGER, ownership or CREATE just to support ordinary inserts. Extension installation is separate: first install its reviewed package for major 18, inspect pg_available_extensions, then CREATE EXTENSION in the intended database using required privileges. Some modules additionally require preloading and a restart.[19][54]

title: Verify permissions, including denials
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL · Objects, roles and administration
text: \du+ \dn+ \dp notes.* \ddp SELECT has_database_privilege('notes_app','adminlab','CONNECT'), has_schema_privilege('notes_app','notes','USAGE'), has_table_privilege('notes_app','notes.orders','INSERT'), has_schema_privilege('notes_app','notes','CREATE'); Connect in a new session as notes_app using the approved endpoint. Do not trust only an inspection query executed as superuser. Use the bootstrap loopback SCRAM endpoint before hardening, or the verified TLS endpoint afterward.[14][18][19] SELECT current_user, current_database(); SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders ORDER BY order_id LIMIT 3; BEGIN; INSERT INTO notes.orders(customer_id, amount, status) VALUES (42, 1.25, 'new') RETURNING order_id; ROLLBACK; The row insert must succeed and leave no row after rollback; its consumed identity value is not reclaimed.[60] Separately, in interactive psql (not in the setup script), run CREATE TABLE notes.denied_test(id integer); and SET ROLE notes_owner;. Both must fail with a permission error. If either succeeds, stop: review unexpected memberships/ownership before any application use. Do not silently drop an unexpectedly created object as though the test passed. Test readers separately because another inherited group can restore a revoked permission. Change Command Limit Block new logins ALTER ROLE notes_app NOLOGIN; Existing sessions remain; separately review termination. Remove a membership REVOKE notes_write FROM notes_app; Direct/other inherited grants may still allow access. Restore login ALTER ROLE notes_app LOGIN; HBA/password/database grants must also permit it. Change password \password notes_app Rotation does not disconnect old sessions. Remove a role DROP ROLE role_name First resolve ownership and dependencies in every database. For decommissioning, inventory owned/shared objects, reassign ownership to the approved successor, and revoke remaining privileges in each database before dropping the role. DROP OWNED can delete objects; it is not a harmless grant cleanup when the role still owns data. Keep a dependency report and backup. HBA is a connection filter, not an alternative to object grants.[14][19]

title: Use psql for inspection and repeatable scripts
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL · Objects, roles and administration
text: Command/option Purpose Scope/caution \conninfo, \l+, \dn+ Connection, databases, schemas Check port/database before mutation. \dt notes.*, \d+ notes.orders, \di notes.* Tables, table detail, indexes Pattern and search path affect what is shown. \df+ notes.*, \dv notes.*, \dx Functions, views, installed extensions Inspect definitions/owners, not only names. \x auto, \pset pager off, \timing on Expanded output, no pager, elapsed time Client presentation, not server settings. \o /secure/report.txt, then \o Begin/end query-output capture Protect files; query results can contain secrets. -f reviewed.sql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -X Script with failure exit status, no startup file Wrap suitable SQL in a transaction if all-or-nothing is needed. --single-transaction / -1 One transaction around -f/-c work Not for CREATE DATABASE, VACUUM, concurrent index creation. \copy ... Client-side file import/export Server COPY '/path' reads server files and needs separate privileges. These flags are psql behavior, not SQL executed by the server.[13] # Local administrator, reviewed script; no password in arguments. sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql \ -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 -d adminlab -f /secure/reviewed.sql The OS account executing psql must be able to read/write its script/output paths. \copy (SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders ORDER BY order_id) TO '/secure/orders.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true) writes on that client. Secure reports and delete them under the same retention policy as exported data.

title: Change settings at the right scope
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL · Objects, roles and administration
text: There is no universal MySQL SET GLOBAL translation. Some parameters are session-settable, some superuser-only, some reloadable, and some startup-only. Query pg_settings.context, source, sourcefile and pending_restart before changing one.[12][58] Mechanism Example Lifetime / reversal Inspect SHOW work_mem; Current session’s effective value. Transaction-local SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '10s'; Ends on commit/rollback; use inside BEGIN. Session SET work_mem = '16MB'; Until reset/disconnect; RESET work_mem. Database default ALTER DATABASE adminlab SET statement_timeout = '30s'; New sessions; ALTER DATABASE adminlab RESET statement_timeout. Role/database default ALTER ROLE notes_app IN DATABASE adminlab SET lock_timeout = '2s'; New matching logins; same command with RESET lock_timeout. Config file Edit postgresql.conf or controlled includes Reload or restart per context; restore recorded previous value. Persistent SQL ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = '500ms'; Writes postgresql.auto.conf; then reload. Undo with ALTER SYSTEM RESET ..., then reload. postgresql.auto.conf overrides the main file; command-line settings can override files; role/database/session settings override applicable defaults. File includes and duplicate entries have order. Do not let automation and manual ALTER SYSTEM silently fight over the same parameter. ALTER SYSTEM cannot run in a transaction block.[12] SELECT name, setting, unit, context, source, sourcefile, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('work_mem','shared_buffers','statement_timeout', 'listen_addresses','log_min_duration_statement'); SELECT pg_reload_conf(); SELECT name, setting, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE pending_restart; Reload returning true means a signal was sent, not that every setting parsed/applied. Check file errors, server logs and a fresh session’s value. Restart settings such as port/shared buffers require a scheduled service restart, not repeated reloads.

title: Inspect and stop a session deliberately
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL · Objects, roles and administration
text: SELECT pid, usename, application_name, client_addr, state, xact_start, query_start, wait_event_type, wait_event, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blockers, left(query, 160) AS query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'adminlab' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid() ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST; Query text can contain sensitive values; monitoring privileges and captured reports must be restricted. Ordinary users see limited information about others; grant monitoring roles deliberately rather than superuser.[25] Action Meaning Decision before use SELECT pg_cancel_backend(<confirmed_pid>); Cancel the active query, keep session Confirm PID, user, query start and application; the transaction may still require rollback. SELECT pg_terminate_backend(<confirmed_pid>, 5000); Disconnect session, abort active transaction; wait up to 5 seconds Coordinate app retry and possible external side effects; does not undo already committed work. The angle-bracket PID is deliberately not runnable SQL. Re-query the exact target immediately before signaling to avoid PID reuse. Permissions depend on role membership/pg_signal_backend; only superusers may signal superuser backends. A true cancellation return is not proof a business action was reversed—read back activity and application state.[23] For an idle-in-transaction blocker, cancelling a nonexistent running query is insufficient: ask its owner to commit/rollback, or terminate only after incident review. Continue with wait and performance analysis.

title: Audit, statistics and performance
context: Databases · See what the server is doing · PostgreSQL
text: Server logs diagnose errors and slow statements; cumulative statistics summarize activity; a statement-audit extension records selected classes of action. None alone is an immutable record of every business event. Decide which actor, operation and retention evidence you need before enabling high-volume logging.[24][25][61] Mechanism Good for Does not prove Error/slow statement log Failed connections, errors, slow SQL, lock waits Every successful row change or tamper-resistant audit. pg_stat_* views Rates, waits, maintenance and replication status Permanent event history; counters reset and queries may be hidden. pg_stat_statements Aggregate cost/calls of normalized query shapes Every execution with every parameter. pgAudit (separate extension) Detailed session/object audit using PostgreSQL logs Independent custody, regulatory compliance or protection from host superusers. Application audit events Business actor/reason/correlation Server-wide changes made outside the application. Example server configuration for a measured starting point. Merge with existing values; do not replace an established logging destination blindly.[24] logging_collector = on log_destination = 'jsonlog' log_directory = 'log' log_filename = 'postgresql-%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S.log' log_rotation_age = '1d' log_rotation_size = '100MB' log_min_duration_statement = '500ms' log_lock_waits = on log_statement = 'none' Use the instance’s PGDATA/log created by PGDG setup (0700, owned by postgres), and restorecon -Rv after restoring/copying it.[100][102] For an external log path, use a persistent postgresql_log_t mapping and inspect actual policy/AVCs as in relocation. Restrict access before restarting for logging_collector; most subsequent log policy changes are reloadable. Check pg_settings.context, then SELECT pg_current_logfile(); and produce a known benign event in a fresh test session. Inspect both server log and remote collector receipt. Rotation creates new files; it is not retention deletion. Enforce bounded retention/off-host delivery outside the database.[24] Statement text, errors and parameters can leak secrets even when password-setting commands are treated specially. Avoid blanket log_statement = 'all'; document who can read logs and exclude secret values from application SQL. Watch disk space, ingestion lag and logging overhead after changing policy. Roll back to recorded settings and reload/restart as required if throughput or disk headroom becomes unsafe. PGDG provides pgAudit as pgaudit_18; the inspected RPM is 18.0-1PGDG.rhel9. Review its dependency resolution against this RHEL minor; a filename suffix alone is not dependency validation. Use sudo dnf install pgaudit_18, verify rpm -q pgaudit_18 and rpm -ql pgaudit_18, and keep signature checking enabled.[106] pgAudit is open source, separate from core, with major-specific builds; use the 18.x extension line for PostgreSQL 18, not an arbitrary build from another major. Install its trusted package/binary on every host that may become primary. Check the installed extension version rather than assuming it ships with the server.[61] Preserve the existing shared_preload_libraries list and append pgaudit. Restart in a maintenance window; a missing library can prevent startup, so keep the prior config available. As administrator, CREATE EXTENSION pgaudit; in each database needing its DDL event-trigger support before setting pgaudit.log. For a narrow initial policy, set pgaudit.log = 'ddl,role' in the server configuration and reload. Include read/write only if required and volume-tested; object auditing can restrict relation coverage but must be maintained when new objects are added. Execute a harmless, approved fixture DDL change, then verify the exact event in server and external logs. Test denied actions and role changes against the requirement too. Record overhead, rotation/retention, collector outage behavior and who can alter policy. To remove the extension, first unset pgaudit.log; removing preload needs a restart.[61] Do not copy the example policy into a compliance claim: it deliberately omits ordinary reads/writes, and server administrators can change both extension policy and local files. Install the approved postgresql18-contrib RPM on each relevant host before preloading pg_stat_statements; confirm /usr/pgsql-18/lib/pg_stat_statements.so and its control files with rpm -ql postgresql18-contrib. The inspected contrib RPM also supplies amcheck, pgcrypto and basic_archive; availability of files is separate from extension SQL installation.[101] pg_stat_statements needs its major-18 module files, preloading and query-ID computation. Merge pg_stat_statements into shared_preload_libraries, retain other entries, keep compute_query_id = auto (or on), restart, then create its SQL extension in adminlab.[26] CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements; SELECT queryid, calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time, rows, shared_blks_hit, shared_blks_read, temp_blks_written, left(query, 180) AS query FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10; Use an authorized monitoring role; other users’ text/query IDs require superuser or pg_read_all_stats. Record the stats reset time and sample interval. A high mean time with one call is different from cheap SQL executed millions of times. Do not reset shared counters merely to make a chart look clean.[26] View Read it for pg_stat_database Transactions, temp bytes, deadlocks, cache/block activity by database. pg_stat_user_tables, pg_stat_user_indexes Scans, writes, live/dead estimates, maintenance and index use. pg_stat_activity, pg_locks Active/idle sessions, transaction age, waits and lock identity. pg_stat_io I/O by backend/object/context; distinguish reads, writes and eviction pressure. pg_stat_wal, pg_stat_checkpointer WAL generation and checkpoint behavior. pg_stat_progress_* Progress of supported vacuum/index/backup operations.[89] These are observation surfaces, not exact bloat gauges or end-to-end application timings.[25] After large imports, run ANALYZE and review estimates; for skewed columns consider a measured higher statistics target, then restore the previous target if extra planning/collection cost is not justified. See vacuum and analyze. Use the exact 2,000-row fixture in adminlab, with no concurrent benchmark workload. The table owner can create/drop the test index. EXPLAIN plans the query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes it, including writes, triggers and function side effects. A transaction rollback cannot undo external effects or sequence allocation, so do not profile unknown DML this way.[27] ANALYZE notes.orders; EXPLAIN (COSTS, VERBOSE) SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'new'; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF) SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'new'; CREATE INDEX orders_customer_status_idx ON notes.orders (customer_id, status) INCLUDE (amount, order_id); ANALYZE notes.orders; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF) SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'new'; Plan item/option Interpretation cost=start..total Planner cost units, not milliseconds. Estimated rows versus actual rows Large mismatch suggests distribution/statistics/correlation issues. Actual rows and loops Repeated nodes report per-loop values; interpret work across loops. BUFFERS Shared hits/reads and temp activity; a shared hit is not an application-cache hit. TIMING OFF Reduces per-node clock overhead while still executing/counting. Rows removed by filter Work done for rows not returned; consider predicate/index fit. Heap fetches in index-only scan Visibility checks may still visit heap pages; vacuum state matters. On this small table a sequential scan may remain cheaper; that is not a failed index. Compare result equality, estimates, logical reads and repeated timings under a declared cache/load condition. No elapsed times or chosen plan are promised here. Keep the index only if i

A transaction rollback cannot undo external effects or sequence allocation, so do not profile unknown DML this way.[27] ANALYZE notes.orders; EXPLAIN (COSTS, VERBOSE) SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'new'; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF) SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'new'; CREATE INDEX orders_customer_status_idx ON notes.orders (customer_id, status) INCLUDE (amount, order_id); ANALYZE notes.orders; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, TIMING OFF) SELECT order_id, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'new'; Plan item/option Interpretation cost=start..total Planner cost units, not milliseconds. BUFFERS Shared hits/reads and temp activity; a shared hit is not an application-cache hit. TIMING OFF Reduces per-node clock overhead while still executing/counting. Rows removed by filter Work done for rows not returned; consider predicate/index fit. Heap fetches in index-only scan Visibility checks may still visit heap pages; vacuum state matters. Keep the index only if it benefits the real read workload enough to pay for write/WAL/storage cost; otherwise DROP INDEX notes.orders_customer_status_idx; removes this exact fixture index.[27][28] For a live table, normal index creation blocks writes. title: Identify blockers and resource pressure
context: Databases · See what the server is doing · PostgreSQL · Audit, statistics and performance
text: SELECT pid, usename, application_name, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, clock_timestamp() - xact_start AS transaction_age, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blockers, left(query, 120) AS query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'adminlab' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid() ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST; SELECT l.pid, l.locktype, l.mode, l.granted, l.relation::regclass AS relation FROM pg_locks AS l WHERE NOT l.granted ORDER BY l.pid; A wait event is not necessarily a lock: it may be I/O, client consumption, WAL flush or synchronous replication. Follow blocker PIDs to the oldest transaction, check application ownership, then ask it to finish. Use cancel versus terminate only after identifying the exact target. Killing the visible victim leaves the root blocker intact.[9][23][25]

title: Budget memory and connections together
context: Databases · See what the server is doing · PostgreSQL · Audit, statistics and performance
text: Lever Why it matters Safer first move work_mem Per sort/hash operation, multiplied by plan nodes/sessions/workers; hashes also use hash_mem_multiplier Set locally for a measured query, not one enormous global allocation. shared_buffers Shared cache competing with OS and private memory Change only with a host budget and restart window. maintenance_work_mem / autovacuum memory Maintenance and worker concurrency Sum concurrent operations before increasing. Connection pool / max_connections Backend memory, contention, reserved admin access Remove idle transactions and cap pools before raising server capacity. Temp-file activity Sort/hash spill or large intermediate results Check query shape and selective indexes before adding RAM. Checkpoints/WAL/archive Bursty I/O or retained WAL Correlate with disk latency, slots and archiver health. PostgreSQL memory is not a single buffer-pool cap.[63] Compare database views with host CPU, filesystem bytes/inodes, storage latency and memory/swap, taking matched time samples. A high buffer hit ratio can coexist with slow locking, CPU-heavy queries or WAL waits. Change one hypothesis at a time; record old values, workload, interval and result, then revert changes that do not improve the chosen objective.

title: Backup and point-in-time recovery
context: Databases · Back up, then restore · PostgreSQL
text: RPO is acceptable lost work; RTO is acceptable time to restore service. A successful backup command measures neither. Budget detection, provisioning, download/decryption, restore, WAL replay, validation and routing—not just copy time. Replication is not backup: it can faithfully reproduce a mistaken delete.[33][38] Method Captures Recovery boundary pg_dump One database’s logical definitions/data in a consistent snapshot Selective restore and major migration; no cluster globals or WAL replay. pg_dumpall --globals-only Roles and tablespaces Complement to per-database dumps; protect role hashes if included. Full pg_basebackup with WAL Whole physical cluster, including all databases/tablespaces Same-major physical restore on a compatible platform. Base backup + continuous WAL archive Cluster state plus later changes PITR to a reachable target, only with an unbroken required WAL chain. Consistent storage snapshot All required volumes at one coordinated point, or a clean stopped copy A casual live directory copy is not a consistent backup. Keep multiple generations in separate failure domains, encrypt off-host copies and restrict delete rights. Retain encryption keys, recovery credentials, extension packages, configs, certificate chains and archive metadata separately from a failed host. Test restoring with the keys the recovery team can actually retrieve. Never delete archive WAL solely by file age: retain all WAL needed by the oldest retained recoverable base and every recovery/replica consumer.[31][33] This bounded procedure backs up adminlab on postgresql-18 and restores it to a fresh, isolated postgresql-18-restore cluster on port 5543. As the OS postgres account: /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_dump -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 \ -U postgres -d adminlab --format=custom \ --file=/srv/pg-backups/logical-drill/adminlab.dump /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_dumpall -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 \ -U postgres --globals-only --no-role-passwords \ --file=/srv/pg-backups/logical-drill/globals.sql /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_restore --list \ /srv/pg-backups/logical-drill/adminlab.dump Require zero exit status and retain stderr for both exports; --list only reads the archive catalog, not every data block. A dump uses one database snapshot and can coexist with writes, but holds locks and can conflict with DDL. Multiple database dumps are not automatically one cluster-wide transaction snapshot.[29][31] Option Use Restriction -Fc / --format=custom Compressed, selective restore archive Parallel dump requires directory format instead. -Fd -j 4 Parallel directory dump Destination must not already exist; adds connections and load. --schema-only / --data-only Definitions or contents only Not a complete backup; dependencies still matter. -n schema / -t pattern Filter objects Dependencies outside selection are not necessarily included. pg_restore --exit-on-error Fail instead of continuing past errors Inspect failures; partial work otherwise may remain. pg_restore --single-transaction Atomic bounded restore Cannot combine with parallel jobs; large restores may need a different plan. --no-owner --no-acl Restore under new ownership without grants Useful for deliberate remapping, not permission-fidelity validation. --clean / --create Drop objects / use database name in archive Destructive; intentionally absent from this drill. Here OS postgres connects over the local socket using the bootstrap replication peer rule; no network superuser exposure is added. title: Decide what must be recoverable
context: Databases · Back up, then restore · PostgreSQL · Backup and point-in-time recovery
text: RPO is acceptable lost work; RTO is acceptable time to restore service. A successful backup command measures neither. Budget detection, provisioning, download/decryption, restore, WAL replay, validation and routing—not just copy time. Replication is not backup: it can faithfully reproduce a mistaken delete.[33][38] Method Captures Recovery boundary pg_dump One database’s logical definitions/data in a consistent snapshot Selective restore and major migration; no cluster globals or WAL replay. pg_dumpall --globals-only Roles and tablespaces Complement to per-database dumps; protect role hashes if included. Full pg_basebackup with WAL Whole physical cluster, including all databases/tablespaces Same-major physical restore on a compatible platform. Base backup + continuous WAL archive Cluster state plus later changes PITR to a reachable target, only with an unbroken required WAL chain. Consistent storage snapshot All required volumes at one coordinated point, or a clean stopped copy A casual live directory copy is not a consistent backup. Keep multiple generations in separate failure domains, encrypt off-host copies and restrict delete rights. Retain encryption keys, recovery credentials, extension packages, configs, certificate chains and archive metadata separately from a failed host. Test restoring with the keys the recovery team can actually retrieve. Never delete archive WAL solely by file age: retain all WAL needed by the oldest retained recoverable base and every recovery/replica consumer.[31][33]

title: Take a full physical base backup
context: Databases · Back up, then restore · PostgreSQL · Backup and point-in-time recovery
text: Use PostgreSQL 18 tools against the 18 server. The baseline below intentionally excludes external tablespaces: inspect pg_tablespace first and stop if any user tablespace exists. For those clusters use a complete reviewed mapping for every external path with --tablespace-mapping=old=new or tar archives and an isolated host. Plain-format backups otherwise use the source’s absolute tablespace paths—a dangerous same-host surprise.[32] The backup account needs replication capability and a matching HBA rule. Here OS postgres connects over the local socket using the bootstrap replication peer rule; no network superuser exposure is added. Check wal_level is replica or higher and enough max_wal_senders are available: --wal-method=stream uses a second connection.[32] As administrator, provision empty /srv/pg-backups/base-drill owned by postgres, mode 0700, with enough free space. Then as OS postgres: /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_basebackup \ --host=/run/postgresql --port=5432 --username=postgres \ --pgdata=/srv/pg-backups/base-drill --format=plain \ --wal-method=stream --checkpoint=spread --progress /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_verifybackup /srv/pg-backups/base-drill Option Meaning / reason --wal-method=stream Includes WAL needed to make the base consistent; temporary slot protection is used when supported and no permanent slot was requested. --checkpoint=spread Spreads checkpoint work; fast can create an I/O burst. --format=plain Direct physical file layout; safest here only because external tablespaces were excluded. --write-recovery-conf / -R Creates standby settings; not used for a standalone backup. --no-sync Skips durable file synchronization; do not use for real backups. --incremental A different backup chain requiring manifests/WAL summaries and combination before restore; not what this full-backup procedure does. A manifest check catches many missing/corrupt files, not every possible server/application failure. Use matching major tools for WAL verification and perform an actual isolated restore. Preserve the completed backup read-only; never start the only backup directory itself.[32][35] PGDG config/HBA/auto.conf normally reside inside PGDATA, so the physical backup includes them; inspect and neutralize source-specific settings before restore. External includes, systemd units/drop-ins, tmpfiles definitions, SELinux local mappings, firewalld rules and any certificates/secrets outside PGDATA still require separate protected backup.[100] Also retain roles’ operational secrets, TLS material, extension versions, system identifier, start/end times, tablespace map and archive/timeline metadata. Do not include secrets in a world-readable job log.

title: Rehearse PITR with a named target
context: Databases · Back up, then restore · PostgreSQL · Backup and point-in-time recovery
text: PITR needs a base backup plus continuous WAL from its starting point through the target. A dump archive cannot substitute. This local, no-tablespace exercise uses core’s example basic_archive module to learn the chain; it is not an off-site production backup system. Production archiving needs monitored durable storage, collision-safe/idempotent delivery, encryption, retention and restore-tested tooling.[33][67] Before the physical backup above, create a new archive directory /srv/pg-archive/main owned by postgres mode 0700 on persistent storage. Install the approved postgresql18-contrib RPM and verify /usr/pgsql-18/lib/basic_archive.so with rpm -ql postgresql18-contrib.[101] The server writes this custom archive path, so check current policy and add a narrow persistent data label, then apply it; do not label a whole backup filesystem indiscriminately:[102][104] sudo semanage fcontext -a -t postgresql_db_t '/srv/pg-archive/main(/.*)?' sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/pg-archive/main Use -a only when the exact local mapping does not already exist; review a conflicting mapping rather than overwrite it. Verify owner/mode, all parent traversal and mount readiness; add RequiresMountsFor=/srv/pg-archive/main to the source unit and reload systemd. Configure the source: wal_level = replica archive_mode = on archive_command = '' archive_library = 'basic_archive' basic_archive.archive_directory = '/srv/pg-archive/main' Restart for archive_mode/any startup settings; inspect the log and pg_stat_archiver. Preserve wal_level = logical if logical replication already needs it; the minimum here is replica, not an instruction to downgrade a working configuration. Do not set archive_command and archive_library simultaneously. Use a different archive namespace per cluster identity, never a shared directory for unrelated primaries.[33][34] Complete and verify the full base backup. Only then, while fixture writers are quiesced, capture baseline counts/sums and the order-1 state. As superuser create a uniquely named restore point and force completed WAL to archive: SELECT pg_create_restore_point('adminlab_before_change'); SELECT pg_switch_wal(); SELECT archived_count, last_archived_wal, last_archived_time, failed_count, last_failed_wal, last_failed_time FROM pg_stat_archiver; Wait for the relevant segment to be archived and verify the archive storage, not merely a non-null historic timestamp. Archive the job’s target name, source timeline and baseline results. Optionally change the fixture afterward to make reversal observable. Do not reuse this target name in a real run: recovery stops at the first matching restore point after backup.[23][33] Use a separate copy of /srv/pg-backups/base-drill at /srv/pg-restore/main, owned by postgres mode 0700. The target must be empty, port 5543 unused, no logical postgresql-18-restore drill running, and no live tablespace paths shared. Verify the copy with pg_verifybackup before modifying recovery configuration. Keep the original base/archive unchanged. Remove any inherited standby.signal from the restore copy only if present. Save its postgresql.auto.conf outside the restored PGDATA and replace it with an empty file owned by postgres mode 0600, so source connection/archive settings cannot override isolation. Save and replace any inherited main/HBA config in the copy. Use the existing tmpfiles-managed /run/postgresql socket directory with the distinct 5543 filename; keep TCP disabled. Put this new postgresql.conf in the restore PGDATA: data_directory = '/srv/pg-restore/main' hba_file = '/srv/pg-restore/main/pg_hba.conf' listen_addresses = '' port = 5543 unix_socket_directories = '/run/postgresql' hot_standby = on archive_mode = off restore_command = 'cp /srv/pg-archive/main/%f %p' recovery_target_name = 'adminlab_before_change' recovery_target_timeline = 'current' recovery_target_action = 'pause' Create pg_hba.conf containing only local all postgres peer. Review compatibility settings from the source before starting: recovery’s max_connections, max_worker_processes, max_wal_senders, max_prepared_transactions and max_locks_per_transaction must not be lower than the source values where required. Install required extension libraries and deliberately choose any preload entries; do not blindly inherit a network or external side-effect configuration.[74] Create recovery.signal as OS postgres in the restore copy only. Register postgresql-18-pitr.service from the inspected vendor unit using multiple instances, with PGDATA=/srv/pg-restore/main and RequiresMountsFor=/srv/pg-restore/main /srv/pg-archive/main. Skip initdb: this is already restored physical data. Keep it disabled at boot. Before launch, create the protected parent/data/log directories and map the copy persistently to the normal PGDATA label tree; do not let a file copy’s old labels silently define access.[100][102] sudo semanage fcontext -a -e /var/lib/pgsql/18/data /srv/pg-restore/main sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/pg-restore/main sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl cat postgresql-18-pitr.service Configure logging_collector = on, log_directory = 'log' in the copy; make PGDATA/log owned by postgres mode 0700 and verify its label. Then: sudo -u postgres touch /srv/pg-restore/main/recovery.signal sudo systemctl start postgresql-18-pitr.service sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql -X \ -h /run/postgresql -p 5543 -d adminlab Verify the intended confined postgresql_t process domain, file labels and absence of relevant AVC denials; journal startup diagnostics belong to postgresql-18-pitr, collector logs to the restored PGDATA/log. The simple restore command copies from a read-only archive to PostgreSQL’s requested file and must fail for absent files; never return success for an unsuccessful restore. The example restricts recovery to the backup’s current timeline; for a post-failover target select the documented descendant timeline and retain its history files. latest is not a substitute for deciding which history is correct.[33][34] Follow journalctl -u postgresql-18-pitr.service and the copy’s collector log. Missing required WAL or an unreached target is failure, not permission to promote early. When the target is reached, verify: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(), pg_is_wal_replay_paused(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(); SELECT count(*), sum(amount) FROM notes.orders; SELECT order_id, status, amount FROM notes.orders WHERE order_id = 1; Compare to the recorded pre-change baseline. A pause allows read-only checks before accepting the recovery point. If the point is too early, a later target may be replayed after stop/reconfiguration; to go backward, restore a fresh base copy. For an approved standalone recovery, SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume(); at the reached pause ends targeted recovery; confirm pg_is_in_recovery() is false and record the new timeline. For a drill, sudo systemctl stop postgresql-18-pitr.service and retain evidence.[34] Target choice Required precision recovery_target_name Unique restore point after backup completion. recovery_target_time Timestamp with explicit UTC offset; inclusivity and transaction commit boundary matter. recovery_target_lsn Known WAL location from the intended timeline. recovery_target_xid Known transaction ID; not a wall-clock ordering shortcut. Set one target selector, not several. Default inclusive behavior applies to time/XID/LSN; for an unwanted committed transaction choose/test the intended boundary explicitly. The selected target cannot precede the base backup’s recoverable state.[34]

title: Prove the restored service is usable
context: Databases · Back up, then restore · PostgreSQL · Backup and point-in-time recovery
text: Validation is acceptance work, not invented command output. Record source snapshot/target, tool versions, backup checksums/manifests, exit codes, elapsed restore stages and each comparison. Identity and recovery: correct system identifier for physical copies; intended major/port/path; target reached; expected primary/standby state; no source connections or live file paths reused. Structure: schemas, extensions/versions, constraints, indexes, functions/triggers, owners and grants. Check invalid indexes and unvalidated constraints rather than counting only tables. Data: per-table counts, null/range checks, totals and deterministic keyed exports/checksums against the same snapshot/target. A count against a source that kept changing is not a valid baseline. Integrity: pg_verifybackup before physical restore; optionally pg_amcheck with installed amcheck and appropriate privileges after start. Checksum/structure checks do not establish business correctness.[35][66] Application: representative reads, join results, a rollback-wrapped write, identity sequence next values, role-denial tests, time zone/collation behavior, external integrations safely disabled. Operations: new backups/archiving, monitoring, alerting and secret recovery work; measured RPO/RTO meet the objective before switching traffic. For the fixture, these read-only catalog checks make structure acceptance explicit. Run in the restored adminlab as an administrator; investigate every returned invalid index or unvalidated constraint, including any documented exception inherited from the source.[28][71] SELECT indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid, indisready FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid OR NOT indisready; SELECT conrelid::regclass, conname, contype FROM pg_constraint WHERE NOT convalidated AND conrelid <> 0; SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension ORDER BY extname; The socket-only logical drill permits only matching OS identities through peer. To exercise the restored notes_app login itself, provision its credentials and temporarily enable a specifically approved loopback/TLS rule and listener, or provide a matching OS test identity; do not switch the drill to trust. A superuser’s SET ROLE notes_app can test grants, but cannot prove login authentication. PITR remains read-only while paused, so defer write/sequence smoke tests until an approved promotion on an isolated copy.[14][34] Logical migration generally loads into the same or newer major; an older pg_dump refuses a newer server, and downgrade restore compatibility is not promised. Physical file/WAL formats are major-specific. Use the target-major dump/restore tools for a planned major migration and read intervening release notes.[29][36] If checks fail, keep the production source unchanged, preserve the failed copy/logs and retry from a clean target after diagnosis. After a real cutover accepts writes, reverting to the old snapshot loses those writes unless reconciled. Keep source log rotation, WAL archive retention and backup retention separate: never rm WAL from PGDATA and never treat archiver success as proof the off-site copy or decryption key is available.

context: Databases · Back up, then restore · PostgreSQL · Backup and point-in-time recovery

title: PostgreSQL foundations and tools
context: Databases · Understand the moving parts · PostgreSQL
text: These notes target community PostgreSQL 18, with server and bundled command-line tools 18.6 as the documentation-review baseline. The official support table lists major 18 through 14 November 2030. Install the maintained 18.x security/bug-fix release available from your approved repository, not an unqualified latest image; record its exact package revision before a change.[1] Linux procedures use RHEL 9.7 x86_64, systemd, SELinux enforcing, PGDG PostgreSQL 18 RPMs. The inspected server/client build is 18.6-1PGDG.rhel9.7 and repository RPM 42.0-66.rhel9.7PGDG. PGDG’s last-two-minors policy is distinct from Red Hat’s RHEL/EUS lifecycle: revalidate the maintained minor and repository dependency match before deployment. These upstream packages are not Red Hat AppStream PostgreSQL or automatically covered by Red Hat database support.[93][94][97] Shell blocks are Bash on that server, not Windows commands. sudo denotes OS administration; sudo -u postgres switches to the database service account. SQL blocks run in psql against the named cluster. The default unit postgresql-18.service manages /var/lib/pgsql/18/data on port 5432; a separate restore drill uses 5543. Paths, addresses and capacity settings called out as examples must be changed for the actual host. Never point a restore drill at the live data directory. Component What it provides Boundary PostgreSQL core Server, SQL, roles, WAL, logical/physical backup and replication Open-source PostgreSQL License; no paid core edition is required for these tasks.[65] PGDG packages Versioned binaries and integration with distro packaging Upstream RPMs, separate from Red Hat’s postgresql-server module/support contract; do not mix service/setup conventions.[97][100] Extensions Additional SQL objects, modules or background workers Availability depends on packages, server major and privileges; CREATE EXTENSION does not download software.[54] Commercial distributions/tools Vendor support or additional features Verify that vendor’s license, compatibility and recovery path; not assumed here. Managed services Provider-operated machines, backups and failover OS access, superuser and supported extensions may differ; these self-hosted procedures are not cloud-console instructions. Call /usr/pgsql-18/bin/<tool> where more than one major is installed. PGDG versioned RPMs place binaries here; postgresql18 supplies clients and postgresql18-server supplies server/setup/unit. Avoid PATH/alternatives ambiguity, especially across majors. A source build commonly uses /usr/local/pgsql; inspect rather than mix trees.[100][105][53] Utility Task Important limit psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d adminlab Run SQL or a reviewed script without user startup customizations Default interactive error handling is not a fail-fast migration runner.[13] pg_isready -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 Check whether the endpoint accepts connections Readiness is not proof of application authentication, schema or recovery health.[73] pg_dump, pg_restore, pg_dumpall Logical archives, restore and cluster globals A database dump excludes cluster-wide roles/tablespaces; logical dumps cannot be replayed with WAL.[29][31][33] pg_basebackup, pg_verifybackup Copy a running cluster and check its manifest/WAL Validation is not a substitute for starting an isolated restore.[32][35] pg_ctl, pg_controldata Control a directly managed server; inspect control metadata Do not run a second controller alongside the package service.[91][92] pg_upgrade, pg_rewind Major-version conversion; rejoin a diverged physical copy Different operations, each with explicit prerequisites and rollback limits.[36][44] Inspect versions with psql --version, /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_dump --version, and SQL SELECT version();. Client and server versions are separate facts. Check extension availability before scheduling a restart: SELECT name, default_version, installed_version FROM pg_available_extensions ORDER BY name; SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension ORDER BY extname; An extension’s files must be installed for this major on every relevant host, then its SQL objects installed in each required database. Superuser is normally required unless the extension is marked trusted; native extension code runs inside the server’s trust boundary.[54] client / driver / psql | Unix socket OR TCP + TLS v postgres supervisor (historically “postmaster”) | matching pg_hba rule + role/database authorization v one backend per connection | parse -> rewrite -> plan -> execute v shared buffers / heap and index pages / WAL The supervisor accepts connections and creates a backend for each; each backend consumes resources, so connection counts need a host budget. The parser checks syntax, rewrite expands views/rules, the planner estimates alternative paths, and the executor reads/modifies rows. title: Choose the server, not just the name
context: Databases · Understand the moving parts · PostgreSQL · PostgreSQL foundations and tools
text: These notes target community PostgreSQL 18, with server and bundled command-line tools 18.6 as the documentation-review baseline. The official support table lists major 18 through 14 November 2030. Install the maintained 18.x security/bug-fix release available from your approved repository, not an unqualified latest image; record its exact package revision before a change.[1] Linux procedures use RHEL 9.7 x86_64, systemd, SELinux enforcing, PGDG PostgreSQL 18 RPMs. The inspected server/client build is 18.6-1PGDG.rhel9.7 and repository RPM 42.0-66.rhel9.7PGDG. PGDG’s last-two-minors policy is distinct from Red Hat’s RHEL/EUS lifecycle: revalidate the maintained minor and repository dependency match before deployment. These upstream packages are not Red Hat AppStream PostgreSQL or automatically covered by Red Hat database support.[93][94][97] Shell blocks are Bash on that server, not Windows commands. sudo denotes OS administration; sudo -u postgres switches to the database service account. SQL blocks run in psql against the named cluster. The default unit postgresql-18.service manages /var/lib/pgsql/18/data on port 5432; a separate restore drill uses 5543. Paths, addresses and capacity settings called out as examples must be changed for the actual host. Never point a restore drill at the live data directory. Component What it provides Boundary PostgreSQL core Server, SQL, roles, WAL, logical/physical backup and replication Open-source PostgreSQL License; no paid core edition is required for these tasks.[65] PGDG packages Versioned binaries and integration with distro packaging Upstream RPMs, separate from Red Hat’s postgresql-server module/support contract; do not mix service/setup conventions.[97][100] Extensions Additional SQL objects, modules or background workers Availability depends on packages, server major and privileges; CREATE EXTENSION does not download software.[54] Commercial distributions/tools Vendor support or additional features Verify that vendor’s license, compatibility and recovery path; not assumed here. title: Use the right utility
context: Databases · Understand the moving parts · PostgreSQL · PostgreSQL foundations and tools
text: Call /usr/pgsql-18/bin/<tool> where more than one major is installed. PGDG versioned RPMs place binaries here; postgresql18 supplies clients and postgresql18-server supplies server/setup/unit. Avoid PATH/alternatives ambiguity, especially across majors. A source build commonly uses /usr/local/pgsql; inspect rather than mix trees.[100][105][53] Utility Task Important limit psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -d adminlab Run SQL or a reviewed script without user startup customizations Default interactive error handling is not a fail-fast migration runner.[13] pg_isready -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 Check whether the endpoint accepts connections Readiness is not proof of application authentication, schema or recovery health.[73] pg_dump, pg_restore, pg_dumpall Logical archives, restore and cluster globals A database dump excludes cluster-wide roles/tablespaces; logical dumps cannot be replayed with WAL.[29][31][33] pg_basebackup, pg_verifybackup Copy a running cluster and check its manifest/WAL Validation is not a substitute for starting an isolated restore.[32][35] pg_ctl, pg_controldata Control a directly managed server; inspect control metadata Do not run a second controller alongside the package service.[91][92] pg_upgrade, pg_rewind Major-version conversion; rejoin a diverged physical copy Different operations, each with explicit prerequisites and rollback limits.[36][44] Inspect versions with psql --version, /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_dump --version, and SQL SELECT version();. title: Authentication, TLS and hardening
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL
text: Network reachability, TLS identity, login authentication and SQL authorization are different controls. A password does not close a public port; TLS does not grant table permissions; an HBA rule does not limit a superuser’s SQL powers. Start local-only and add the smallest required path.[14][16][19] Method/control Use Avoid Local peer OS service/admin identity over protected Unix socket Assuming a TCP password affects peer mapping. scram-sha-256 Password authentication with modern clients Reusing MD5 hashes; PostgreSQL 18 deprecates MD5 password authentication.[15] cert or clientcert=verify-full Client certificate identity, optionally alongside SCRAM Confusing client CN/role verification with server hostname verification. trust No authentication at all Network or routine recovery configuration. password Cleartext password exchange inside a separately secured transport Using without TLS; prefer SCRAM here. Object grants / owner separation Bound what a logged-in role can do Application superuser/owner to “fix permissions.” Keep the OS postgres account noninteractive for normal human use, control sudo access and protect its Unix socket directory. An authorized OS administrator can already act as the database owner; do not pretend the database password protects against host root. For a forgotten database password, retain controlled local peer administration and use psql \password role_name; do not start a public trust-auth server.[13][14][45] Changing password_encryption affects newly set passwords, not existing hashes. For an MD5-to-SCRAM migration, first verify every driver/tool supports SCRAM, select SCRAM, rotate affected passwords securely, then change the relevant HBA rules and test new logins. Keep an authorized local session open until the tests pass.[15] For the RHEL PGDG primary, obtain a certificate from the organization’s trusted CA with the real database DNS name in its subject alternative names. The examples use primary.example.test; replace it with the intended identity. Do not ship a sample private key, publicly trusted wildcard assumption or production self-signed bootstrap here. Obtain/manage CA trust through the organization’s certificate process.[16][69] Place server chain and key at the following example paths, owned by postgres; private key mode 0600, parent directories accessible only as necessary. Alternatively a root-owned 0640 key may be group-readable by the server account, but do not mix that model accidentally. Public CA/certificate files can be readable without exposing the private key.[16] For this RHEL layout, create /var/lib/pgsql/tls owned by postgres, mode 0700; provision the files through secret management. Inspect semanage fcontext -l and matchpathcon first. If a custom path lacks an appropriate existing mapping, add the narrow PostgreSQL-readable data type (postgresql_db_t) to that directory, then apply restorecon -Rv /var/lib/pgsql/tls and verify ls -lZ/AVCs. Preserve key mode 0600: a SELinux label does not grant Unix access. Do the same after atomic certificate replacement because a moved file can retain its old label. Do not enable permissive mode to work around a denied key read.[102][104] # /var/lib/pgsql/18/data/postgresql.conf listen_addresses = 'localhost,192.0.2.10' ssl = on ssl_cert_file = '/var/lib/pgsql/tls/server.crt' ssl_key_file = '/var/lib/pgsql/tls/server.key' ssl_min_protocol_version = 'TLSv1.2' password_encryption = 'scram-sha-256' 192.0.2.10 is a documentation address, not a real interface to bind. The server certificate file must begin with the leaf matching the key, followed by any required intermediate chain. The client separately trusts the issuing root. Confirm package OpenSSL support and certificate/key readability before changing the listener.[16] Use explicit, narrow HBA rules, adapting addresses for the actual private network: # Keep local break-glass administration; peer still checks OS identity. local all postgres peer local all all peer local replication postgres peer # Application host and physical standby, separately authorized. hostssl adminlab notes_app 198.51.100.10/32 scram-sha-256 hostssl replication notes_repl 192.0.2.20/32 scram-sha-256 # Explicit rejections make accidental broad access visible. host all all 0.0.0.0/0 reject host all all ::0/0 reject host replication all 0.0.0.0/0 reject host replication all ::0/0 reject HBA uses the first matching line and never falls through after failed authentication. host matches encrypted and unencrypted TCP; hostssl matches only TLS. Database all does not match physical replication, hence the separate rules. Add any loopback TCP app or logical-subscriber rule narrowly before rejects; keep it hostssl once this policy replaces bootstrap loopback access.[14] The host/provider firewall must independently allow only the intended clients to the intended interface/5432. Use RHEL firewalld, keeping SELinux enforcing. Inspect firewall-cmd --get-active-zones, the actual interface’s zone, --zone=ZONE --list-all and --permanent --zone=ZONE --list-all first. An existing broad postgresql service, 5432 port, trusted zone, rich rule, direct rule or forwarding policy can defeat a new narrow rule; reconcile it under change control before proceeding. Do not remove unrelated management access.[103] After verifying that public really is the intended restricted interface zone, substitute the actual client/standby addresses below. Add runtime rules first, test permitted and denied sources, then persist exactly those rules. No database port is needed on a socket-only drill or on a standby solely receiving outbound streaming connections.[103] DB_ZONE=public # replace only after checking interface/zone assignment APP_RULE='rule family="ipv4" source address="198.51.100.10/32" port port="5432" protocol="tcp" accept' REPL_RULE='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.0.2.20/32" port port="5432" protocol="tcp" accept' sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$DB_ZONE" --add-rich-rule="$APP_RULE" sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$DB_ZONE" --add-rich-rule="$REPL_RULE" # Test actual allowed clients and an unauthorized host before persistence. sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone="$DB_ZONE" --add-rich-rule="$APP_RULE" sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone="$DB_ZONE" --add-rich-rule="$REPL_RULE" sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$DB_ZONE" --list-rich-rules sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone="$DB_ZONE" --list-rich-rules If validation fails, remove these exact rules from both runtime and permanent configuration with --remove-rich-rule, retaining the prior policy; do not blindly --runtime-to-permanent unrelated changes. Reboot/reload persistence must be tested in the approved window. IPv6 needs a separate deliberate source rule or remains denied; provider ACLs require the same narrow policy. postgresql_port_t on 5432/any alternate TCP port permits SELinux binding but is not a firewall allowance. Inspect the installed port map rather than assuming an alternate port works.[102][103] Do not open 0.0.0.0/0 as a diagnostic shortcut. In a maintenance window, restart for listen_addresses; reload for HBA/certificate changes where supported. Inspect pg_file_settings, pg_hba_file_rules, logs and pending_restart—sending a reload signal is not successful validation.[12][16][58] Client example, with no secret in the connection string: /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql -X 'host=primary.example.test port=5432 dbname=adminlab user=notes_app sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=/secure/ca.crt gssencmode=disable' verify-full verifies both trust chain and hostname. sslmode=require does not promise hostname verification: with a root CA file it can also validate the chain for compatibility, but that is still not verify-full. Specify the intended verification mode explicitly. gssencmode=disable keeps this TLS-specific example from selecting a separately configured GSS encrypted path.[17][69] SELECT current_user, current_database(), inet_server_addr(), inet_server_port(); SELECT ssl, version, cipher FROM pg_stat_ssl WHERE pid = pg_backend_p

title: Authenticate clients with certificates
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL · Authentication, TLS and hardening
text: When policy requires mutual TLS, set ssl_ca_file to the CA(s) trusted to issue client certificates. Add clientcert=verify-full to the narrow hostssl ... scram-sha-256 rule to require both a valid matching client certificate and password authentication. Without a configured mapping, the certificate common name must match the requested database role.[16] hostssl adminlab notes_app 198.51.100.10/32 scram-sha-256 clientcert=verify-full Client sslcert/sslkey supply its certificate and owner-only key; its sslrootcert still verifies the server. The cert authentication method instead uses certificate authentication without a second password. Review role mappings in pg_ident.conf if certificate names differ; do not grant every valid client certificate the same privileged role.[14][16][69]

title: Rotate certificates and credentials without lockout
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL · Authentication, TLS and hardening
text: Inventory certificate expiry, hostname/SAN, chain, key algorithm, client trust stores, standby/backup clients and CA revocation requirements. Decide whether old/new trust must overlap. Stage a matching certificate/key pair under the intended ownership/modes and validate the chain/identity. Retain the old valid pair securely for rollback. Use an atomic replacement strategy so the server never reads a half-written pair. Reload the PostgreSQL TLS files on the RHEL target, inspect errors and test new connections from every client class. Existing sessions do not prove the new files work. Passphrase-protected keys have additional reload/startup constraints; unattended services need an approved passphrase retrieval mechanism, not a password embedded in a script.[16] Rotate client trust/certificates or SCRAM passwords through their secret channel, reconnect pools and replication/backup clients, then remove expired/revoked trust after the overlap window. Monitor connection failures and standby lag throughout. If validation fails, restore the still-valid pair/trust policy and reload; verify a fresh connection. If compromise is suspected, rollback to a compromised key is not acceptable—reissue/revoke and follow incident policy. Use ssl_crl_file/ssl_crl_dir where certificate-revocation policy requires it. Revoking a certificate or changing a password does not itself disconnect an established database session; plan termination/reconnect separately if the incident demands it.[16]

title: Bound SQL and filesystem privileges
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL · Authentication, TLS and hardening
text: Use the role/ownership matrix. Runtime identities normally need database CONNECT, schema USAGE, precise table privileges and sequence USAGE, not CREATE in a schema, role administration or ownership. Keep migration credentials separate and revoke temporary elevated access after the change.[19] Capability Why it is sensitive Control Superuser / BYPASSRLS Bypasses ordinary authorization/row policy Dedicated break-glass use with independent recording. CREATEROLE, powerful memberships Can delegate/escalate authority under their rules Review membership ADMIN, INHERIT and SET options. Server file/program roles Read/write server files or execute commands as server OS account Never grant to ordinary import/report users; use client \copy. Writable schema on search_path Untrusted objects can change name resolution Schema-qualify sensitive SQL; remove untrusted create privileges. SECURITY DEFINER routine Executes with owner’s privileges Minimal owner, safe fixed search path, reviewed body and restricted EXECUTE. Extension/native code Executes inside database server trust boundary Signed/trusted packaging, major compatibility, change review. A hardened function is not achieved merely by adding SECURITY DEFINER. Prefer invoker security where possible; malicious shadow objects and overly broad public execute grants can defeat an otherwise narrow role model.[19][21][54]

title: Encrypt the storage and protect recovery material
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL · Authentication, TLS and hardening
text: Community PostgreSQL 18 does not provide a general core switch for transparent whole-cluster data-file encryption. Use OS/block/filesystem encryption and storage/provider controls for that boundary; verify that data, WAL, tablespaces, temporary files, swap and snapshots are all included. TLS protects traffic, not stored files.[45] Storage encryption protects offline media, not a compromised running host: while the filesystem is mounted, the OS exposes plaintext to authorized processes and a sufficiently privileged attacker. Keep recovery keys available through separate protected custody rather than relying only on the host being recovered.[45] pgcrypto provides field-level cryptographic functions; it is not transparent database encryption, and plaintext/key handling in server-side functions has a different trust model. Client-side encryption can keep plaintext away from the server but changes indexing/query/recovery design. Pick a threat model before selecting either; neither makes superuser-controlled application access safe by itself.[45] Secret/data location Required handling libpq passfile Owner-only mode 0600 on Unix; exact host/port/database/user matching; ignored when permissions are too broad.[55] Connection URI/environment Avoid embedded passwords; arguments, logs, process inspection and error reports can leak them. Logical globals dump May contain password hashes unless --no-role-passwords; preserve grants without casually exposing credentials.[31] Base backups/WAL/snapshots Treat as the entire database; encrypt, access-control, separate delete rights and test recovery. TLS/storage encryption keys Separate protected custody, rotation records and tested recovery access. A backup without its key is not recoverable. Logs/exports/support bundles Redact/minimize secrets and personal data; bounded retention and authorized readers. Verify the backup restore drill using the recovery team’s access rather than the original machine’s cached credentials. Revisit hardening after promotion or upgrade: a new primary must inherit an intentional security policy, not accidental defaults from a copied file.

title: Installation, services and instances
context: Databases · Get a server running · PostgreSQL
text: Use a new authorized RHEL 9.7 x86_64 host, systemd, SELinux Enforcing, persistent storage and working DNS/time. The selected upstream PGDG RPM build is PostgreSQL 18.6-1PGDG.rhel9.7, not Red Hat’s AppStream PostgreSQL. PGDG supports the last two RHEL minors and publishes minor-specific repositories because OpenSSL changes broke cross-minor dependencies. If 9.7 is no longer maintained, stop and qualify the current RHEL minor, not a different OS.[93][94][98] Red Hat’s RHEL 9 guide documents its own postgresql-server/module streams, postgresql-setup --initdb, /var/lib/pgsql/data and postgresql.service. Those are not this PGDG 18 installation or a promise of Red Hat support for upstream RPMs. Obtain any required database support separately. These bootstrap steps must not be applied to existing data. Use the official minor-specific repository RPM rather than pinning every OS repository through a global releasever override. Never use --nogpgcheck. The inspected repository RPM is 42.0-66.rhel9.7PGDG: its pgdg18 and pgdg-common URLs explicitly contain rhel-9.7-$basearch, with gpgcheck=1, repo_gpgcheck=1 and the RHEL PGDG key. Review /etc/yum.repos.d/pgdg-redhat-all.repo, enabled repositories and candidate origins; leave testing/extras/non-free disabled unless separately approved. Preserve both package and metadata verification for these PGDG repositories; inspect other repositories separately rather than assuming identical policy.[99] On this clean host disable the distribution’s PostgreSQL module to prevent modular filtering/package mixing. Review the transaction; do not reset/switch a production module as a migration technique. PGDG documents EPEL dependencies for some packages and CodeReady Builder for GIS/development dependencies. Enable those only through approved repository/key procedures when the selected packages need them; never solve dependency errors using another RHEL minor’s RPMs or --skip-broken.[94][95] sudo dnf module disable postgresql sudo dnf install policycoreutils-python-utils sudo dnf --refresh list --showduplicates postgresql18 postgresql18-server postgresql18-contrib sudo dnf install postgresql18 postgresql18-server postgresql18-contrib rpm -q postgresql18 postgresql18-server postgresql18-libs postgresql18-contrib pgdg-redhat-repo /usr/pgsql-18/bin/postgres --version /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql --version sudo systemctl cat postgresql-18.service postgresql18 supplies clients; postgresql18-server supplies the server/setup/unit; postgresql18-contrib supplies modules including pg_stat_statements, amcheck, pgcrypto and basic_archive. pgAudit is separate: pgaudit_18. Record exact package NEVRAs/origins and review the whole DNF transaction before accepting it. Install a maintained approved 18.x, not an unversioned server package.[100][101][105][106] RPM installation does not initialize a database. The inspected PGDG setup script reads PGDATA from the named systemd unit, then calls major-18 initdb as postgres; it does not use a separate distribution cluster registry. Its current auth defaults are SCRAM with local peer, but set them explicitly. The documentation’s HOWTO contains an inconsistent major-17 path in its 18 example; use the actual packaged /usr/pgsql-18/bin/postgresql-18-setup. Check an empty target and available C.utf8 locale (locale -a) before running:[11][95][100] sudo env PGSETUP_INITDB_OPTIONS='--encoding=UTF8 --locale=C.utf8 --data-checksums --auth-local=peer --auth-host=scram-sha-256' \ /usr/pgsql-18/bin/postgresql-18-setup initdb initdb creates a cluster, not merely a database; never run upstream initdb as root. The service account owns /var/lib/pgsql/18/data mode 0700. PostgreSQL 18 enables checksums by default; the option makes the choice explicit. Inspect /var/lib/pgsql/18/initdb.log, PG_VERSION and generated configuration before first start. The wrapper creates PGDATA/log; PostgreSQL logs and WAL are different.[11][100] # /var/lib/pgsql/18/data/postgresql.conf # memory/connection values are examples for a small host listen_addresses = 'localhost' port = 5432 unix_socket_directories = '/run/postgresql' shared_buffers = '128MB' max_connections = 50 password_encryption = 'scram-sha-256' fsync = on full_page_writes = on logging_collector = on log_directory = 'log' Before first service startup, inspect matchpathcon /usr/pgsql-18/bin/postgres and ls -lZ /usr/pgsql-18/bin/postgres. Upstream RPM paths are not proof that the installed RHEL policy labels the executable correctly. If it lacks the required postgresql_exec_t label, have the SELinux policy owner verify that type/domain transition, add a narrow persistent mapping with semanage fcontext -a -t postgresql_exec_t '/usr/pgsql-18/bin/postgres' (only if no conflicting local record), then restorecon -v /usr/pgsql-18/bin/postgres. Do not proceed if the running service remains unconfined; keep enforcing mode and resolve the installed policy explicitly. Repeat this gate for any other major’s executable.[102] Set the socket directory explicitly instead of relying on a compiled default that may include /tmp. PGDG’s tmpfiles rule recreates /run/postgresql as postgres:postgres mode 0755 at boot. Different ports have different socket filenames; socket permissions and peer identity remain separate controls.[100] # /var/lib/pgsql/18/data/pg_hba.conf, ordered initial policy local all postgres peer local all all peer host all all 127.0.0.1/32 scram-sha-256 host all all ::1/128 scram-sha-256 local replication postgres peer Keep local peer administration and local replication for backups. Do not add remote access until TLS and firewalld are ready. No trust rule or database-superuser network password is needed.[14][15] sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/postgresql-18.conf sudo restorecon -Rv /var/lib/pgsql/18 /run/postgresql getenforce sudo systemctl start postgresql-18.service /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_isready -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \ -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 -d postgres In psql inspect SELECT version();, SHOW data_directory;, SHOW config_file;, SHOW unix_socket_directories;, SHOW data_checksums; and \conninfo. Verify the intended cluster, not only “accepting connections”. Check ps -eZ shows the server’s confined postgresql_t domain and n

title: Initialize and enter through the local socket
context: Databases · Get a server running · PostgreSQL · Installation, services and instances
