title: Operate the named service
context: Databases · Get a server running · PostgreSQL · Installation, services and instances
text: Command Effect / interpretation sudo systemctl show postgresql-18 -p Environment -p FragmentPath -p DropInPaths Resolve effective PGDATA, vendor unit and local overrides. sudo systemctl status postgresql-18.service Exact default-major unit; verify SQL identity too. sudo systemctl reload postgresql-18.service HUP reload; inspect parse errors and actual values. sudo systemctl restart postgresql-18.service Disconnects clients; scheduled restart for startup settings. sudo systemctl stop postgresql-18.service Packaged SIGINT fast shutdown aborts active transactions cleanly. sudo journalctl -u postgresql-18.service --since '1 hour ago' Startup/service diagnostics; also inspect pg_current_logfile()/collector logs. The inspected unit uses Type=notify, OS postgres, a PGDATA guard, direct postgres -D ${PGDATA}, KillMode=mixed, KillSignal=SIGINT, restart-on-failure, unlimited startup time and a one-hour stop timeout. Do not run pg_ctl alongside systemd for the same cluster or routinely kill processes. Use systemctl edit drop-ins, not edits to /usr/lib/systemd/system. RPM update scriptlets call try-restart for the default unit; updates therefore need a controlled outage and explicit validation of every separately named instance.[100]

title: Consider a source build only when needed
context: Databases · Get a server running · PostgreSQL · Installation, services and instances
text: A source build is an alternative when approved RPMs cannot meet a requirement, not this production baseline. Obtain the official 18.x archive and verify the published checksum/signature; install documented compiler/library prerequisites. In the extracted source tree, as an unprivileged build account:[53] ./configure --prefix=/opt/postgresql/18 --with-ssl=openssl make make check # Only after real test success and approval of this separate prefix: sudo make install make check starts temporary servers and must not run as root. Keep actual results. A source install supplies neither PGDG’s unit/setup script nor automatic SELinux integration; qualify executable labels/domain transitions, service supervision, extensions, patching and recovery separately before production. Never overwrite RPM-managed files or claim this alternative was tested here.[11][53][102]

title: Diagnose before changing authentication or files
context: Databases · Get a server running · PostgreSQL · Installation, services and instances
text: Symptom Inspect Safe action Service fails Journal, PGDATA/log, mounts/free bytes/inodes, unit/drop-ins Revert last change; never initialize over existing data. Address in use ss -ltnp, socket files, unit inventory and SQL identity Find the exact competing instance, not all postgres processes. Peer failure OS user, socket path, first local HBA match A database password does not repair OS identity. No HBA entry Database/user/source/TLS and ordered rules Add only the intended rule, not network trust. Permission denied namei -l PATH, ls -ldZ PATH, matchpathcon -V PATH, ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC -ts recent Correct DAC/labels/mount access; keep SELinux enforcing. Timeout Route, listener, active firewalld zone/provider ACL, DNS HBA cannot permit packets not reaching PostgreSQL. Connection/memory pressure Pool budget, idle transactions, work_mem, other instances Reduce pressure before raising limits. WAL growth Slots, archive failure, write rate Repair retention/consumer; never delete live WAL. Use getenforce, sestatus, ps -eZ, semanage fcontext -l and semanage port -l on the actual RHEL host. policycoreutils-python-utils supplies semanage. Persistent mappings require both semanage fcontext and restorecon; chcon alone is not durable. Investigate AVC causes instead of disabling SELinux or generating an unrestricted audit2allow policy. Red Hat’s older PostgreSQL example establishes the data-label concept, not proof of this host’s current policy; inspect the installed RHEL 9 types and labels before applying custom mappings.[102][104] SELECT sourcefile, sourceline, name, setting, applied, error FROM pg_file_settings WHERE error IS NOT NULL; SELECT line_number, type, database, user_name, address, auth_method, error FROM pg_hba_file_rules ORDER BY line_number; SELECT name, setting, source, sourcefile, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('port','listen_addresses','shared_buffers'); A clean parse is not proof a restart setting is active. Keep local admin access while changing HBA; reload, test new allowed and denied sessions, and revert the recorded prior file if needed.[12][14][58]

title: Run a second cluster without crossing wires
context: Databases · Get a server running · PostgreSQL · Installation, services and instances
text: PGDG ships one default unit per major, not an instance template or cluster-name registry. Create an explicitly named local unit for each additional instance. This example uses postgresql-18-lab2.service, /var/lib/pgsql/18/lab2, port 5542, shared /run/postgresql and its own PGDATA/log. The socket directory can be shared because port-specific filenames differ; PGDATA must never be shared.[100] Verify the path is empty, unit name unused and port free. Copy the inspected vendor unit to a new local name, preserving its notify/shutdown/user behavior, then override its data path. Do not copy an already customized primary unit inadvertently: sudo cp /usr/lib/systemd/system/postgresql-18.service \ /etc/systemd/system/postgresql-18-lab2.service sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl edit postgresql-18-lab2.service [Unit] Description=PostgreSQL 18 isolated lab2 RequiresMountsFor=/var/lib/pgsql/18/lab2 [Service] Environment=PGDATA=/var/lib/pgsql/18/lab2 Run sudo systemctl daemon-reload, inspect systemctl cat and systemctl show ... -p Environment, then initialize this empty target with the same explicit options as bootstrap, passing the service name as the setup script’s second argument: sudo env PGSETUP_INITDB_OPTIONS='--encoding=UTF8 --locale=C.utf8 --data-checksums --auth-local=peer --auth-host=scram-sha-256' \ /usr/pgsql-18/bin/postgresql-18-setup initdb postgresql-18-lab2 Edit this target’s config/HBA, not the primary’s: use the bootstrap policy, port = 5542, listen_addresses = 'localhost', unix_socket_directories = '/run/postgresql', logging_collector = on, log_directory = 'log'. Inspect SELinux’s port inventory; if 5542 is not allocated, add it as below. If another type owns it, select a different port or review that service before modifying policy. A label permits a bind; it does not open firewalld.[102] sudo semanage port -l # Only after confirming 5542 is available and not already labeled correctly: sudo semanage port -a -t postgresql_port_t -p tcp 5542 sudo restorecon -Rv /var/lib/pgsql/18/lab2 sudo systemctl start postgresql-18-lab2.service sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql -X -h /run/postgresql -p 5542 -d postgres Verify SHOW data_directory, port, system identifier, effective paths and ps -eZ; test clean stop/start. Do not enable a drill at boot or open its firewall. Stop postgresql-18-lab2 afterward; deleting data is a separate decision. New copied units do not automatically inherit later vendor-unit fixes: compare them after package updates and restart each instance in its approved window. Reuse this registration pattern for restore/upgrade/standby names, substituting all paths/ports; never run initdb on restored data.[100] Distinct clusters isolate SQL namespaces and restart schedules, not CPU, disk or memory. Budget aggregate connections/buffers/workers and use resource controls/volumes as needed. A shared OS account can access all those files; use separate accounts/hosts for stronger isolation, with separately reviewed policy.

title: Relocate data during a clean outage
context: Databases · Get a server running · PostgreSQL · Installation, services and instances
text: This is a stopped same-host move, not a live-copy backup. Take a verified backup; record system identifier, effective PGDATA, data_directory, config/HBA paths, external tablespaces and mounts. The destination /srv/pgsql/18/data must be empty/persistent and must not belong to another cluster.[6][22] Drain clients; sudo systemctl stop postgresql-18.service; verify no process owns the source. Create the destination with postgres:postgres, mode 0700 and traversable protected parents. Copy all of stopped PGDATA, including hidden files/configs: sudo rsync -aH /var/lib/pgsql/18/data/ /srv/pgsql/18/data/. External tablespace symlinks remain references: inventory/migrate their storage separately. Compare with sudo rsync -aHn --checksum /var/lib/pgsql/18/data/ /srv/pgsql/18/data/ and investigate differences. Preserve the data/log label distinctions with a persistent equivalence mapping, after checking no conflicting local mapping exists:[102][104] sudo semanage fcontext -a -e /var/lib/pgsql/18/data /srv/pgsql/18/data sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/pgsql/18/data sudo systemctl edit postgresql-18.service [Unit] RequiresMountsFor=/srv/pgsql/18/data [Service] Environment=PGDATA=/srv/pgsql/18/data Configuration moved with PGDATA. Review absolute data_directory, HBA/includes, TLS, archive, socket and log references in both postgresql.conf and postgresql.auto.conf; they must not redirect to the old copy. Do not add a split config layout by accident. Run daemon-reload, inspect effective unit/environment, ownership, mount and matchpathcon -V labels; start only this unit. Verify SQL identity/paths, pg_current_logfile(), confined domain/no AVC denials, representative reads/writes and backup jobs before clients return. Before new writes, rollback can stop this unit and restore its prior drop-in/configs. After new writes, the old copy is stale; reconcile or perform another clean copy-back. Never start both. Retain the original securely through the rollback window. Apply the same custom-path checks to archive/restore/tablespace directories: PostgreSQL-written data needs reviewed postgresql_db_t, external collector logs postgresql_log_t, sockets postgresql_var_run_t; validate available types on the installed policy. Persistent mappings alone do not create directories or grant Unix permissions. Keep backup-only exports accessible only to their tool accounts, not globally labeled writable by every database process.[102][104]

title: Sources
context: Databases · Get a server running · PostgreSQL · Installation, services and instances

title: Joins: keep the rows you mean
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL
text: An inner join keeps only rows that find a partner. Here, the customer id is the shared fact: orders.customer_id points to customers.id. SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY c.id, o.id; name order_id total Ada 101 42 Ada 102 18 Grace 103 35 Ada appears twice because she has two orders. Linus is absent because an inner join has no row to return for a customer without an order. A left join preserves every row from the table on the left. Put customers there when the question is “which customers have—or have not—ordered?”PostgreSQL lesson · customer / orderA missing match is not a missing customerCustomers and their matching ordersSolid curves link Ada to orders 101 and 102, and Grace to order 103. Linus has no connecting curve because he has no matching order. A left join still returns Linus with NULL order columns; no order row is invented.CUSTOMERSORDERSAdaGraceLinusOrder 101Ada · total 42Order 102Ada · total 18Order 103Grace · total 35Linus: no matching orderAda → two matchesOrder 101 · total 42; order 102 · total 18.Grace → one matchOrder 103 · total 35.Linus → no matchNo connecting line and no stored order row.Relationship ≠ result row. The join matches orders.customer_id = customers.id. In this unfiltered left join, Linus produces one result row whose order columns are NULL—not a stored order with zero values. An inner join omits him.Teaching illustration of the lesson’s data, not an exact engine schematic. A customer can have zero or more orders. Every curve represents a real match; the unmatched customer is deliberately unconnected. The text key carries the same information at narrow widths.Read the lesson evidence Why Ada appears twice · Linus and NULL · How filtering changes the result SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY c.id, o.id; name order_id total Ada 101 42 Ada 102 18 Grace 103 35 Linus NULL NULL NULL is useful information here: Linus exists, but no matching order does. It is not zero and it is not an empty string. The location of a filter changes a left join. A WHERE clause runs after the join, so this query removes both low-value orders and the unmatched Linus row: SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.total > 30 ORDER BY c.id, o.id; It returns Ada’s 42 order and Grace’s 35 order: 2 rows. Move the same condition into ON when you want all customers but only qualifying order matches: SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 30 ORDER BY c.id, o.id; That version returns 3 customer rows: Ada with 42, Grace with 35, and Linus with NULL. Ada’s 18 order no longer qualifies as a match. The practical rule is to say the question aloud: “filter the final rows” suggests WHERE; “limit what may match” suggests ON. Run the left join, then move o.total > 30 between WHERE and ON. Predict which people remain before pressing Run. The database is disposable and local to this page; Reset restores the three customers and three orders.

title: Inner join
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL · Joins: keep the rows you mean
text: An inner join keeps only rows that find a partner. Here, the customer id is the shared fact: orders.customer_id points to customers.id. SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY c.id, o.id; name order_id total Ada 101 42 Ada 102 18 Grace 103 35 Ada appears twice because she has two orders. Linus is absent because an inner join has no row to return for a customer without an order.

title: Left join
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL · Joins: keep the rows you mean
text: A left join preserves every row from the table on the left. Put customers there when the question is “which customers have—or have not—ordered?”PostgreSQL lesson · customer / orderA missing match is not a missing customerCustomers and their matching ordersSolid curves link Ada to orders 101 and 102, and Grace to order 103. Linus has no connecting curve because he has no matching order. A left join still returns Linus with NULL order columns; no order row is invented.CUSTOMERSORDERSAdaGraceLinusOrder 101Ada · total 42Order 102Ada · total 18Order 103Grace · total 35Linus: no matching orderAda → two matchesOrder 101 · total 42; order 102 · total 18.Grace → one matchOrder 103 · total 35.Linus → no matchNo connecting line and no stored order row.Relationship ≠ result row. The join matches orders.customer_id = customers.id. In this unfiltered left join, Linus produces one result row whose order columns are NULL—not a stored order with zero values. An inner join omits him.Teaching illustration of the lesson’s data, not an exact engine schematic. A customer can have zero or more orders. Every curve represents a real match; the unmatched customer is deliberately unconnected. The text key carries the same information at narrow widths.Read the lesson evidence Why Ada appears twice · Linus and NULL · How filtering changes the result SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY c.id, o.id; name order_id total Ada 101 42 Ada 102 18 Grace 103 35 Linus NULL NULL NULL is useful information here: Linus exists, but no matching order does. It is not zero and it is not an empty string.

title: Filter placement
context: Databases · Work with objects and access · PostgreSQL · Joins: keep the rows you mean
text: The location of a filter changes a left join. A WHERE clause runs after the join, so this query removes both low-value orders and the unmatched Linus row: SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.total > 30 ORDER BY c.id, o.id; It returns Ada’s 42 order and Grace’s 35 order: 2 rows. Move the same condition into ON when you want all customers but only qualifying order matches: SELECT c.name, o.total FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 30 ORDER BY c.id, o.id; That version returns 3 customer rows: Ada with 42, Grace with 35, and Linus with NULL. Ada’s 18 order no longer qualifies as a match. The practical rule is to say the question aloud: “filter the final rows” suggests WHERE; “limit what may match” suggests ON.

title: Migrating to PostgreSQL
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL
text: A MySQL SQL dump is not a PostgreSQL restore script. Convert the model, SQL behavior and application contract before the outage, then move data under a documented snapshot/change boundary. PostgreSQL logical replication cannot consume MySQL’s binary log directly; cross-engine CDC needs a separately selected connector whose source version, privileges, initial snapshot and offset semantics are verified. Record source server/tool versions, storage engines, SQL modes, charsets/collations, time zones, table sizes, PK/FK/unique constraints, views, triggers, routines, generated columns, events and application queries. Include nontransactional source tables and external side effects when deciding whether a consistent export is possible. The target remains community PostgreSQL 18 on RHEL/PGDG; no migration tool or managed service is silently assumed. Provision that RPM/service/TLS/firewalld/SELinux baseline before loading. Use /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql with the explicit /run/postgresql socket/5432 for local peer administration; target extensions need their RHEL-major-specific RPMs on all recovery/HA hosts. Client \copy below reads the client filesystem, so grant that client account access rather than relabeling exports as server-writable data.[100][105][13] Source concept PostgreSQL target / conversion decision Validate before loading MySQL database used as namespace PostgreSQL database plus named schema Cross-database SQL must be redesigned; schema is inside one database.[21] Backtick/mixed-case identifiers Prefer lowercase unquoted names; double quotes preserve exact case Rewrite application SQL and collisions; do not just replace quoting characters in arbitrary SQL.[78] Signed integer types smallint, integer, bigint by actual range Overflow and negative-value constraints. Unsigned integer / unsigned bigint Wider signed type, or numeric(20,0) where bigint cannot hold the range Add nonnegative/range checks; do not silently wrap or truncate.[79] Auto-increment GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY plus explicit PK/unique constraint Imported IDs, sequence next value, application generated-key API.[48] Decimal currency numeric(precision, scale) Rounding, scale and maximum aggregate values; not floating point.[79] Tiny integer used as boolean boolean only after proving the actual value domain Values other than intended true/false/null need explicit mapping. Datetime / timestamp timestamp for wall-clock facts; timestamptz for instants Source session zone, DST ambiguity, invalid/zero dates and precision.[80] Text/charset/collation Usually UTF-8 plus chosen libc/ICU/builtin collation Case/accent comparisons, trailing-space behavior, ordering and unique collisions.[49] JSON json or jsonb by required semantics/operators Formatting/key-order/duplicate-key expectations; index design.[81] Binary/blob bytea, or an explicitly designed large-object/external store Byte-for-byte comparison, encoding and backup lifecycle.[47] Enum/set Enum, check-constrained text or normalized relation Allowed values, ordering and future schema evolution. The table is a conversion checklist, not a universal mechanical mapping. Inspect actual values and source-version semantics; target data types and operators are defined by the PostgreSQL 18 manual.[47] Use a no-login owner and separate runtime roles as in administration. Keep a checked-in conversion manifest mapping each source object to its target name, type, default, constraint and application change. Avoid importing source administrators or broad grants. Object/behavior Conversion work Defaults/generated columns Rewrite expressions and volatile/time-zone behavior; PostgreSQL 18 defaults generated columns to virtual, so specify STORED when required by the design.[4][70] Views/procedures/functions Rewrite SQL dialect and security semantics; PL/pgSQL is not source-compatible stored-routine syntax. Triggers PostgreSQL uses trigger functions; preserve timing, row/statement scope and privileges explicitly.[50] Scheduled events Choose an external scheduler or separately reviewed extension; not an automatic core event-scheduler import. Upsert / duplicate handling Rewrite to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT with a deliberate arbiter: DO UPDATE requires a supported unique constraint/index, not an exclusion constraint. Do not assume identical affected-row semantics.[82] Indexes Recreate constraints first; redesign useful B-tree/expression/partial/GIN indexes for actual PostgreSQL predicates.[28] Prefix/collation-sensitive unique index Model the intended uniqueness explicitly and detect collisions before enforcement. Sequences They are not gapless and not rolled back; test generated-key handling and post-import alignment.[60] Changing collation can change equality and sort behavior, not just display order. Run duplicate checks under the target comparison before creating a unique index. Do not merely refresh a recorded collation version after an OS/library upgrade; rebuild affected indexes first.[49][87] Test application transaction boundaries, error SQLSTATE handling/retries, pagination stability, boolean/date serialization, parameter placeholders, identifier quoting, connection pooling and permissions. A schema that loads successfully can still implement different business rules. This bounded example assumes a quiesced, consistent CSV export of one source orders table has already been produced and validated by the source owner. It is not a MySQL export or CDC tool recipe. The file contract is UTF-8 RFC-style CSV with header, comma delimiter, double-quote escaping, \N for null, dot decimal, and timestamps already normalized to explicit UTC offsets. If the export uses different escaping/null conventions, convert it explicitly rather than guessing.[46] Example file shape (illustrative input, not captured production output): id,customer_id,total,status,created_at 1,42,12.50,new,2026-01-01T10:00:00+00:00 2,17,8.00,paid,2026-01-02T09:30:00+00:00 3,42,0.00,cancelled,2026-01-03T12:00:00+00:00 Create a new migrationlab database and migration_owner no-login owner using controlled local peer administration. Stop on name collisions; do not reuse a database containing application data. As postgres in psql, outside a transaction for CREATE DATABASE:[13][59] \set ON_ERROR_STOP on CREATE ROLE migration_owner NOLOGIN; CREATE DATABASE migrationlab OWNER migration_owner; REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE migrationlab FROM PUBLIC; \connect migrationlab REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC; SET ROLE migration_owner; Continue in that same owner session. The client OS account must be allowed to read /secure/orders.csv. No application login receives access until mapping and validation are accepted. \set ON_ERROR_STOP on CREATE SCHEMA staging; CREATE SCHEMA sales; CREATE TABLE staging.orders_raw ( id text, customer_id text, total text, status text, created_at text ); \copy staging.orders_raw FROM '/secure/orders.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true, NULL '\N', ENCODING 'UTF8') -- Inspect rejects; resolve them, do not discard them silently. SELECT * FROM staging.orders_raw WHERE id IS NULL OR id !~ '^[0-9]+$' OR customer_id IS NULL OR customer_id !~ '^[0-9]+$' OR total IS NULL OR total !~ '^[0-9]+([.][0-9]{1,2})?$' OR status IS NULL OR status NOT IN ('new','paid','cancelled') OR created_at IS NULL OR created_at LIKE '0000-%' OR created_at !~ '[+]00:00$'; SELECT id, count(*) FROM staging.orders_raw GROUP BY id HAVING count(*) > 1; The reject query is a preliminary screen, not a complete date/range validator. Casts and constraints below are the decisive fail-fast gate. Text duplicates such as 1 versus 01 can still collide numerically; the primary key catches them. If actual source IDs can exceed signed bigint, change the target design before importing, not after an overflow. BEGIN; CREATE TABLE sales.orders ( order_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY CHECK (order_id > 0), customer_id integer NOT NULL CHECK (customer_id > 0), amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount >= 0), status text NOT

SELECT * FROM staging.orders_raw WHERE id IS NULL OR id !~ '^[0-9]+$' OR customer_id IS NULL OR customer_id !~ '^[0-9]+$' OR total IS NULL OR total !~ '^[0-9]+([.][0-9]{1,2})?$' OR status IS NULL OR status NOT IN ('new','paid','cancelled') OR created_at IS NULL OR created_at LIKE '0000-%' OR created_at !~ '[+]00:00$'; SELECT id, count(*) FROM staging.orders_raw GROUP BY id HAVING count(*) > 1; The reject query is a preliminary screen, not a complete date/range validator. title: Validate at a common boundary
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL · Migrating to PostgreSQL
text: SELECT count(*) AS rows, min(order_id), max(order_id), sum(amount) FROM sales.orders; SELECT status, count(*), sum(amount) FROM sales.orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status; SELECT count(*) FROM sales.orders WHERE customer_id <= 0 OR amount < 0; SELECT conname, convalidated FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'sales.orders'::regclass; Compare these with the source at the exported snapshot or final CDC watermark. Equal counts do not prove equal rows: compare ordered primary-key ranges and canonical per-row/per-batch digests or exports. Define identical null, decimal, Unicode, time-zone and binary serialization on both engines before hashing; database-native hash functions over different string formats are not comparable. Include orphan/FK checks, duplicate detection under target collation, bounds/null distributions, money totals, time-zone edge cases and representative joins. Test target grants and expected denials, routine/trigger side effects, generated IDs and application read/write workflows in an isolated environment. Inspect plans after ANALYZE; do not require identical MySQL and PostgreSQL plans, only equivalent results and the agreed performance objective.[27][46][49] Keep a per-table reconciliation report: source snapshot/watermark, target count, comparison definition, rejected rows, owner decision and final acceptance. No rows are “close enough” without an explicit business decision. Masked rehearsals must preserve the data distributions relevant to uniqueness and plan tests.

title: Cut over once, with a rollback boundary
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL · Migrating to PostgreSQL
text: Phase Required proof before continuing Rehearsal Complete conversion, restore/reload timings, application/permission tests and repeatable reconciliation. Initial copy Consistent source snapshot and its CDC start position, or a documented full write outage. Catch-up Connector reports durable applied position, no unresolved conflicts/rejects, DDL changes coordinated. Write fence Source application writers/jobs disabled; remaining transactions completed; final source position recorded. Final sync All changes through the fence applied; sequence state/routines/privileges validated; totals/checks pass. Switch One write authority, endpoint/driver/pool updated, controlled smoke write/readback succeeds. Observe Error/latency/business checks pass, backups and recovery monitoring active, old source kept read-only. For a small system, a full outage plus consistent export/import may be safer than an unproven CDC stack. For low downtime, choose a connector with documented MySQL-version/binlog/snapshot requirements and PostgreSQL delivery semantics; test duplicates, restart/replay, deletes, schema changes and offset retention. This is a product-selection boundary, not a missing command to fake with PostgreSQL’s native subscription syntax. Before target writes are accepted, rollback can leave the source authoritative and discard/rebuild the target. After target writes, the old MySQL source is stale. Returning traffic requires tested reverse movement/reconciliation or an explicitly accepted loss window. Dual-writing both databases is not a free rollback mechanism: ordering, retries, partial success and conflict handling require application design. Retain source backups, normalized export definitions, conversion scripts, source/CDC positions and validation reports through the agreed rollback period. After acceptance, remove migration-only privileges/connector secrets, securely retire staging data and prove a PostgreSQL restore. The migration is not finished merely because the final row loaded.

title: Replication and high availability
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · PostgreSQL
text: physical WAL (whole cluster) applications -> primary ----------------------------> standby | | | WAL archive + base backups | read-only queries v v independent recovery storage promotion only after fencing publisher database -- publication/table changes --> subscriber database logical replication; separate schema/sequence policy Mechanism Replicates Does not supply Physical streaming WAL for the entire cluster, same major and compatible platform Selective table filtering, cross-major upgrade or automatic leader election. Logical publication/subscription Selected tables’ data changes plus optional initial copy DDL, sequences, large objects, all extension state or a transparent HA copy. WAL archive Durable retained segments for recovery/standby catch-up Live failure detection/routing. External HA controller Failure decision, fencing, routing and rejoin policy A replacement for PostgreSQL backups or tested consistency settings. Core PostgreSQL provides replication and promotion primitives, not the software that decides a primary has failed and fences it. A heartbeat alone cannot distinguish failure from network partition.[38][41][64] Two separate RHEL/PGDG hosts, both major 18 with compatible extensions, checksums/platform and maintained minor versions. Primary postgresql-18 is already running; standby has no running cluster at its target path. This bounded setup uses no external tablespaces. With tablespaces, stop and plan all target mappings. Require verified TLS, time/DNS, private routing and a restore-tested backup first.[32][38] Example names/addresses are reserved documentation values: primary primary.example.test at 192.0.2.10, standby at 192.0.2.20. Replace them with actual private addresses and certificate identities. On the primary as administrator: CREATE ROLE notes_repl LOGIN REPLICATION NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE; \password notes_repl Set the password through the prompt with SCRAM selected, not in SQL history. Allow only the standby’s address, and only replication connections, before any broad reject rules: hostssl replication notes_repl 192.0.2.20/32 scram-sha-256 Review settings on the primary. The following capacities are examples, not a formula for every topology: wal_level = replica max_wal_senders = 10 max_replication_slots = 10 max_slot_wal_keep_size = '10GB' Changing wal_level, senders or slot capacity needs a restart; HBA and retention changes are reloadable according to pg_settings.context. Keep at least two sender connections free for a streaming base backup. The retention cap limits slot-induced growth at checkpoints but can invalidate a lagging consumer; it is not a guarantee of uninterrupted catch-up.[32][39] On the separate RHEL 9.7 standby host install the same approved PGDG major-18 server/client/contrib and extension RPMs as the primary. Do not initialize its target: RPM installation alone does not create a writable database. Leave postgresql-18.service stopped/disabled and verify /var/lib/pgsql/18/data is empty, owned by postgres, mode 0700, with no process using it. If it contains data, stop and preserve/inventory it; do not delete it to make this recipe fit.[100] Provision the primary CA at /var/lib/pgsql/tls/ca.crt and a passfile /var/lib/pgsql/.pgpass owned by postgres mode 0600 through secret management. Its matching database field is replication, with primary hostname/port and notes_repl. Use the TLS file-label checks; do not store credentials in primary_conninfo. Check primary firewalld allows only this standby source; the receiving standby needs outbound primary access, not a broadly opened inbound database port.[55][102][103] As OS postgres on the standby: /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_basebackup \ --dbname='host=primary.example.test port=5432 user=notes_repl sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=/var/lib/pgsql/tls/ca.crt gssencmode=disable passfile=/var/lib/pgsql/.pgpass application_name=standby1' \ --pgdata=/var/lib/pgsql/18/data --format=plain --wal-method=stream \ --write-recovery-conf --create-slot --slot=standby1 --progress /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_verifybackup /var/lib/pgsql/18/data -R creates standby.signal and connection/slot settings in postgresql.auto.conf; do not remove them. --create-slot fails if the named slot exists; inspect and determine ownership rather than dropping an unknown slot. If backup fails after creating a slot, review/remove the unused slot or it can keep retaining WAL.[32] PGDG primary configuration lives inside PGDATA and is copied by this base backup. Save and replace/review it with standby-local postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf; do not inherit the primary’s listener, TLS server identity, external includes, archive destination or local paths.[100] Review inherited postgresql.auto.conf for unrelated source overrides, retaining the intended primary_conninfo and primary_slot_name; never inherit a source data_directory, port or archive destination unchecked. data_directory = '/var/lib/pgsql/18/data' hba_file = '/var/lib/pgsql/18/data/pg_hba.conf' listen_addresses = 'localhost' port = 5432 unix_socket_directories = '/run/postgresql' hot_standby = on archive_mode = off Set standby max_connections, max_worker_processes, max_wal_senders, max_prepared_transactions and max_locks_per_transaction no lower than required source values; install required libraries. For this admin-only standby, HBA can contain just local all postgres peer; enable any reporting TCP access separately with TLS/least privilege. On this second host 5432 must be free.[74] Before streaming or a logical subscription starts, inspect getsebool -a, the installed postgresql_selinux(8) policy documentation and AVC denials for server-originated outbound connections. If policy requires a PostgreSQL database-network boolean, enable only the verified installed boolean after a security review and record its prior value; do not enable all network booleans or generate broad allow rules. A successful unconfined pg_basebackup client is not proof that the confined WAL receiver/subscription worker can connect.[102] sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/postgresql-18.conf sudo restorecon -Rv /var/lib/pgsql/18/data /run/postgresql sudo systemctl start postgresql-18.service sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql -X -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 -d postgres \ -c 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();' This is the default PGDG service on the second host, not a second controller for the primary. Configure its own PGDATA/log, check ps -eZ/AVCs and journal/collector output, then verify SHOW data_directory, system identifier, pg_is_in_recovery(), primary streaming state and a new fixture commit becoming visible. Rehearse clean stop/start and boot recovery before sudo systemctl enable postgresql-18.service; keep applications away until read-only state and security policy are proved. For nondefault paths use the PGDATA/drop-in/SELinux/mount relocation procedure, not a detached pg_ctl daemon.[100][102] On the primary, using an authorized monitoring role; slot restart_lsn is a retention boundary, not proof that the subscriber has applied every transaction:[25][90] SELECT application_name, client_addr, state, sync_state, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn, write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication; SELECT slot_name, slot_type, active, restart_lsn, wal_status, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots; On a physical standby: SELECT status, sender_host, sender_port, slot_name FROM pg_stat_wal_receiver; SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(), pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(); Lag intervals are not guaranteed forecasts of catch-up time; an idle source can have an old replay timestamp without a backlog. title: Replicate the right unit
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · PostgreSQL · Replication and high availability
text: physical WAL (whole cluster) applications -> primary ----------------------------> standby | | | WAL archive + base backups | read-only queries v v independent recovery storage promotion only after fencing publisher database -- publication/table changes --> subscriber database logical replication; separate schema/sequence policy Mechanism Replicates Does not supply Physical streaming WAL for the entire cluster, same major and compatible platform Selective table filtering, cross-major upgrade or automatic leader election. Logical publication/subscription Selected tables’ data changes plus optional initial copy DDL, sequences, large objects, all extension state or a transparent HA copy. WAL archive Durable retained segments for recovery/standby catch-up Live failure detection/routing. External HA controller Failure decision, fencing, routing and rejoin policy A replacement for PostgreSQL backups or tested consistency settings. Core PostgreSQL provides replication and promotion primitives, not the software that decides a primary has failed and fences it. A heartbeat alone cannot distinguish failure from network partition.[38][41][64]

title: Build an asynchronous physical standby
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · PostgreSQL · Replication and high availability
text: Two separate RHEL/PGDG hosts, both major 18 with compatible extensions, checksums/platform and maintained minor versions. Primary postgresql-18 is already running; standby has no running cluster at its target path. This bounded setup uses no external tablespaces. With tablespaces, stop and plan all target mappings. Require verified TLS, time/DNS, private routing and a restore-tested backup first.[32][38] Example names/addresses are reserved documentation values: primary primary.example.test at 192.0.2.10, standby at 192.0.2.20. Replace them with actual private addresses and certificate identities. On the primary as administrator: CREATE ROLE notes_repl LOGIN REPLICATION NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE; \password notes_repl Set the password through the prompt with SCRAM selected, not in SQL history. Allow only the standby’s address, and only replication connections, before any broad reject rules: hostssl replication notes_repl 192.0.2.20/32 scram-sha-256 Review settings on the primary. The following capacities are examples, not a formula for every topology: wal_level = replica max_wal_senders = 10 max_replication_slots = 10 max_slot_wal_keep_size = '10GB' Changing wal_level, senders or slot capacity needs a restart; HBA and retention changes are reloadable according to pg_settings.context. Keep at least two sender connections free for a streaming base backup. The retention cap limits slot-induced growth at checkpoints but can invalidate a lagging consumer; it is not a guarantee of uninterrupted catch-up.[32][39] On the separate RHEL 9.7 standby host install the same approved PGDG major-18 server/client/contrib and extension RPMs as the primary. Do not initialize its target: RPM installation alone does not create a writable database. Leave postgresql-18.service stopped/disabled and verify /var/lib/pgsql/18/data is empty, owned by postgres, mode 0700, with no process using it. If it contains data, stop and preserve/inventory it; do not delete it to make this recipe fit.[100] Provision the primary CA at /var/lib/pgsql/tls/ca.crt and a passfile /var/lib/pgsql/.pgpass owned by postgres mode 0600 through secret management. Its matching database field is replication, with primary hostname/port and notes_repl. Use the TLS file-label checks; do not store credentials in primary_conninfo. Check primary firewalld allows only this standby source; the receiving standby needs outbound primary access, not a broadly opened inbound database port.[55][102][103] As OS postgres on the standby: /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_basebackup \ --dbname='host=primary.example.test port=5432 user=notes_repl sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=/var/lib/pgsql/tls/ca.crt gssencmode=disable passfile=/var/lib/pgsql/.pgpass application_name=standby1' \ --pgdata=/var/lib/pgsql/18/data --format=plain --wal-method=stream \ --write-recovery-conf --create-slot --slot=standby1 --progress /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_verifybackup /var/lib/pgsql/18/data -R creates standby.signal and connection/slot settings in postgresql.auto.conf; do not remove them. --create-slot fails if the named slot exists; inspect and determine ownership rather than dropping an unknown slot. If backup fails after creating a slot, review/remove the unused slot or it can keep retaining WAL.[32] PGDG primary configuration lives inside PGDATA and is copied by this base backup. Save and replace/review it with standby-local postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf; do not inherit the primary’s listener, TLS server identity, external includes, archive destination or local paths.[100] Review inherited postgresql.auto.conf for unrelated source overrides, retaining the intended primary_conninfo and primary_slot_name; never inherit a source data_directory, port or archive destination unchecked. data_directory = '/var/lib/pgsql/18/data' hba_file = '/var/lib/pgsql/18/data/pg_hba.conf' listen_addresses = 'localhost' port = 5432 unix_socket_directories = '/run/postgresql' hot_standby = on archive_mode = off Set standby max_connections, max_worker_processes, max_wal_senders, max_prepared_transactions and max_locks_per_transaction no lower than required source values; install required libraries. For this admin-only standby, HBA can contain just local all postgres peer; enable any reporting TCP access separately with TLS/least privilege. On this second host 5432 must be free.[74] Before streaming or a logical subscription starts, inspect getsebool -a, the installed postgresql_selinux(8) policy documentation and AVC denials for server-originated outbound connections. If policy requires a PostgreSQL database-network boolean, enable only the verified installed boolean after a security review and record its prior value; do not enable all network booleans or generate broad allow rules. A successful unconfined pg_basebackup client is not proof that the confined WAL receiver/subscription worker can connect.[102] sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/postgresql-18.conf sudo restorecon -Rv /var/lib/pgsql/18/data /run/postgresql sudo systemctl start postgresql-18.service sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql -X -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 -d postgres \ -c 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();' This is the default PGDG service on the second host, not a second controller for the primary. Configure its own PGDATA/log, check ps -eZ/AVCs and journal/collector output, then verify SHOW data_directory, system identifier, pg_is_in_recovery(), primary streaming state and a new fixture commit becoming visible. Rehearse clean stop/start and boot recovery before sudo systemctl enable postgresql-18.service; keep applications away until read-only state and security policy are proved. For nondefault paths use the PGDATA/drop-in/SELinux/mount relocation procedure, not a detached pg_ctl daemon.[100][102]

title: Monitor lag, slots and durability
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · PostgreSQL · Replication and high availability
text: On the primary, using an authorized monitoring role; slot restart_lsn is a retention boundary, not proof that the subscriber has applied every transaction:[25][90] SELECT application_name, client_addr, state, sync_state, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn, write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication; SELECT slot_name, slot_type, active, restart_lsn, wal_status, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained FROM pg_replication_slots; On a physical standby: SELECT status, sender_host, sender_port, slot_name FROM pg_stat_wal_receiver; SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(), pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(); Lag intervals are not guaranteed forecasts of catch-up time; an idle source can have an old replay timestamp without a backlog. Compare LSN positions, generation rate, receiver/apply state and storage throughput. A disconnected slot can fill primary disk; a cap can instead force a new base backup. Never delete pg_wal files or drop a consumer’s active slot to hide an alarm.[25][39] Failure Response TLS/authentication failure Inspect certificate hostname/CA, passfile ownership, HBA and SCRAM role; do not relax to trust. Required WAL removed Retrieve from a valid archive if configured/available, otherwise rebuild from a new base. Receive advances but replay stalls Check replay pause, conflicts with standby queries, resource settings and I/O. Long standby queries conflict with recovery Choose delay versus cancellation consciously; hot_standby_feedback can reduce cleanup conflicts but retain bloat on primary. Abandoned slot Confirm consumer retirement and rebuild consequence, then pg_drop_replication_slot for that exact inactive slot. A production standby can add an authenticated restore_command for archive catch-up; access must be read-only and point to the same cluster/timeline history. Streaming alone cannot fetch WAL the primary has already recycled.[38]

title: Synchronous is a commit policy, not automatic HA
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · PostgreSQL · Replication and high availability
text: Asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged transactions if the primary fails before the standby durably receives them. To wait for this particular standby, set synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (standby1)', where the name matches its application_name; reload and verify sync_state on the primary.[38][39] synchronous_commit Wait condition (with a selected synchronous standby) on Local durable WAL plus synchronous standby durable WAL. remote_apply Also waits for standby replay/visibility; increases latency. remote_write Standby OS has written WAL but may not have durably flushed it. local Local flush only, not a standby acknowledgment. off Does not wait for local durable commit; acknowledged recent work can be lost. With no qualifying synchronous standby, commits can wait indefinitely. Changing the policy to resume writes is an explicit durability tradeoff, not an invisible health fix. Test loss of a standby, network partition and recovery while measuring both latency and data loss. Keep synchronous nodes in meaningful failure domains, and verify clients are not overriding the commit policy.[34][38]

title: Publish a bounded set of tables
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · PostgreSQL · Replication and high availability
text: Logical replication is useful for a selected-table copy or major migration, not an automatic full-cluster standby. For this example use adminlab on the publisher and a new adminlab_sub on a separate subscriber, with no application writes to the destination. A table’s primary key normally supplies replica identity for updates/deletes; REPLICA IDENTITY FULL is a fallback with performance/type limitations, not a default recommendation.[40][41] On the publisher set wal_level = logical, budget replication slots/senders, restart as required and retain the physical replication configuration if also used. Give notes_repl CONNECT on adminlab, USAGE on notes and SELECT on notes.orders for initial copy. Add a separate narrow TLS HBA rule for database adminlab from the subscriber; the special replication rule does not match logical database connections.[14][88] Copy the reviewed schema, not rows, to an empty destination. For the fixture, export only notes and exclude topology definitions so an existing publication/subscription is not recreated accidentally:[29][41] # Publisher, as OS postgres; /secure must be owned/protected appropriately. /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_dump -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 \ -U postgres -d adminlab --schema-only --schema=notes --no-owner --no-acl \ --no-publications --no-subscriptions --file=/secure/notes-schema.sql Transfer the file through an approved secure channel and inspect it. On a separate subscriber cluster, create a no-login notes_owner and fresh adminlab_sub owned by it; if either already exists, stop and review, not overwrite. Revoke public database access. Install any required extensions first, then restore the fixture schema with correct ownership:[18][29] # Subscriber, as OS postgres, after checking its identity/path/port. /usr/pgsql-18/bin/psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \ -h /run/postgresql -p 5432 -d adminlab_sub \ -c 'SET ROLE notes_owner' -f /secure/notes-schema.sql Do not create the fixture’s 2,000 rows there; initial synchronization will copy them. Review owners/grants independently because --no-acl intentionally omits source grants. A filtered schema dump can omit external dependencies; this bounded fixture has none, but a real schema needs an explicit dependency inventory. 3. As the table owner or appropriate administrator on the publisher: CREATE PUBLICATION notes_pub FOR TABLE notes.orders; On the subscriber as a trusted superuser subscription owner for this bounded example, use a protected server-side passfile (matching database adminlab) and verified CA. This avoids embedding a secret in SQL/catalog connection text; non-superuser ownership has additional password/security restrictions that must not be bypassed casually.[42] CREATE SUBSCRIPTION notes_sub CONNECTION 'host=primary.example.test port=5432 dbname=adminlab user=notes_repl sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=/var/lib/pgsql/tls/ca.crt gssencmode=disable passfile=/var/lib/pgsql/.pgpass' PUBLICATION notes_pub WITH (copy_data = true, create_slot = true, enabled = true, run_as_owner = false); Do not run slot-creating subscription setup inside a transaction block. Default run_as_owner = false uses table-owner permissions for apply. Restrict who can alter subscriber table definitions/ownership; replication is a trust boundary, not merely a connection string.[42] Inspect pg_stat_subscription and pg_subscription_rel, wait for all subscribed tables to finish synchronization, and compare a quiet-source count plus keyed checks. Commit an approved fixture change on the source and verify it arrives. Watch the publisher slot and subscriber logs for conflicts/schema errors. Apply DDL deliberately to both sides (often additive subscriber changes first). Before subscriber cutover, stop source writes, prove all final changes applied, copy/update sequences and validate application state. Logical replication does not replicate sequences, schema changes or large objects.[41] To abandon this copy, disable notes_sub, then drop it while the publisher is reachable so its slot is cleaned up. If the publisher is unavailable, follow the documented disassociation/slot-removal procedure and track the orphan explicitly; disabling alone keeps retention. Do not skip conflicting transactions to make replication appear green without reconciling missing data.

title: Promote only after fencing
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · PostgreSQL · Replication and high availability
text: Establish whether the primary is truly failed or merely unreachable from one observer. Stop/reroute clients under the HA incident procedure; identify the best eligible standby and accepted RPO. Fence the former primary using a verified power/storage/network mechanism that prevents it accepting writes. Merely removing a DNS record or failing a health check is not fencing. If exclusive write authority cannot be established, do not promote into split brain.[64] Inspect replay/receive positions, pause state and required logical-slot readiness. For a planned switchover, stop writes and wait for the final committed position to replay. For an unplanned failure, explicitly record the possible data-loss window. On the chosen standby, run SELECT pg_promote(true, 60); as an authorized administrator. Verify pg_is_in_recovery() becomes false, perform a controlled write and readback, check the new timeline, then update the application endpoint/pool and confirm reconnect behavior.[23][64] Preserve old-primary files/logs for reconciliation. Reconfigure backups/archives for the new primary, create/rejoin a standby and test the degraded-period alert. Promotion does not automatically recreate redundancy.

title: Rejoin without creating a second primary
context: Databases · Keep more than one copy · PostgreSQL · Replication and high availability
text: Safest general path: keep the old primary fenced, preserve any divergent data needed for reconciliation, replace its cluster with a fresh base backup from the new primary and start it as a standby using the physical procedure. This discards divergence only after an explicit decision. pg_rewind can be faster for a compatible diverged cluster with common history. It needs target checksums or wal_log_hints enabled before divergence, full_page_writes = on, the required old WAL and a cleanly stopped target. Run --dry-run first with correct source/target and credentials; review exact official prerequisites before the write. A failed rewind can leave the target unusable—rebuild from base backup, not repeated improvisation.[44] Rewind can copy source configuration. On RHEL, stop the exact target systemd unit before rewind and keep its boot/restart path fenced; restore file contexts with restorecon and inspect unit/drop-ins before allowing systemd to start it.[100][102] Before restart, correct local paths/ports/archive identity, create/verify standby recovery settings, and test pg_is_in_recovery(); starting it without standby configuration can diverge again. Restore client routing only after lag and consistency checks. Keep failover/rejoin drills, fencing evidence and measured RPO/RTO alongside the backup restore report.

title: Storage, transactions and tablespaces
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · PostgreSQL
text: A PostgreSQL cluster is one initialized data directory served by one server instance, containing multiple databases. It does not by itself mean an HA group. Roles and tablespaces are cluster-wide; a schema is a namespace inside a database. Unlike MySQL’s common usage, database and schema are not synonyms.[6][21][22] For the RHEL/PGDG target, main config, HBA and data are together under PGDATA unless explicitly relocated. The service takes PGDATA from its systemd environment. Do not invent a separate distribution cluster registry or external config tree.[6][100] /usr/pgsql-18/bin/ versioned server and client executables /usr/pgsql-18/lib/ major-specific extension libraries /usr/pgsql-18/share/extension/ extension control/SQL files /usr/lib/systemd/system/postgresql-18.service vendor unit (do not edit) /etc/systemd/system/postgresql-18.service.d/ local drop-ins /var/lib/pgsql/18/data/ default PGDATA postgresql.conf main settings / reviewed includes pg_hba.conf ordered connection authentication pg_ident.conf OS/certificate-to-role maps postgresql.auto.conf ALTER SYSTEM overrides PG_VERSION major, not full minor base/<database-OID>/ per-database relation files global/ cluster-wide catalogs/control pg_wal/ write-ahead log, not disposable logs pg_xact/ transaction status pg_multixact/ shared row-lock state pg_tblspc/ links to external tablespaces log/ collector output (configured here) /run/postgresql/ explicit socket directory; tmpfiles-managed Use the server’s answers as authority, not a remembered package path: SHOW data_directory; SHOW config_file; SHOW hba_file; SHOW ident_file; SELECT system_identifier FROM pg_control_system(); SELECT oid, datname FROM pg_database ORDER BY datname; SELECT pg_relation_filepath('pg_catalog.pg_class'); Control information and some paths require elevated privileges. Record system identifier, major version, host, port and tablespace map with every physical backup. A relation OID is not necessarily its current filenode; rewrites and reindexing can change files without changing the SQL object’s identity. Never repair a table by renaming files or editing catalogs.[6][23] A dirty page in shared buffers is not yet a durable data-file write. WAL records describing the change must reach durable storage before the corresponding changed data page. With normal synchronous commit, the commit waits for local WAL flush; the checkpointer later establishes a redo starting point so crash recovery need not scan all historical WAL.[7][34] Component/setting Purpose Operational consequence shared_buffers Shared database page cache Startup setting; leave memory for OS cache, sessions and maintenance.[63] wal_buffers In-memory staging for WAL Not retained backup history. fsync = on Request durable writes Turning it off risks unrecoverable corruption after OS/power failure.[34] full_page_writes = on Protect against torn page writes during recovery Keep on; also a rewind prerequisite.[34][44] synchronous_commit = on Wait for commit durability at configured level off can lose acknowledged recent transactions after crash, even without corruption; not an optimization to apply blindly.[34] checkpoint_timeout, max_wal_size Time/volume pressure for checkpoints More frequent checkpoints increase write load; max_wal_size is a soft limit, not a disk-space cap.[34] WAL archive / replication slot Retain changes for recovery or consumers Failures can fill disk independently of checkpoint limits.[33][39] Crash recovery replays WAL automatically on restart. It does not repair deleted files, restore a dropped table or reverse valid but unwanted transactions. Those require backups and PITR. Leave pg_wal under server control; deleting files there to make room can destroy the recovery path. Ordinary tables use heap storage; their primary-key index is a separate structure, not an InnoDB-style clustered row store. An index entry leads to a heap tuple whose visibility must normally be checked. The visibility map allows an index-only scan to avoid some heap visits; having all selected columns in an index alone does not promise zero heap fetches.[6][10][76] Structure Use Cost/limit Heap relation Row versions, pages with free space Updates/deletes leave old versions until safe cleanup. B-tree Equality, range and ordered access Extra writes/WAL/storage; column order and selectivity matter. GIN Inverted access for suitable array, JSONB and text-search operators Write/maintenance cost; requires matching operators/classes. BRIN Summaries of ranges of physical pages Useful for correlated large data; lossy checks may visit many rows. TOAST Out-of-line/compressed large values Include TOAST in size/maintenance investigations. Free-space / visibility map Reusable page space / visibility information Maintained by normal operations and vacuum, not hand-edited. Index methods and operator classes are choices for measured access patterns, not interchangeable speed switches.[28][75] SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size('notes.orders')) AS table_with_toast, pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('notes.orders')) AS indexes, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('notes.orders')) AS total; This inspection assumes the adminlab fixture. Growth is not proof of bloat: compare live row counts, row widths and workload before proposing a rewrite. MVCC lets readers use snapshots while writers create new row versions. It does not eliminate locks. Updates to the same row serialize; DDL can block readers and writers. Keep transactions short, acquire locks in a consistent order and retry the whole transaction after deadlock or serialization failure—not just the last statement.[8][9] Isolation Snapshot behavior Application obligation Read Committed (default) New snapshot for each statement Recheck assumptions across statements; an earlier read is not a reservation. Repeatable Read Stable transaction snapshot Concurrent update conflicts can abort; retry from the beginning. Serializable Detects anomalies inconsistent with serial execution Handle SQLSTATE 40001 and bounded retry with backoff. Read Uncommitted Behaves as Read Committed in PostgreSQL No dirty-read mode.[8] Example: reserve a known row while changing it. Run only against the fixture, and replace the proposed update with the real business invariant before production use. BEGIN; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2s'; SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '10s'; SELECT order_id, status FROM notes.orders WHERE order_id = 1 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE notes.orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE order_id = 1 AND status = 'new'; COMMIT; A zero-row update can mean the row already changed; it is not automatically success. A lock timeout aborts the statement and leaves this transaction needing ROLLBACK. ROLLBACK undoes transactional row changes, but sequence allocations are not gapless and are not rolled back.[60] Do not hold the lock while waiting for a user or remote API. A two-session lock investigation is explicit: session A opens a transaction and locks the row; session B attempts the update with the short timeout; inspect pg_blocking_pids() before rolling back A. Do not reproduce this on an unknown production row. Use wait diagnostics, not random process termination. CREATE TEMP TABLE creates a session-local object; ON COMMIT DROP makes its lifecycle transaction-local. Autovacuum cannot maintain another session’s temporary table, so analyze it after a substantial load if subsequent plans depend on its distribution. Unlogged tables are different: persistent objects whose contents are not crash-safe or physically replicated; they are not a substitute for durable application tables.[10][70] Run this example as the database owner or administrator. The fixture intentionally revokes public database privileges and grants notes_app no TEMPORARY privilege; do not widen runtime permissions just to run this maintenance example.[19] BEGIN; CREATE TEMP TABLE order_batch (order_id bigint PRIMARY KEY) ON COMMIT DROP; INSERT INTO order_batch VALUES (1), (2); ANALYZE order_batch; SELECT o.* FROM

Serializable Detects anomalies inconsistent with serial execution Handle SQLSTATE 40001 and bounded retry with backoff. Read Uncommitted Behaves as Read Committed in PostgreSQL No dirty-read mode.[8] Example: reserve a known row while changing it. Run only against the fixture, and replace the proposed update with the real business invariant before production use. BEGIN; SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2s'; SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '10s'; SELECT order_id, status FROM notes.orders WHERE order_id = 1 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE notes.orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE order_id = 1 AND status = 'new'; COMMIT; A zero-row update can mean the row already changed; it is not automatically success. A lock timeout aborts the statement and leaves this transaction needing ROLLBACK. ROLLBACK undoes transactional row changes, but sequence allocations are not gapless and are not rolled back.[60] Do not hold the lock while waiting for a user or remote API. A two-session lock investigation is explicit: session A opens a transaction and locks the row; session B attempts the update with the short timeout; inspect pg_blocking_pids() before rolling back A. Do not reproduce this on an unknown production row. Use wait diagnostics, not random process termination.

title: Temporary objects and external storage
context: Databases · Store data and handle change · PostgreSQL · Storage, transactions and tablespaces
text: CREATE TEMP TABLE creates a session-local object; ON COMMIT DROP makes its lifecycle transaction-local. Autovacuum cannot maintain another session’s temporary table, so analyze it after a substantial load if subsequent plans depend on its distribution. Unlogged tables are different: persistent objects whose contents are not crash-safe or physically replicated; they are not a substitute for durable application tables.[10][70] Run this example as the database owner or administrator. The fixture intentionally revokes public database privileges and grants notes_app no TEMPORARY privilege; do not widen runtime permissions just to run this maintenance example.[19] BEGIN; CREATE TEMP TABLE order_batch (order_id bigint PRIMARY KEY) ON COMMIT DROP; INSERT INTO order_batch VALUES (1), (2); ANALYZE order_batch; SELECT o.* FROM notes.orders AS o JOIN order_batch USING (order_id); COMMIT; A tablespace assigns objects to an existing empty, persistent directory owned by the PostgreSQL OS account. On RHEL, mount it persistently, add RequiresMountsFor=/srv/postgresql/fastspace to the owning unit, and check parent traversal. Before SQL creation, inspect existing local labels, then use sudo semanage fcontext -a -t postgresql_db_t '/srv/postgresql/fastspace(/.*)?' and sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/postgresql/fastspace; verify ownership/mode 0700 and matchpathcon -V. Do not replace an existing conflicting mapping blindly or disable enforcing mode.[102][104] Creating one requires superuser; using it requires CREATE on that tablespace. It is part of the same cluster, not an independent backup or portable collection of tables.[22] -- Prerequisite: /srv/postgresql/fastspace exists, empty, owned by postgres. CREATE TABLESPACE fastspace LOCATION '/srv/postgresql/fastspace'; GRANT CREATE ON TABLESPACE fastspace TO notes_owner; SELECT spcname, pg_tablespace_location(oid) FROM pg_tablespace; Moving notes.orders with ALTER TABLE notes.orders SET TABLESPACE fastspace takes a strong lock, consumes copy space and does not move its separate indexes automatically.[71] Schedule and verify every object; reverse the move to the original tablespace if needed. Drop a tablespace only once all databases’ objects have been moved out. A missing mount can make the entire cluster unusable. Base-backup/restore plans must include every tablespace, and same-host drills must remap them rather than reuse live paths.[22][32] Next: vacuum, freezing and bloat.

title: Minor and major upgrades
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL
text: A minor update (18.x to a later 18.x) replaces binaries without a major-format conversion. A major update (for example 17 to 18) requires pg_upgrade, logical dump/restore or a planned logical-replication migration. Never start an 18 binary on a 17 data directory. PostgreSQL does not require visiting every intervening major, but you must review their compatibility notes.[1][37] Route Strength Main constraint Minor package update Short restart, unchanged major format Read that minor’s release notes for extra actions; binaries/extensions must remain compatible. pg_upgrade default copy Fast catalog conversion without logical row reload Both major binaries, compatible physical settings/extensions and extra disk space. pg_upgrade --clone Copy-on-write speed with independent old cluster Supported OS/filesystem and same filesystem requirements; verify in rehearsal. pg_upgrade --link Less copying/storage After new cluster starts, shared files make old cluster unsafe to restart. Dump/restore Clean rebuild; portability and selected redesign Longer copy/index-build outage unless separately synchronized. Logical replication Can reduce final write outage DDL, sequences, large objects and cutover consistency need separate handling. PostgreSQL 18 also has swap/copy-file-range modes; this procedure deliberately uses default copy, not a space-saving mode with different rollback properties.[36] The bounded major procedure is PGDG PostgreSQL 17 to 18 on the same RHEL 9.7 x86_64 host, old unit postgresql-17 with /var/lib/pgsql/17/data, new unit postgresql-18-upgrade with /var/lib/pgsql/18/upgrade on 5544. Both package families must resolve against this maintained OS minor, including OpenSSL and all extension dependencies. It is not an AppStream stream-switch recipe or an instruction to downgrade the existing 18 learning cluster.[94][100] SELECT version(); SHOW data_directory; SHOW data_checksums; SHOW server_encoding; SHOW lc_collate; SHOW lc_ctype; SELECT datname, datlocprovider, datcollate, datctype, datcollversion FROM pg_database ORDER BY datname; SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension ORDER BY extname; SELECT spcname, pg_tablespace_location(oid) FROM pg_tablespace; SELECT * FROM pg_prepared_xacts; Collect extension inventory from every database, native library paths, replication topology/slots, publications/subscriptions, external integrations and package versions. Check drivers, SCRAM/TLS support, reserved words, query behavior and extension vendor upgrade instructions. A compatible binary package is not proof its SQL extension version was upgraded.[36][54] PostgreSQL 18 enables checksums by default; pg_upgrade requires matching old/new checksum settings. For a no-checksum source, initialize the target with --no-data-checksums or follow an independently reviewed offline checksum-enablement plan. Match locale/provider/encoding and other checked physical settings; do not “fix” a check failure by editing control files.[4][11] Use a restored production copy for rehearsal. Measure the entire outage through extension updates, stats, reindex work and application validation. Freeze schema changes before the final run, take a verified recoverable backup and retain source binaries/configuration. Confirm capacity for both copied data and later WAL/index work. Default-copy rollback still cannot recover writes accepted only by the new server.[36] Read the exact old-to-new 18.x release notes, check repository candidates and extension package updates, verify backup/recovery access, then drain applications. Inventory every unit using /usr/pgsql-18; drain and stop affected clusters cleanly. Review dnf --refresh list --showduplicates postgresql18 postgresql18-server postgresql18-contrib, then use sudo dnf upgrade postgresql18 postgresql18-server postgresql18-libs postgresql18-contrib with approved matching extension updates. Preview/review the whole transaction; retain gpgcheck=1. The inspected server RPM calls systemctl try-restart postgresql-18 on upgrade; a stopped service is not started by that action. Separately named local units are not updated/restarted for you. Compare copied units to the new vendor unit and inspect .rpmnew files.[99][100] Start postgresql-18.service (and each affected named instance in order), verify SQL SELECT version() and tool versions, inspect logs, connect as the actual application role and run representative reads/writes. Follow any release-specific reindex/extension tasks. Observe replication/archive health and new backup completion before closing the change.[1][100] If startup fails, preserve logs and diagnose config/library mismatches. Binary rollback is a release-specific decision, not a universal safety guarantee; keep a restore path for changes that cannot be reversed by reinstalling an older package. The OS account running pg_upgrade must own both clusters and a writable work directory. Use the new major’s utility. No applications may connect during conversion. Ensure the fresh target’s HBA permits local peer connections for postgres; do not enable network trust to make the tool work.[36] Install approved postgresql17, postgresql17-server and corresponding old extensions if not already retained, plus target postgresql18, postgresql18-server, postgresql18-contrib and all matching target extension libraries. Do not replace the old major or install extension SQL manually into the empty target. Register postgresql-18-upgrade.service using multiple instances, with PGDATA=/var/lib/pgsql/18/upgrade and mount ordering. Leave it disabled/stopped. Initialize that empty directory as postgres with /usr/pgsql-18/bin/initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/upgrade, adding the source’s encoding/locale/provider/checksum choices and --auth-local=peer --auth-host=scram-sha-256; never use learning defaults blindly. Set target port 5544, listen_addresses = '', socket /run/postgresql, and local peer HBA. Create/label its owned log directory. Inspect the port inventory; if TCP will later be enabled on 5544, allocate postgresql_port_t after checking conflicts. No broad firewall opening is needed for this local upgrade.[11][102] Create /var/lib/pgsql/upgrade-work owned by postgres, mode 0700. Use direct new-major pg_upgrade in default copy mode: the inspected PGDG setup wrapper’s upgrade action uses --link and its check action rewrites HBA/has destructive failure cleanup, so it is not a harmless substitute for this workflow.[100] Both clusters must be cleanly stopped for the following rehearsal/final sequence. Prevent unattended package/service starts during conversion. sudo systemctl stop postgresql-17.service sudo systemctl stop postgresql-18-upgrade.service sudo restorecon -Rv /var/lib/pgsql/18/upgrade /var/lib/pgsql/upgrade-work sudo -u postgres -H bash cd /var/lib/pgsql/upgrade-work /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_upgrade \ --old-bindir=/usr/pgsql-17/bin \ --new-bindir=/usr/pgsql-18/bin \ --old-datadir=/var/lib/pgsql/17/data \ --new-datadir=/var/lib/pgsql/18/upgrade \ --old-port=5432 --new-port=5544 \ --socketdir=/var/lib/pgsql/upgrade-work --check PGDG configs are inside these PGDATA paths, so no external --old-options/--new-options config-file override is needed. If discovery showed a nonstandard split layout, explicitly adapt and rehearse it. pg_upgrade starts temporary postmasters itself: do not also start their systemd units. Keep SELinux enforcing; diagnose path/domain/AVC failures instead of turning confinement off.[36][100][102] --check reports incompatibilities, not successful application migration. Resolve every reported library/type/setting/prepared-transaction issue and rerun. Keep the generated logs. Before final execution, confirm backup and cutover authorization; run the same command without --check, still from the owned work directory. Do not add --link, --swap or --no-sync to save time.[36] Exit the OS postgres maintenance shell before host-administrator service commands. Follow pg_upgrade’s generated, version-specific completion instructions. Review and apply

title: Keep rollback honest
context: Databases · Protect it and change it safely · PostgreSQL · Minor and major upgrades
text: Point Copy-mode rollback What must not happen Precheck failed Source remains the authority; restart it after inspection Do not promote/populate the target to bypass checks. Conversion failed before target use Preserve logs, confirm source unchanged, restart source Do not reuse half-upgraded target without cleanup/reinitialization plan. New target tested without accepted writes Stop target, restore routing/config to retained source Never run both writable behind the same endpoint. New target accepted writes Reconcile/export those writes or restore under an agreed loss decision Old source is now stale; starting it is not lossless rollback. Link/swap mode was used instead Follow that mode’s strict destructive boundary; restore backup when required Do not restart shared or moved source files after the unsafe boundary. Keep old cluster data, packages, tablespaces and generated cleanup scripts through the agreed rollback period. Do not run delete_old_cluster.sh merely because the upgrade tool produced it. End the window only after new backups can be restored and the performance/application acceptance checks pass.[36] For dump/restore migration, use the logical restore workflow with target-major clients. For a low-outage table migration, use logical replication and a separate sequence/DDL/cutover plan—not an assumed automatic upgrade of every database object.
